Title: Getting started
Text:
Elemenx is a framework for applications in the browser. It is one file, elemenx.js, written in ES5 with no dependencies: components with reactive state and templates, a router, services, a network layer (requests, streams, sockets, WebRTC, transfers), storage, messaging between tabs, frames and workers, and languages. Its library, ElemenxUI, brings about 130 components, 36 services and 13 directives with themes. The command line makes projects, serves them while they are written, and builds them into a site, one file, a widget, a browser extension or native programs. A few rules run through all of it: - Names. Components, services, guards and the members of their definitions are written in PascalCase: Elemenx.Component('UserCard', {Name: '', Save: function () {...}}). Every name that starts with $ belongs to Elemenx: $Template, $OnCreate, this.$Emit(...). - No Promises. What takes time reports through callbacks (error, result) or events. The code of an Application stays plain ES5 and runs in any browser. - State is plain data. A field of a component is its state: assign it, push into its list, and the template follows. There is nothing to declare. A page with the framework Without a build and without a server step, a page can load the framework and ElemenxUI from the files of the distribution (npm run dist makes them; elemenx.all.min.js holds both):

Title: Applications
Text:
An Application is the root of a page made with Elemenx: its root component and where it renders, the folder of its sources, the libraries it uses, its routes, its languages and the services it owns. A page may hold several Applications, each in its own element, each with its own services and router. Elemenx.Application('Shop', { $Title: 'Shop', $Component: 'Layout', $Mount: '#app', $Root: 'application', $Use: ['ElemenxUI'], $Locales: {URL: 'locales/{language}.json', Languages: ['en', 'ru']}, $Pending: '

Loading the shop...

Text:

Title: Templates
Text:
A template is HTML with the bindings of Elemenx. Its expressions are JavaScript, read against the fields of the component (its methods, and the helpers it set in $OnCreate), and every binding follows the fields it reads: change a field, and exactly the texts, attributes and elements that use it change. | Syntax | What it does | | --- | --- | | {{Expression}} | text, in the content of an element or inside an attribute: title="Hello, {{Name}}" | | [value]="Expression" | a property of an element (value, checked, disabled, hidden...), or a prop of a component | | [property.innerHTML]="Html" | a property of the element by its name (HTML reads it in small letters: the property with that name in any case is found) | | [attribute.aria-label]="Label" | an attribute; null or undefined removes it | | [class]="['card', Kind, Active ? 'active' : '']" | classes from a list (empty items are skipped), added to the classes written in the tag | | [class.selected]="Selected" | one class, while the value is true | | [style]="{'width': Width + 'px', '--accent': Color}" | styles from an object of CSS names; null removes one | | [style.width]="Width + 'px'" | one style; custom properties too: [style.--size] | | (click)="Method" | an event: the method gets (event, element); on a component tag, (data, component) | | (click)="Pick(item, $event)", (click)="Open = !Open" | an expression run on the event: $event is the event (on a component tag, what it told), $node the element (the component) | | \{{ | a {{ of the template itself, not an expression | | [(value)]="Name" | two-way, on an input, textarea or select: the field follows what is typed (input), and the element follows the field | | [(checked)]="Agreed", [(selected)]="Picked" | two-way, on a check box, a radio, an option (on change) | | #name | marks an element for this.$Ref('name') (all of them, the rows of a for: this.$Refs('name')) | | if, for, key... | structure: see below and Directives | | {{$T('key', params)}} | a phrase in the language of the page (Languages) | An expression that names a field that does not exist is quiet (it gives undefined); any other error is written to the console with the expression.

Title: State and reactivity
Text:
The state of a component is its fields. Elemenx watches them: every text, attribute, condition and list of the template remembers which fields it read, and when one of them changes, those parts, and only those, are updated. There is no setState, no list of dependencies and no comparison of trees. Elemenx.Component('Cart', { $Template: '

{{Items.length}} items, {{Total(Items)}} €

', Items: [], $OnCreate: function () { this.Total = function (items) { return items.reduce(function (sum, item) { return sum + item.Price item.Count; }, 0); }; }, Add: function (product) { this.Items.push({ID: product.ID, Price: product.Price, Count: 1}); }, More: function (index) { this.Items[index].Count++; } }); What is watched - Fields of the component: assigning one (this.Name = 'Ada') updates what reads it. Assigning the same value again does nothing. - Plain objects and lists inside them, at any depth: this.User.Address.City = 'Riga', this.Items.push(item), this.Items.splice(0, 1), this.Items[2] = item, delete this.Filters.Color. A list that changes its length, and an object that gains or loses a key, update the for over them. - Not watched: the inside of other objects (a Date, a Map, an instance of a class, a DOM node, a resource of the network). Replace them to update: this.Since = new Date(...). The changes are synchronous: once the assignment is done, the DOM shows it. A method of a list (push, splice, sort...) counts as one change, however many items it moves. Several changes at once this.$Batch(function (state) {...}) makes several changes and updates the template once, at the end. state is the state itself: this.$Batch(function (state) { state.Loading = false; state.Items = response.Items; state.Total = response.Total; }); this.$Update({Loading: false, Items: items}) sets several fields in one batch; a $ name there throws Elemenx component value uses reserved $ namespace. Helpers and computed values A template expression is computed again when the fields it reads change. A computed value that several places use belongs in a method that takes the fields as arguments: Visible: function (items, filter) { return items.filter(function (item) { return !filter || item.Tags.indexOf(filter) !== -1; }); }
  • {{item.Title}}
    • A helper only computes: one that assigns a field the template reads makes the template compute it again, without end (Maximum call stack size exceeded). The helper reads items and filter through the arguments, so the list follows both. A helper that reads this.Items inside works too, as long as the template calls it, but naming what it depends on keeps it clear. Outside the component - Services are not reactive: a component copies what it shows into its own fields, and the service tells it when to (OnChange(callback)), or the component reads the service in a helper whose argument changes. - Callbacks of the network, timers and events of other objects run outside the template: they only assign fields, and the template follows. - The hooks ($OnCreate, $OnReady, $OnProps, $OnDestroy, $OnSleep, $OnWake) run untracked: what they read does not tie the component that created them to it. Title: Lifecycle
Text:
A component is created, rendered, maybe put to sleep and woken, and destroyed; an Application starts and is ready or fails. Hooks in the definition run at each of these moments, with the component (or the Application) as this. A component | Hook | When | For | | --- | --- | --- | | $OnCreate(data) | the state has its first values (the defaults, then the props of the tag in data), before the first rendering | the helpers of the template, values computed from the props, listeners of services | | $OnReady() | the template is rendered and in the component's element; the values of the route are there | measuring the DOM, focusing a field, starting a request, a timer | | $OnProps(changed) | its tag (or the page of a widget) gives it new values of props: changed holds the props that changed, the state already holds them; not called for the first values | recomputing what depends on a prop, reloading data for a new id | | $OnSleep() | the component leaves the page but is kept (see Lazy rendering and cache) | pausing timers, media, sockets | | $OnWake() | it comes back as it was | resuming them | | $OnDestroy() | it goes for good | removing what it added outside itself: listeners of window and of services, timers | Elemenx.Component('Clock', { $Template: '{{Now}}', Now: '', $OnCreate: function () { this.Tick = this.Tick.bind(this); }, $OnReady: function () { this.Tick(); this.Timer = setInterval(this.Tick, 1000); }, $OnSleep: function () { clearInterval(this.Timer); }, $OnWake: function () { this.$OnReady(); }, $OnDestroy: function () { clearInterval(this.Timer); }, Tick: function () { this.Now = new Date().toLocaleTimeString(); } }); What a component owns ends with it without a hook: its requests and sockets ($Network), event and message sockets ($Events, $Messaging), workers ($WebWorker), the listeners of its template, its directives and the components of its template. $OnDestroy runs before its children are destroyed, while its element is still in the page. The listeners of its tag and its $Parent() are there before $OnCreate: an event it emits from $OnCreate or $OnReady reaches its owner. $OnCreate, $OnReady, $OnProps, $OnDestroy, $OnSleep and $OnWake run untracked: what they read does not make the template of the parent that creates the component (a row of a for) depend on it. Components that load later In development, a component named by a template may not be loaded yet: its tag holds its place while its files come. The component around it hears about it: | Hook | When | | --- | --- | | $OnChildPending(child) | a component inside it started loading | | $OnChildReady(child) | it is rendered | | $OnChildError(child) | it could not load (child.Error) | child is {Name, $Element, Error}. Without hooks, the tag may show its own status: pending shows markup while it loads and error when it failed, each a template of the page ('#id') or a text: A component that fails with nobody to hear it writes the error to the console. The root of an Application reports to the Application. An Application | Hook | When | | --- | --- | | $Bootstrap() | first, before anything loads | | $OnPending() | the root started loading (the mount shows $Pending) | | $OnReady() | the root is rendered | | $OnError(error) | the root, or a component it needs to start, failed (the mount shows $Error) | The router of an Application starts with its root: the page of the first route is rendered after $OnReady of the root, and a Waiting component shows meanwhile (see Router). The order For a component with children in its template: the parent's $OnCreate, then its rendering, which creates every child (each with its $OnCreate, rendering and $OnReady), then the parent's $OnReady. Destroying goes the other way: the parent's $OnDestroy, then its children. The content of the tag of a component (what goes into its slots:
) is made with the first instance of that component, before its $OnCreate, so its hooks see it built. A component never shown (
) makes nothing of its content, and a lazy in that content waits too. A component a if hides takes that content with it (its components hear $OnDestroy), and the next time it shows the content is made again from the template; with keep the content sleeps with the component and comes back as it was. Title: Directives
Text:
A directive is an attribute that starts with . A structural directive decides whether, and how many times, its element is built; a behavioral one adds behavior to an element that is there. Elemenx has the structural ones; ElemenxUI and the Applications add behavioral ones. Built in | Directive | What it does | | --- | --- | | if="Condition" | builds the element while the condition holds, destroys it when it does not | | for="item of List" | builds it for each item; item in Object for the keys, i = 0; i < 5; i++ for a counted loop; $index is the place | | key="item.ID" | names each item of a for, so its element and components move with it | | keep | a component hidden by if sleeps instead of going, when the cache keeps instances (see Lazy rendering and cache) | | lazy="Placeholder" | builds the element near the screen, or when the browser is idle | | outlet="Content" | where the router puts the page of a route (see Router) | | pending="#id", error="#id" | what a component that is still loading, or failed, shows (see Lifecycle) | An element has at most one structural directive (if, for, lazy); key and keep are arguments of the one there. For a condition around a list, nest two elements. Behavioral directives may be as many as needed on one element.

A behavioral directive Elemenx.Directive('tooltip', { $OnCreate: function (context) { context.Data.Show = function () { context.Element.setAttribute('title', context.Value || ''); }; context.Element.addEventListener('mouseenter', context.Data.Show); }, $OnUpdate: function (context) { context.Data.Show(); }, $OnDestroy: function (context) { context.Element.removeEventListener('mouseenter', context.Data.Show); } }); | Hook | When | | --- | --- | | $OnCreate(context) | the element is in the template, before the first value | | $OnUpdate(context) | the value of the expression is computed: the first time, and at every change of what it reads | | $OnDestroy(context) | the element goes | | $OnSleep(context), $OnWake(context) | the component around it sleeps and wakes | The context is {Name, Element, Component, Expression, Value, Data}: the element, the component of the template (also this in the hooks), the text of the expression, its value now, and Data, an object of the directive's own for this element. A directive without a value (autofocus) has Value undefined. The name of a directive is written in lower case letters, digits, - and , and starts with a letter; it is matched without case (Tooltip is tooltip). A name registered twice throws Elemenx directive already registered: . A structural directive Elemenx.Directive('unless', { Structural: true, $OnUpdate: function (context) { if (context.Value) context.Unmount(); else context.Mount(); } });

The cart is empty.

A structural directive owns its element: the element becomes a template that the directive builds and takes away. Its context has Mount() (builds it, once), Unmount() (takes it away; with keep and a cache that keeps it, it sleeps), Mounted(), and Marker, the node that marks its place. A collection directive (Structural: true, Collection: true) builds the element for many items: its context has Source(expression) (the value of an expression in the scope of the template), Argument(name) (an argument such as key) and Render(items, {Mode, Variable, Key}), as for does. An argument directive (Kind: 'argument', For: 'collection' or 'structural') is a setting read by them. The policy - An element has at most one structural directive; nest elements for two. - An argument is valid only next to a structural directive of the host it is made For. - Behavioral directives are created in the order of their attributes, updated in that order, and destroyed in the opposite order. - A behavioral directive under a structural one lives with the subtree that one builds: it is created when that is built, and destroyed when it goes. Title: Services
Text:
A service is one object that the components of an Application share: the session of the user, a client of an API, a cart, the settings. It is made the first time something asks for it, lives as long as its Application, and every Application of the page has an instance of its own. Elemenx.Service('Cart', { Items: [], Listeners: null, $OnCreate: function () { this.Items = []; this.Listeners = []; }, $OnDestroy: function () { this.Listeners = []; }, Add: function (product) { this.Items.push({ID: product.ID, Title: product.Title, Price: product.Price}); this.Changed(); }, Count: function () { return this.Items.length; }, OnChange: function (listener) { this.Listeners.push(listener); }, OffChange: function (listener) { this.Listeners = this.Listeners.filter(function (item) { return item !== listener; }); }, Changed: function () { var self = this; this.Listeners.slice().forEach(function (listener) { listener(self); }); } }); Using a service this.$Service('Cart') in a component, a service or a guard returns the instance of its Application. Outside an Application, Elemenx.Service('Cart') returns an instance of the page. Elemenx.Component('CartBadge', { $Template: '{{Count}}', Count: 0, $OnCreate: function () { var self = this; this.Update = function () { self.Count = self.$Service('Cart').Count(); }; this.$Service('Cart').OnChange(this.Update); this.Update(); }, $OnDestroy: function () { this.$Service('Cart').OffChange(this.Update); } }); A service is not reactive: its fields change without the templates knowing. A component keeps what it shows in its own fields, and the service tells it when to read them again (a callback, an event). Report what takes time with callbacks (error, result) or events, never with a Promise. The definition | Key | Meaning | | --- | --- | | a field | its first value (each instance gets its own; give lists and objects their value in $OnCreate, so instances do not share them) | | a method | called on the instance: this is the service | | $OnCreate() | the instance is made | | $OnDestroy() | its Application is destroyed, or the service is declared again | | $Events and $OnEvent, $Messaging and $OnMessage | its channels | The instance also has $Application(), $Service(name) (another service of the same Application), $Network(context), $Storage(context), $Events(), $Messaging(context), $WebWorker(...), $ServiceWorker(...) (its resources end with it), $Generation() and $StartedAt(). Loading and declaring In development, a service of the graph of an Application is loaded before the root renders. One that is asked for later (a name built at run time) is loaded then; the calls made meanwhile are queued and run once it is there. Elemenx.Service(name, definition) declares a service anywhere; an Application declares one of its own with this.$Service(name, definition) in $Bootstrap. Declaring a name again replaces the definition: the instances made from the old one are destroyed ($OnDestroy) and the next request makes a new one. $Destroy() on the instance an Application holds destroys it; the next request makes another. A build leaves out the services an Application does not use: it keeps the ones named in quotes in its code ($Service('Cart')). A name built at run time needs to be named somewhere, or a build with --full. ElemenxUI The library brings services of its own: Theme, Toast, Dialogs, Hotkeys, Clipboard, Format, Formats, Forms, Icons, Emoji, Cities, Countries, Currencies, Gamepad, Platform, Push, Print, Syntax, Diff, RichText and more: see the section Services. Title: Router
Text:
The router of an Application puts the component of the route into an outlet of its layout, follows the links of the page and the steps of the browser history, asks the guards, shows a waiting component while a route loads, and reports every step of a navigation as an event. Elemenx.Application('Shop', { $Component: 'Layout', $Mount: 'body', $Router: { Mode: 'history', Waiting: 'PageLoading', NotFound: 'PageNotFound', Routes: [ {Path: '/', Component: 'HomePage'}, {Path: '/product/:id', Component: 'ProductPage'}, {Path: '/account', Component: 'AccountLayout', Guard: 'SignedIn', GuardFailed: 'SignIn', Routes: [ {Path: 'orders', Component: 'OrdersPage'}, {Path: 'orders/:order', Component: 'OrderPage', Outlet: 'Detail'} ]} ] } });
Home A lamp Orders
The settings | Setting | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Routes | the routes, in order: the first that matches wins | | Mode | where the route lives: 'history', 'hash' or 'memory' (below) | | Outlet | the name of the outlet of the root for the routes of the first level, 'Content' | | Waiting | the component shown while a route loads or a guard waits | | WaitingOutlet | where the waiting component shows, the outlet of the route by default | | NotFound | the component of a path no route matches | Elemenx.Router({Root: component, Routes: [...]}) makes a router for any component outside the declaration of an Application; Start() starts it. A route | Key | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Path | /product/:id: a part that starts with : is a parameter. A trailing slash and a missing leading one do not matter. A child's path continues its parent's | | Component | the component of the route: a name, or a factory | | Routes | the children: their component goes into an outlet of this component's template | | Outlet | the outlet of the parent it goes into, 'Content' by default (several outlets show several children) | | Guard, Guards | a guard or a list of them, by name or as functions (see Guards) | | GuardFailed | what shows when a guard says no: a component, or {GuardName: component, Default: component} | | Waiting | the waiting component of this route, instead of the router's | A routed component A component the router renders gets the values of its route, which its template reads too: | Value | For /product/7?tab=photos#reviews | | --- | --- | | $Path | '/product/7' | | $Params | {id: '7'} | | $Query | {tab: 'photos'} (a key without = is '') | | $Hash | 'reviews' | They are there from $OnReady on. A navigation to the same route with other parameters, query or hash keeps the component and changes these values: a template that reads them follows, and code that loads data by them reads them in a helper or watches them through the router's events. A navigation keeps the components the old and the new route share (a common layout of nested routes). A component that holds an outlet (outlet="Content") is a layout: the outlets of its template receive the children of its route. Navigating - Links: a click on an of the same origin goes through the router (not a link with target or download, a click with Ctrl, Shift, Alt, Command or another button, a click whose default a listener prevented, or a path no route matches when there is no NotFound: those the browser follows itself). - Code: this.$Router() in a component returns the router: Go(url) (a new entry of the history), Replace(url) (the same entry), Back(), Forward(), Current() (the routes of now, from the outer one in), On(event, callback). Go and Replace never throw: a navigation that fails is an event. - The history: Back and Forward of the browser go through the router and its guards. Modes - 'history': the route is the path of the URL, through the History API. The default for a page served over http. The server answers every path of the Application with its index.html (the elemenx dev and serve commands do). - 'hash': the route is after the # (index.html#/orders/5?tab=2#comments); a link to #/path goes to a route, and a link to #name sets the hash of the current route. - 'memory': the route lives in the entries of the browser history, and the URL of the page does not change. The default for a page that is not served over http (a file, a browser extension, an Electron window); its first route is /. A relative link or Go('details') is read against the current route outside the history mode. Events this.$Router().On(name, callback) hears a navigation (the listener of a component goes with it; on the router itself, router.Owner(owner).On(name, callback) ties a listener to an owner and router.OffOwner(owner) removes them), as callback(context): context.$From and context.$To are {Path, Params, Query, Hash}, context.$Route the route, context.$Guard the guard. | Event | When | | --- | --- | | NavigationStart | a navigation begins | | GuardStart, GuardWait, GuardEnd, GuardFailed | a guard is asked, waits, answers, says no | | NavigationWaiting | the waiting component shows | | NavigationCommit | the URL is the new one | | NavigationEnd | the components of the route, and the ones inside them that load later, are rendered | | NavigationCancel | a newer navigation replaced it, or a guard said no | | NavigationError | a component of the route could not be loaded or rendered (context.$Error); the URL goes back | Titles A component with $Title sets the title of the document when it renders: a page of the router names the tab. this.$Title(text) changes it later (a page that loaded its data). Title: Guards
Text:
A guard decides whether a navigation may enter a route: a signed-in user, a role, an unsaved form, data that must load first. It is a function, named and declared once, and routes name it. Elemenx.Guard('SignedIn', function () { if (this.$Service('Session').SignedIn()) return true; return this.$Fail('Sign in first', {Return: this.$To.Path}); }); $Router: { Routes: [ {Path: '/account', Component: 'Account', Guard: 'SignedIn', GuardFailed: 'SignIn'}, {Path: '/admin', Component: 'Admin', Guards: ['SignedIn', 'Admin'], GuardFailed: {SignedIn: 'SignIn', Admin: 'Forbidden', Default: 'Forbidden'}} ] } What a guard returns | Result | Meaning | | --- | --- | | true, or nothing | enter | | false | stay: the navigation is cancelled | | this.$Fail(reason, data) | refuse with a reason: the GuardFailed component shows at the protected URL | | a path, '/sign-in' | go there instead (a redirect) | | this.$Wait(function (done) {...}) | the answer comes later: done(result) with any of the results above | A guard of a route with Guards runs in order; the first one that does not say true decides. $Wait given a Promise refuses the navigation with the reason 'InvalidWait'. What a guard sees The guard runs with a context as this: | Member | Meaning | | --- | --- | | $To, $From | the target and the current place: {Path, Params, Query, Hash} | | $Route | the route that is guarded | | $Service(name) | a service of the Application of the router | | $Fail(reason, data), $Wait(operation) | the answers above | Waiting Elemenx.Guard('ProjectAccess', function () { var self = this; return this.$Wait(function (done) { self.$Service('API').CanOpen(self.$To.Params.id, function (error, allowed) { done(!error && allowed ? true : self.$Fail('No access to this project')); }); }); }); While a guard waits, the router shows the Waiting component of the route (or of the router) and emits GuardWait. A newer navigation makes the answer of an older one count for nothing. When a guard says no With GuardFailed, the URL stays the protected one and its component shows in the place of the route's: 'SignIn', or by guard {SignedIn: 'SignIn', Admin: 'Forbidden', Default: 'Forbidden'}. That component reads this.$GuardFailure: {Reason, Data, $Guard, $To, $Route}, so a sign-in page knows where to return. Without it, the navigation is cancelled and the current page stays. Leaving a page A component of the current route may refuse to be left (unsaved changes): its $OnRouteLeave(context) returns the same results as a guard, with context.$From, context.$To, context.$Route, context.$Wait and context.$Fail; this is the component. Elemenx.Component('Editor', { $OnRouteLeave: function (context) { var self = this; if (!this.Dirty) return true; return context.$Wait(function (done) { self.$Service('Dialogs').Confirm({Title: 'Leave without saving?', Variant: 'danger'}, function (action) { done(action === 'ok'); }); }); } }); A redirect does not ask the leave hooks a second time: the pages already agreed to leave. Events of guards The router emits GuardStart, GuardWait, GuardEnd and GuardFailed with the context of the navigation (context.$Guard names the guard, '$OnRouteLeave' for a leave hook). See Router. Example The pages of this reference have no guard, so the example asks one directly: the function a guard is, with the context a router would give it.

Title: Languages
Text:
Elemenx.Locale keeps the phrases of the Applications and of their libraries in the language of the page. Templates show them with $T(key, params), and when the language changes, every phrase on the page follows, with the lang and dir of the document. The dictionaries are JSON files, one for each language; nested objects make keys with dots: { "cart": { "title": "Cart", "total": "Total: {sum}", "items": {"one": "{count} item", "other": "{count} items"} } } Elemenx.Application('Shop', { $Locales: {URL: 'locales/{language}.json', Languages: ['en', 'ru', 'de']} });

{{$T('cart.title')}}

{{$T('cart.items', {count: Items.length})}} · {{$T('cart.total', {sum: Total})}}

The root of an Application renders once the dictionaries of the language are in, so the first screen shows its phrases, not their keys. The language | Method | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Language() | the language of the page ('en', 'pt-br'...) | | Language(code, callback) | loads the dictionaries of that language, then switches to it and calls back (error); the lang and dir of the page follow | | Fallback(code) | the language of the phrases a dictionary lacks, 'en' by default; Fallback() returns it | | Direction(code) | 'ltr' or 'rtl' (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu...) | | OnChange(callback), OffChange(callback) | the language changed | The first language is the lang of the page, or the language of the browser. Phrases | Method | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Text(key, params) | the phrase of the key: in the language, else its base language (pt for pt-BR), else the fallback language, else the key itself; {name} is replaced by params.name | | Has(key) | whether a phrase of that key exists | | Add(language, entries) | adds phrases in code: Add('de', {cart: {title: 'Warenkorb'}}) | | Source(url, languages) | names dictionary files: '/locales/{language}.json', only for the languages listed when a list is given | | Key(event) | the key of a keyboard event, with ArrowLeft and ArrowRight swapped on a right-to-left element: code written for left to right keeps its meaning | A phrase that is an object of plural forms (zero, one, two, few, many, other) is chosen by params.count through Intl.PluralRules of the language: Russian has one (1, 21), few (2–4, 22–24) and many (5–20), English one and other. $T in a template follows the language: a template that shows a phrase is updated when the language changes, with nothing else to do. A component that needs a phrase in code calls Elemenx.Locale.Text(key, params), and listens to OnChange if it keeps the result. Libraries A library declares its dictionaries in its own $Locales (relative to its root). ElemenxUI speaks English and Russian: every label, placeholder and message of its components is a key under ui. (ui.common.clear), and an Application may add another language (Add('de', {ui: {...}})) or change a phrase. The dates, numbers, countries and currencies of the components follow the language too, and a right-to-left language mirrors them (see ElemenxUI). This reference The pages of this reference are Markdown files of each language: pages/guide/start.en.md, pages/guide/start.ru.md; a page missing in a language shows its English one with a note. The buttons of its header call Elemenx.Locale.Language, and the language is kept in localStorage for the next visit. Example The phrases of the example are added in code, in English and in Russian; the plural form follows the count in the language of this page:

{{$T('docs.example.items', {count: Count})}}

{{$T('docs.example.language', {language: $T('docs.example.name')})}} · {{Direction}}

Title: Forms
Text:
ElemenxUI collects and validates forms in two ways on one model, as Angular does: declared in the template with Form and Field, or made in code with the Forms service and handed to the template. Both give the same nodes: a value, its errors, its state (touched, dirty, pending, disabled) and the events of its changes. In the template A Form makes its model of its Fields. A field with a Name and validators adds a control to it; its value comes from the control inside it, a native field or a component of ElemenxUI (Input, Select, Checkbox, DateInput...). The errors of a field show once it is touched (it lost the focus, or the form was submitted); a submit touches every field, waits for the validators that take time, and emits submit with {Value, Model} only when the form is valid, invalid with {Errors, Model} otherwise, and the first field in error takes the focus.

{{Note}}

The validators of a Field: Required, Email, Min, Max, MinLength, MaxLength, Pattern (a regular expression as a text) and Match (the Name of another field that must hold the same value). Messages replaces the text of an error by its key ({required: 'Tell us your name'}). A form with Disabled disables every field; Submit() and Reset() do in code what its buttons do. Names of parts A Name is read as the forms of a server read it: user[name] and user[address][city] (or user.address.city) put their controls in a group user and a group address in it, items[2][title] in an array items, and every tags[] adds one more item to the array tags. The value of the form is nested the same way: {user: {name, address: {city}}, items: [{title}], tags: ['red', 'blue']}; an array holds only the items that have a field (items[2] alone is the first item of the value). A field of a row of for names its item by its key ([name]="'items[' + item.ID + '][title]'"): when the row goes, its control goes, and with the last one the group and the array made for them. Get takes the same names (Model.Get('items[2][title]')), and the errors of invalid are by the path of their control (user.address.city). In code The Forms service makes the model: Control(value, validators), Group({name: node}, validators) and Array([node], validators). A form takes it by [model], and a field takes a control of it by its Name (a path: 'address.city') or by [control]. var forms = this.$Service('Forms'); var Validators = forms.Validators; this.Profile = forms.Group({ Name: forms.Control('', [Validators.Required, Validators.MaxLength(40)]), Age: forms.Control(18, [Validators.Min(18)]), Address: forms.Group({ City: forms.Control(''), Zip: forms.Control('', [Validators.Pattern('^[0-9]{5}$')]) }), Phones: forms.Array([forms.Control('')]) }); this.Profile.Value; / {Name: '', Age: 18, Address: {City: '', Zip: ''}, Phones: ['']} / this.Profile.Get('Address.City').Value = 'Riga'; this.Profile.Get('Phones').Push(forms.Control('+371')); this.Profile.Valid; / false: Name is required / Every node has: | Member | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Value | its value; setting it sets the value (a group takes an object, an array a list) | | Errors | null, or {key: params} of its own validators | | Valid, Invalid, Pending, Status | Status is valid, invalid, pending or disabled | | Touched, Dirty, Disabled | it was left, it was changed, it is off (a disabled node is left out of the value and the validity of its group) | | Get(path) | a node inside: 'address.city', 'items.0', or a list of names | | SetValue(value), Patch(value), Reset(value) | sets all, sets the names given, goes back to the first value (or to this one), untouched and clean | | Touch(), Disable(), Enable() | with everything inside | | Error(key), Message() | the params of one error, the phrase of the first error | | Validate(callback) | calls back (null, {Valid, Errors}) once no validator is pending; Errors by the path of each invalid node | | OnChange(listener), OffChange(listener) | listener(node) after a change of a value or a state inside | | ID | a number of its own, for the key of a list | An array also has Push(node), Insert(index, node), RemoveAt(index) and Clear(); a group Add(name, node) and Remove(name). Validators forms.Validators holds Required, RequiredTrue (a check box that must be checked), Email, Min(number), Max(number), MinLength(length), MaxLength(length), Pattern(expression), Equal(name, other) (for a group: two of its controls must match) and Custom(key, test(value, control)). A validator is any function (control) -> null or {key: params}. An async validator is function (control, callback), calling back the errors or null later; while it runs the control is pending, and only the answer for its present value counts: var name = forms.Control('', { Validators: [Validators.Required], Async: [function (control, callback) { api.IsFree(control.Value, function (error, free) { callback(free ? null : {taken: true}); }); }] }); forms.Message(errors) is the phrase of the first error in the language of the page (ui.forms.), or the text an error gives itself ({taken: 'This name is taken'}). Example A model made in code, its value and status shown as they change, and a list of phones that grows:

Title: Styles and shadow DOM
Text: A component carries its CSS with it: $Style holds it as a text, $StyleURL names a file next to its script. The stylesheet is placed once, when the first instance of the component renders, and stays for the next ones; a production build inlines the file. The rules are plain CSS of the page: name the classes of a component after it (.product-card, .product-card-title) so they do not meet others. Elemenx.Component('ProductCard', { $TemplateURL: 'ProductCard.html', $StyleURL: 'ProductCard.css' }); Elemenx.Component('Badge', { $Template: '{{Text}}', $Style: '.badge { padding: 0 6px; border-radius: 999px; background: var(--elemenx-accent); color: var(--elemenx-accent-text); }', Text: '' }); The colors, corners, sizes and timings of ElemenxUI are tokens of the theme (--elemenx-accent, --elemenx-radius...): a component that uses them follows every theme and both schemes (see Themes). Styles from code Elemenx.Style(name, text) keeps a stylesheet of a name in the document: a new text replaces the old one, an empty one removes it. The stylesheets of components and libraries go the same way, so every Application in a shadow root gets them too. Elemenx.Style('print', '@media print { .no-print { display: none; } }'); Bindings of style In a template, [class], [class.name], [style] and [style.property] change classes and styles with the state (see Templates); [style.--size]="Size + 'px'" sets a custom property that the CSS of the component reads. An Application in a shadow root $Shadow (true, 'open' or 'closed') renders the root of an Application in a shadow root of its mount: Elemenx.Application('Widget', {$Component: 'WidgetRoot', $Mount: '#widget', $Shadow: true, $Use: ['ElemenxUI']}); - The styles of the page do not reach the Application, and its styles do not reach the page. - Elemenx.Style places every stylesheet of the framework, of its components and of its libraries in that shadow root too. In a shadow root, html, body and :root of a selector mean its host: body[data-theme='dark'] .card becomes :host([data-theme='dark']) .card, so the themes of ElemenxUI work there. - The links of the Application go through its router; its host takes the lang and dir of Elemenx.Locale. - A widget build renders in a shadow root by default ($Shadow: false turns it off). The page and its parts ElemenxUI styles html and body (the font, the background of the theme, the scrollbars) and gives layout classes: elemenx-screen (a full window), elemenx-container (a row; fill, centered, wrappable, grid...), elemenx-column (a column), typography (elemenx-title, elemenx-text, elemenx-caption...), blocks (elemenx-panel, elemenx-card, elemenx-callout...) and tables. Every class is listed in the THEMING-CLASSES list of the repository; they are public: a theme written against them keeps working. Title: Lazy rendering and cache
Text:
Two tools keep a large Application fast: lazy builds the parts of a long page only when they come near the screen, and Elemenx.Cache keeps components that leave the page asleep instead of destroying them (keep-alive), and unloads the definitions nobody uses. lazy
The host of lazy (an element or a component) renders when it comes within a screen of the viewport, or when the browser is idle, whichever is first, one host at a time in the order of the page; once rendered, it stays. A long page shows its first screen at once and builds the rest in the background, instead of freezing the tab until all of it is built. Meanwhile a placeholder holds its place ([data-elemenx-lazy]): - no value: a line high; - a number or a length: that height (lazy="320" pixels, lazy="'20rem'"); ElemenxUI draws it as a shimmer (data-elemenx-lazy="sized"); - '#id': the markup of a template of the page or of the registry (data-elemenx-lazy="template"), as a skeleton of the content. What the host declares exists only once it renders: its hotkeys, listeners and services start then. A list of them follows their changes (Hotkeys.OnChange of ElemenxUI) rather than reading them once. A host whose component goes before its turn never renders. The cache Everything is off by default: a component that leaves is destroyed, a definition stays loaded. Elemenx.Cache(policy) sets the policy; Elemenx.Cache() returns it. A key that is not given keeps its value; ages are milliseconds, 0 means no limit. Elemenx.Cache({ Definitions: {MaxAge: 600000, Max: 200}, Instances: {Scope: 'router', MaxAge: 300000, Max: 20} }); Instances: keep-alive An instance that leaves its place sleeps out of the page and wakes as it was, its DOM, its state and its scroll, when its place shows it again. Scope says which: | Scope | What sleeps | | --- | --- | | 'none' | nothing (the default) | | 'marked' | a host of if with keep, and a component with $KeepAlive: true | | 'router' | the above, and every page of a router: by its level, its component and the parameters of its route (not its query) | | 'all' | the above, and every host of if | keep="false" and $KeepAlive: false keep an instance out of every scope. The items of a for never sleep (keep there throws). An instance asleep for MaxAge, beyond the Max asleep (the longest asleep first), or whose place goes away, is destroyed. Going to sleep, a component or a directive with $OnSleep hears it, and so do the ones inside it; $OnWake follows when it comes back. Timers, global listeners, media, sockets and data that ages pause and resume there. Before it sleeps, the fields of passwords and of payment cards (autocomplete="cc-") inside it are emptied: a page asleep keeps no secret. Definitions A definition no instance uses for MaxAge, or beyond the Max definitions loaded (the longest idle first), unloads the text of its template and style, its stylesheet and its compiled expressions. A definition from files loads them again for its next instance; a definition of code keeps its object and places its style again. Statistics Elemenx.Cache.Stats() returns {Definitions: [{Name, Instances, Cached, Idle}], Instances: [{Name, Asleep}]}; Elemenx.Cache.Clear() destroys every instance asleep and unloads every unused definition, whatever the policy. A wrong policy throws: Elemenx.Cache expects a policy object, Elemenx.Cache does not know , Elemenx.Cache expects Instances.Scope to be none, marked, router or all, Elemenx.Cache expects to be a number of 0 or more. Example Forty sections built lazily, and the counters of the cache of this reference (its policy is {Instances: {Scope: 'marked'}}):

Title: Resources and bundles
Text: In development, Elemenx loads the files of an Application one by one, when they are first needed. A production build carries them inside its scripts instead. Three registries make that work, and they are open to an Application too: embedded files (Elemenx.Resource), bundled entities (Elemenx.Bundle) and precompiled expressions (Elemenx.Expressions). Embedded files Elemenx.Resource keeps the text of a file under its URL, so code that would fetch it finds it already there: the sprites of the icons, the data of a library, a dictionary. | Call | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Elemenx.Resource(url, text) | embeds a text under a URL (resolved against the page) | | Elemenx.Resource(url) | the embedded text, or null | | Elemenx.Resource.Load(url, callback) | calls back (error, text): the embedded text at once, or the text fetched from the URL | A component or a service that reads a file through Resource.Load works the same in development, from a server, and in a build in one file that runs from file://, where nothing can be fetched. Elemenx.Resource.Load('/data/countries.json', function (error, text) { if (error) return; self.Countries = JSON.parse(text); }); The bundle Elemenx.Bundle({Type: {Name: loader}}) registers entities a build carries: a loader is a function that declares the entity (Elemenx.Component(...), Elemenx.Service(...), a guard, a directive) the first time it is needed. A production app.js begins with one call of it for the whole graph, its templates and styles inlined: Elemenx.Bundle({ Component: { HomePage: function () { Elemenx.Component('HomePage', {$Template: '<main>...</main>', $Style: '.home { ... }'}); } }, Service: { Cart: function () { Elemenx.Service('Cart', {...}); } } }); The bundle is asked first, Discovery (the files of the graph) after: an Application can mix bundled entities and ones it still loads from files. Two bundled graphs may not declare the same name of the same type; the builder stops and says so. Precompiled expressions A page whose Content Security Policy forbids eval (a browser extension, script-src 'self') cannot compile the expressions of its templates. elemenx build --precompile writes them as code into the build: one Elemenx.Expressions({source: function ($globals, $scope) {...}}) call with a function for each expression the builder found in the templates. The compiler takes them and compiles nothing; an expression missing there throws Elemenx expression is not precompiled and the page forbids eval: <source> (a template made at run time cannot be read by the builder). See Builds. The framework itself | Member | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Elemenx.Version | the version of this copy | | Elemenx.NoConflict() | gives the name Elemenx back to what had it before this copy, and returns the copy | | Elemenx.RuntimeID() | the identifier of this runtime (a tab, a frame, a worker): runtime-… | | Elemenx.StartedAt() | when this copy started | | Elemenx.Title(text) | sets the title of the document; Elemenx.Title() returns it | Each copy of elemenx.js has a namespace of its own. A second copy of the same version leaves the first in place and does nothing; a copy of another version starts, but the window keeps the first Elemenx (the page it serves goes on working) and the console warns. An isolated build (elemenx build --widget) keeps its copy to itself: the page may have an Elemenx of any version. Example A text embedded by the example, read by Resource.Load with no request, and a file of this reference read from the server: <Button Label="Read both" Variant="primary" (click)="Read" /> <Properties> <Property Label="Embedded" [value]="Embedded" /> <Property Label="Fetched (/pages/index.json)" [value]="Fetched" /> <Property Label="The framework" [value]="Version" /> <Property Label="This runtime" [value]="Runtime" /> </Properties> <script> ({ Embedded: '—', Fetched: '—', Version: Elemenx.Version, Runtime: Elemenx.RuntimeID(), $OnCreate: function () { Elemenx.Resource('/docs-example/greeting.txt', 'Hello from an embedded file'); }, Read: function () { var self = this; Elemenx.Resource.Load('/docs-example/greeting.txt', function (error, text) { self.Embedded = error ? error.message : text; }); Elemenx.Resource.Load('/pages/index.json', function (error, text) { self.Fetched = error ? error.message : JSON.parse(text).Sections.length + ' sections, ' + text.length + ' characters'; }); } }) </script>

Title: Libraries and ElemenxUI
Text: A library is a graph of components, services, guards and directives that Applications share: the same index.js files, the same loading in development, the same bundling in a build. ElemenxUI is the library that comes with Elemenx. Using a library Elemenx.Library('Mosaic', { $Root: 'libraries/Mosaic', $Locales: {URL: 'locales/{language}.json', Languages: ['en', 'de']} }); Elemenx.Application('Shop', { $Use: ['ElemenxUI', 'Mosaic'], $Component: 'Layout', $Root: 'application' }); Elemenx.Library(name, {$Root, $Locales}) declares a library before the Applications that use it; $Use names it (a name or a list), and $Libraries() of the Application lists them. ElemenxUI needs no declaration: $Use: ['ElemenxUI'] takes its files from libraries/ElemenxUI next to the elemenx.js that runs, so a framework from a CDN takes its library from there. In development, a component the Application does not have is looked for in its libraries; their services and directives load before the root starts, and the CSS files their index.js lists are attached once. An unknown name in $Use is skipped with a warning. In a build, the library components the Application renders (by their tags in its templates, then in theirs) are bundled, and the others are left out (see Builds). A library of your own A library is a folder with an index.js, laid out as the graph of an Application: libraries/Mosaic/ ├── index.js ['index.css', 'components', 'services', 'directives'] ├── index.css ├── components/ │ ├── index.js ['Tile/Tile.js', 'TileList/TileList.js'] │ └── Tile/... ├── services/... └── locales/en.json, de.json packs.json in its root names the large files few pages need, so a build in one file carries them only when an Application uses them: {"brands": {"Files": ["icons/brands.svg"], "Uses": ["brands:"]}} (Uses are the texts that show a use; Language makes a pack of one language). Without a declaration, $Discovery of the Application finds libraries by their paths (from the file of the definition, as $Root): $Discovery: ['vendor/charts', 'vendor/kit/kit.js', {Path: 'shared/ui', Name: 'SharedUI'}]. A path is a folder with its index.js, or a graph file of any name; a library is named by Name, by its graph file other than index.js, or by its folder. They load as the libraries of $Use, and the dictionaries their graph lists (locales/{language}.json next to it) come in the languages it lists. A build reads $Discovery from the entry and bundles them, with their packs.json. ElemenxUI About 130 components, 36 services and 13 directives, with English and Russian phrases, light and dark schemes, themes, right-to-left layout and keyboard and screen reader support. Every one has a page in the sections Components, Services and Directives; by subject: | Subject | Components | | --- | --- | | Actions | Button, ButtonGroup, Menu, MenuList, MenuItem, ContextMenu, CommandPalette | | Text fields | Input, TextArea, NumberInput, MoneyInput, PhoneInput, OTPInput, TagInput, Combobox, ColorInput, Field, Form | | Dates and places | DateInput, DateRangeInput, TimeInput, Calendar, CityInput, CurrencySelect | | Payment | CardNumberInput, CardExpiryInput, CVVInput, PlanCard, PlanPicker | | Choice | Checkbox, Radio, RadioGroup, Toggle, Select, MultiSelect, Slider, Knob, Rating, Tabs | | Navigation | Breadcrumbs, NavList, Pagination, Steps, Tree, SettingsMenu | | Data | Table, VirtualList, Properties, Property, Chronicle, Chart, Sparkline, Meter, Progress | | Layout | Section, Block, Card, Centered, Splitter, MasterDetail, Dashboard, DashboardWidget, Settings, TileGrid, Tile, TileGroup | | Application frames | Workspace, WorkspaceToolbar, WorkspaceToolWindow, Ribbon, RibbonTab, RibbonGroup, RibbonButton, RibbonGallery, RibbonBackstage, RibbonPage, Window | | Overlays | Dialog, DialogHost, Drawer, Popover, ToastHost, Tour, AchievementHost | | Feedback | Spinner, Skeleton, EmptyState, Presence | | Editors and viewers | RichEditor, CodeEditor, Terminal, Markdown, CodeView, Formula, FindBar | | People and media | Avatar, Image, Gallery, FileUpload, FileIcon, Icon | | Cards | PostCard, ProductCard, ProfileCard, CommentCard | | Messaging | Chat, ChatMessage, ChatComposer, EmojiPicker, StickerPicker, ExpressionPicker | | Input devices and sound | Keyboard, DialPad, Piano, Mixer, MixerChannel, GameKey | | Games | GameHud, GameBar, GameSlot, GameInventory, GameItemCard, GameDialogue, GameMenu, GameTabs, GameQuests, GameMinimap, GameLeaderboard | | Theme | ThemeSwitch | The services: the page (Theme, Toast, Dialogs, Hotkeys, Windows, Print, PictureInPicture, Idle), data (Forms, FieldFormats, Format, Countries, Currencies, Cities, Emoji, Stickers), text (RichText, Syntax, Diff, Find, Formulas), the device (Clipboard, Permissions, Biometric, Push, Platform, Gamepad, Serial, USB, NFC) and the rest (Icons, Badges, Menus, Reveal, Achievements, GameItems). Phrases and directions Every phrase ElemenxUI shows is a key of Elemenx.Locale under ui., with dictionaries in English and Russian; a text prop of a component (Placeholder, Empty...) is empty by default, so the phrase of the language shows, and a value of the owner takes its place. Dates, numbers, countries and currencies follow the language too. A right-to-left language mirrors the components: logical CSS properties, arrows that keep their meaning, sliders from right to left, popups at the start of their anchor, the icons of a direction turned. Icons draws an icon of the sprite of the library; a name with a set before it draws another set: files:pdf, brands:github, weather:rain, music:, sport:, racing:, science:, art:, cinema:, games:. A set loads when one of its icons first shows. The Icons service adds the sets of an Application and replaces icons (Override); elemenx icons makes a set from a folder of SVG files (see The CLI). Styles index.css of the library holds the base of the page (fonts, the colors of the theme, scrollbars), the layout classes (elemenx-screen, elemenx-container, elemenx-column and their modifiers), typography, lists, blocks, tables and the shared parts of the controls; every other component carries its own stylesheet. Sizes follow a grid of 8-4-2-1: controls are 24, 32, 40 and 56 pixels high (small, medium, large, giant), the text 14 on 20. See Themes. Example

Title: Themes
Text:
The look of ElemenxUI is its tokens: CSS variables --elemenx- for the colors, the type, the corners, the sizes and the motion, and the variables of each component. A theme sets them, and where tokens are not enough it restyles a component by its classes. A theme is one plain CSS file: no build step, no cascade layers, any browser that runs ElemenxUI. The scheme and the theme body carries two attributes, set by the Theme service: - data-theme: the policy of the scheme under the default theme (system, light, dark; index.css applies it before any script runs), or the name of a named theme (contrast, ocean...); - data-scheme: the scheme shown, light or dark, whatever the theme. var theme = this.$Service('Theme'); theme.Policy('dark'); / or 'light', or 'system' to follow the operating system / theme.Use('soft'); / a named theme; Use('default') goes back / theme.Resolved(); / 'dark': the scheme shown / The policy and the theme are kept in localStorage and come back on the next visit. To avoid a flash of the default theme on load, the page may name its theme in its markup: . | Method | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Policy(value), Policy() | sets or returns the policy: system, light, dark | | Next() | the next policy (what ThemeSwitch does) | | Resolved() | the scheme shown | | Register(name, {URL, Label, Schemes}) | adds a theme: its stylesheet loads when it is first used; Schemes: ['dark'] for a theme of one scheme | | Use(name, callback) | shows a theme, after loading its stylesheet; callback(error) | | Theme(), Themes() | the theme shown, every theme [{Name, Label, Schemes}] | | Scope(element, name, callback) | one part of the page in a theme or a policy of its own; null gives it back to the page | | Channels(color) | the channels of a color ('75, 68, 61') for the -rgb tokens | | OnChange(callback), OffChange(callback) | {Policy, Theme, Name} after every change, including a change of the system under system | ElemenxUI brings contrast (high contrast, light and dark), darcula (the dark theme of the JetBrains IDEs), soft (round corners, roomier controls, a violet accent), and two themes for games, fantasy and scifi. A build takes a theme only when the Application names it (Theme.Use('soft'), data-theme="soft") or lists the themes (Theme.Themes()); --packs soft adds one it cannot see. A theme file Every rule of a theme starts with its attribute, written twice so it works on any element. Tokens of both schemes go under [data-theme][data-theme='ocean'], the colors of each scheme under ...[data-scheme='light'] and ...[data-scheme='dark']: [data-theme][data-theme='ocean'] { --elemenx-radius: 6px; --elemenx-control: 36px; } [data-theme][data-theme='ocean'][data-scheme='light'] { --elemenx-accent: #0b6e99; --elemenx-accent-rgb: 11, 110, 153; --elemenx-background: #f1f6f8; } [data-theme][data-theme='ocean'][data-scheme='dark'] { --elemenx-accent: #6cc4e8; --elemenx-accent-rgb: 108, 196, 232; --elemenx-background: #0d1a20; } [data-theme][data-theme='ocean'] .elemenx-button.primary { text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.04em; } The prefix makes a theme apply only while it is on (its file may stay on the page), and makes its rules more specific than the rules of the components they override, so the order of the stylesheets does not matter. A token you do not set keeps its default. libraries/ElemenxUI/themes/template.css lists every token with its value: copy it, rename it, keep what you change. The classes of the components are public: the full list is docs/THEMING-CLASSES.md of the repository. theme.Register('ocean', {URL: 'themes/ocean.css', Label: 'Ocean'}); theme.Use('ocean', function (error) {}); The tokens | Group | Tokens | | --- | --- | | Type | --elemenx-font, --elemenx-font-mono, --elemenx-font-math, --elemenx-font-size-small / -size / -size-large (12, 14, 16px), --elemenx-font-size-field (16px on a touch screen), --elemenx-line-height-small / -height / -height-large, --elemenx-font-weight-strong, --elemenx-font-weight-bold | | Geometry | --elemenx-control-small / --elemenx-control / -large / -giant (24, 32, 40, 56px; larger on a touch screen), --elemenx-grid-min, --elemenx-radius-small / --elemenx-radius / -large / -huge / -giant / -pill | | Motion | --elemenx-duration, --elemenx-duration-slow, --elemenx-easing | | Colors of a scheme | --elemenx-background, --elemenx-surface, --elemenx-surface-raised, --elemenx-surface-hover, --elemenx-text, --elemenx-text-muted, --elemenx-accent, --elemenx-accent-hover, --elemenx-accent-text, --elemenx-danger, --elemenx-success, --elemenx-warning, --elemenx-info, --elemenx-border, --elemenx-border-strong, --elemenx-shadow, --elemenx-focus, and their -rgb channels | | Both schemes | --elemenx-shadow-small, --elemenx-shadow-subtle, --elemenx-backdrop, --elemenx-overlay, the scrollbars, the badges and avatars, the gamepad buttons | | Components | --elemenx-block-, --elemenx-property-, --elemenx-rating-color, --elemenx-tile-color, --elemenx-weather-, --elemenx-syntax- (highlighted code), --elemenx-achievement-, and the --elemenx-game- tokens of the game components | A component has variables of its own, set by its variants (--elemenx-progress-color, --elemenx-drawer-size...): a theme changes them on its class. A part of the page Any element with data-theme and data-scheme gives itself and everything in it a theme of its own; Theme.Scope(element, name) does it from code, loading the stylesheet of a named theme first:
...
...

Title: The CLI
Text: The package @qybercom/elemenx gives the command elemenx (npx elemenx in a project, or the script elemenx-cli.js). It makes projects and their parts, serves them while they are written, serves their builds as a production server would, builds them, and makes icon sets. elemenx generate application <Name> [path] [--native [desktop|mobile]] [--force] elemenx generate <component|service|guard|directive> <path/Name> [project] [--application Name] [--force] elemenx dev [project] [--port 4173] [--host 127.0.0.1] elemenx serve [project] [--port 4175] [--host 127.0.0.1] [--out dist] [--compression true|false] [--compression-threshold 1024] [--cache-control "..."] elemenx build [project] [options] elemenx docs [--port 4179] [--open] elemenx native add [desktop|mobile|all] [project] elemenx icons <directory> <output.svg> [--current-color] elemenx version elemenx help [command] elemenx help <command>, or elemenx <command> --help, shows the use and the options of one command; g is short for generate. generate npx elemenx generate application Shop npx elemenx g component pages/HomePage npx elemenx g service services/Cart npx elemenx g guard SignedIn npx elemenx g directive Tooltip - generate application Shop makes the folder of its sources, Shop/, with index.js and the root component App; and app.js, index.html, elemenx.config.js and package.json (with the scripts dev, build, serve) when the project has none. A second Application beside it (generate application Admin) keeps the files that are there. --native makes it ready for native programs (see Builds). - An entity goes under the root of the sources of its Application (Application of elemenx.config.js, or --application): a component gets <Name>/<Name>.js and <Name>/<Name>.html, the others <Name>.js. Its path is yours (pages/HomePage, ./auth/Session); the generator walks up from it to the nearest index.js and adds the entity there, relative to it, or to the index.js of the root. A path that leaves the root is refused. - Nothing is written over without --force, and an entity already in a graph is not added twice. dev elemenx dev serves the project as it is, with the framework and ElemenxUI of the package: the page loads the files of the graph one by one, and a reload shows every change (each file goes with Cache-Control: no-cache: the browser checks it again by its ETag). It answers every path that is not a file with index.html, so the routes of the router work on a reload. --host 0.0.0.0 opens it to the other devices of the network. serve elemenx serve serves the build in dist as a production server would: gzip and brotli for the responses of 1024 bytes and more, ETag, Last-Modified, Cache-Control, Vary: Accept-Encoding, 304 for the conditional requests, HEAD with the headers and no body. Development and production can run at once on their two ports. docs elemenx docs serves this reference, of the version of Elemenx the project installed, from the package itself: no network is needed, and its live examples run (the ones of the network too, against the server of the command). --open opens it in the browser of the system; the port is 4179 (--port). The configuration elemenx.config.js in the root of a project gives the defaults; an option of the command line wins over it, and it wins over the defaults of Elemenx. module.exports = { Application: 'Shop', Entry: 'app.js', Index: 'index.html', Output: 'dist', Server: { DevelopmentPort: 4173, ProductionPort: 4175, Compression: true, CompressionThreshold: 1024, Request: function (request, response, pathname) { if (pathname !== '/api/hello') return false; response.writeHead(200, {'Content-Type': 'application/json'}); response.end(JSON.stringify({Message: 'Hello'})); return true; }, WebSocket: { Path: '/api/socket', Message: function (connection, message) { connection.Send(message); } } } }; | Key | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Application, Applications | the root of the sources, or the list of the Applications of a project with several | | Entry, Index, Output | the script of the Applications, the page, the folder of the build | | Server | the ports and the compression; Templates: false sends the pages as they are (by default the <template id> of a page goes as a <script type="text/html" id>, see Templates); Request(request, response, pathname) answers paths of its own (an API of the project while it is developed: return true when it answered); WebSocket: {Path, Message(connection, message)} answers a socket (connection.Send(text), connection.Close()) | | Single, Widget, Full, Precompile, Packs | the defaults of the options of build | | Extension | Surface, Name, Description, Version, ID, Icons, Manifest of a browser extension | | Native | Desktop and Mobile: the settings of the native programs | The server of this reference uses Request and WebSocket for the live examples of the section Network. icons npx elemenx icons ./svg/lucide ./application/icons/lucide.svg --current-color Every SVG file of the folder becomes a <symbol> of the sprite, named by its file (Arrow Left.svg becomes arrow-left), with its viewBox and the fill and stroke of its root; the ids inside an icon get its name before them, so icons do not collide. --current-color makes every color but none the color of the text. The Icons service of ElemenxUI shows the sprite as a set: Icons.Register('lucide', 'icons/lucide.svg'), then <Icon Name="lucide:arrow-left" />. native and version elemenx native add desktop installs Electron and its packager into the project, native add mobile Capacitor and its plugins, native add both (see Builds). elemenx version prints the version.

Title: Builds
Text: elemenx build turns a project into what a server, a file, another site, a browser or a system runs. Every kind of build takes only what the Application uses, inlines its templates and styles, and minifies it. | Build | Command | What it makes | | --- | --- | --- | | A site | elemenx build | dist/ for any static server | | One file | elemenx build --single | one index.html that runs from a server or from file:// | | A widget | elemenx build --widget | one isolated widget.js for a page of another site | | A browser extension | elemenx build --extension | Chrome, Edge and Firefox extensions, zipped for the stores | | Native programs | elemenx build --native | a desktop program (Electron), Android and iOS programs (Capacitor) | A site dist/ holds index.html (copied from the project), elemenx.js, and app.js: the bundle of the graph of the Application (Elemenx.Bundle({...}), see Resources and bundles) followed by the original app.js. The other public files of the project (images, fonts, data) are copied; the sources, nodemodules and the package files are not. elemenx serve serves it as production would. What a build leaves out - Components the Application does not render: the build follows the tags of its templates, then the templates of the components it took. - Services, guards and directives it does not name: it keeps the ones named in quotes in its code ($Service('Toast'), Guards: ['SignedIn']) and the directives its templates put on elements, and the ones these use in turn. - Files of the libraries: of the packs (emoji, cities, icon sets, game themes) a build in a folder copies the ones the Application uses, with every language of them (see below). - Phrases of the libraries: their dictionaries keep the phrases the code of the build names, by their key or the start of one; a build in one file, a widget, an extension and a native program keep only the languages of the Application (its $Locales, the lang of its page, and en), all of them when it names none. - Parts of the framework: Router, Network, Storage, Events, Messaging, WebWorker and ServiceWorker stay only when the code of the build uses them ($Router, $Network, $Storage, $Events or $OnEvent, $Messaging or $OnMessage, $WebWorker, $ServiceWorker, Elemenx.Network...). Messaging keeps Events; an Application with workers keeps all of the framework, since their scripts are files the build does not read. The build says what it left out. A name built at run time ($Service(name)) cannot show a use: name it in quotes somewhere, or build with --full, which keeps all of the framework and every file of the libraries. The icon of the Application Icon: '/icon.png' in elemenx.config.js, a square PNG of the project (1024 pixels), is the icon everywhere: the icon of the page and of Apple, the icons of a PWA, the ICO, ICNS and PNG of the desktop programs with their installers, and the icons of Android and iOS. Icons: {Favicon, Windows, Mac, Linux, Android, IOS} gives a platform a file of its own. A splash screen Splash: true in elemenx.config.js (or {Image, Background, Color, Text, Spinner, MinTime, Timeout}, or a splash.html in the project) shows a splash from the first paint of the page until the first Application is ready: the build puts it at the top of the body, with no script, and elemenx dev serves it too. Elemenx.Splash.Hold() keeps it until Elemenx.Splash.Hide(), for an Application that loads its data first. The window of a desktop program and the screen of a phone while the program starts take its background. An installable application (PWA) PWA: true in elemenx.config.js (or {Name, ShortName, Description, Icon, Theme, Background, Display, Start, Offline}) makes the build of a site installable: manifest.webmanifest linked from its page and, with Offline (by default), a service worker that keeps the files of the build so it runs without the network. The Application offers the installation when it chooses: Elemenx.Install.Available() tells the browser can install it, Elemenx.Install.Prompt(callback) shows its prompt, Elemenx.Install.Manual() is true on Safari of iOS, which installs by its Share menu. Expressions as code --precompile writes the expressions of the templates into the build as functions (Elemenx.Expressions({...})), so it runs on a page whose Content Security Policy forbids eval. The builder reads $Template texts (and sums of texts), $TemplateURL files, Elemenx.Template(name, text) and the

Title: Widgets on other sites
Text:
A widget is a Component of an Application that lives on a page of another site: a cart in the header of a shop, a booking form in a hotel page, a chat button on a blog. The page is not an Elemenx application and may have any framework of its own; it loads one script and marks the places of the widgets. elemenx build --widget (or Widget: true in elemenx.config.js) makes that script, widget.js: the framework, the Libraries the Application uses and the Application, minified and isolated. module.exports = { Application: 'Shop', Entry: 'app.js', Widget: true }; Isolation - The window gets no Elemenx: the widget runs its own copy of the framework, and a page with an Elemenx of its own, of any version, keeps it untouched. - Each widget renders in a shadow root of its place: the styles of the page do not reach it, and its styles (ElemenxUI included) do not reach the page. Shadow: false renders it in the element itself. - The language (lang, dir) and the theme go to the host of the widget, not to the html and body of the page. - widget.js loaded twice (two parts of the page that each bring it) runs once. Limits: a URL in the widget (an image, a file) is read against the page, so give absolute URLs; a widget starts no worker. Defining the widgets The Application needs no $Component and no $Mount: Elemenx.Widgets names its widgets. Elemenx.Application('Shop', { $Root: 'Shop', $Use: ['ElemenxUI'] }); Elemenx.Widgets .Define('Cart', {Component: 'CartButton', Application: 'Shop', Events: ['checkout']}) .Define('AddToCart', {Component: 'AddToCart', Application: 'Shop', Events: ['added']}) .Define('Reviews', {Component: 'Reviews', Application: 'Shop'}); / Every place of the page, now and later. / Elemenx.Widgets.Watch(); / The code of the page reaches them too. / window.ShopWidgets = Elemenx.Widgets; Define(name, {Component, Application, Props, Events, Shadow}): the Component of the widget, the name of its Application, the props it starts with, the events of the Component the page hears, and Shadow: false to render without a shadow root. The page The page loads widget.js once, in its head, and marks the places; data-props holds the props as JSON:

Brass lamp

Watch(root) mounts every place of root (the document by default) and the places added later, takes away the widgets of the places removed, and passes a change of data-props to the widget. It returns the function that stops watching. A place of a widget it does not define is left alone. The events named in Events bubble from the place as DOM events, their data in detail: document.addEventListener('checkout', function (event) { console.log(event.detail.Items.length, event.detail.Total); }); From code | Method | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Mount(element, name, props) | mounts a widget into an element; returns {Name, Element, Update(props), On(event, callback), Unmount()} | | Unmount(element) | takes the widget of an element away; false when there was none | | Names() | the names of the widgets defined | var reviews = ShopWidgets.Mount(document.querySelector('#reviews'), 'Reviews', {Product: 'Lamp'}); reviews.Update({Product: 'Shelf'}); reviews.Unmount(); One Application The widgets of a page are one Application: they share its Services. In the example the Cart Service holds the products, so the button of every product and the cart in the header show the same cart: Elemenx.Component('CartButton', { $TemplateURL: 'CartButton.html', Currency: 'EUR', Count: 0, $OnCreate: function () { var self = this; var cart = this.$Service('Cart'); this.Read = function () { self.Count = cart.Count(); }; this.Read(); cart.OnChange(this.Read); }, $OnDestroy: function () { this.$Service('Cart').OffChange(this.Read); }, CheckedOut: function () { this.$Emit('checkout', {Items: this.$Service('Cart').Items, Total: this.$Service('Cart').Total()}); } }); examples/Widgets is such a project: a shop of another site with its cart, the buttons of its products and their reviews (npm run dev there, npm run build for dist/widget.js). See also Builds.

Title: The Designer
Text: examples/Designer is the Designer, a builder of pages: the components of ElemenxUI are taken from a palette onto a canvas, arranged, given their props and their layout, and the result is a template of Elemenx, a Component or a whole Application. It builds the layout and the props of a page, not its bindings or its handlers: those are written in code afterwards. npm run example:designer Projects A project is one of three kinds, chosen when it is created (File → Create), and it stays that kind: - template: one page; its result is a template to paste into a Component; - component: a Component with its public props and slots; - application: pages and components, the routes, the guards and the settings of the Application (its name, title, language, theme and router). The projects are kept in the storage of the browser (File → Open lists them) and can be saved into a file and read back from one. The screen - The Ribbon: Home (undo, redo, copy, remove, move the selected element), Project (a new page or component, the settings of the Application), Insert (every component of ElemenxUI and the classes of its layouts, by group, with a search) and View (the width of the canvas, its outlines, gaps and rulers). - The canvas in the middle: a sample pressed goes into the selected element, or after it; a sample dragged goes where it is dropped. Run shows the page as it works, and the inspector shows its elements while it runs. - The structure of the page on the left, a tree to select and move elements. - The layout and the props of the selected element on the right; with nothing selected, the document itself (the name and route of a page, the props and slots of a component). The rules of CSS of an element can depend on its state (hover, focus), the width of the screen and the theme. - The template at the bottom, always in step with the canvas. Keys: Mod+Z, Mod+Shift+Z (or Mod+Y), Mod+D (a copy), Delete, Escape (no selection), and Alt for the key tips of the Ribbon. The result File → Export gives the template of the page, its rules first in a <style>; Import reads a template back. File → Application downloads the page or the application as one HTML file that runs alone (the framework and ElemenxUI inside it), or as a project in a zip (index.html, app.js, elemenx.config.js and the Components under application/) ready for elemenx dev and elemenx build; its icon, splash screen and PWA settings go with it. The palette The palette is not a list kept by hand: it is the $Meta the Components of the Library declare (their group, icon, description, props with their options, events and the sample the palette inserts), which elemenx meta (npm run meta in the repository) collects into data/meta.json. The type of a prop comes from its default value. A Component of your own Library with a $Meta appears in the palette of a builder that uses that Library. Elemenx.Component('PriceTag', { $Meta: { Group: 'commerce', Icon: 'tag', Description: 'A price with its currency.', Props: { Value: 'The amount.', Currency: {Options: ['EUR', 'USD'], Description: 'The currency of the amount.'} }, Sample: {Value: 25, Currency: 'EUR'} }, Value: 0, Currency: 'EUR' }); A Designer of your own The parts of the Designer are Components of ElemenxUI around the Designer Service, which holds the document, its history and the projects: DesignerPalette, DesignerCanvas, DesignerTree, DesignerInspector (with DesignerStyle and DesignerRules), DesignerDocument, DesignerProject and DesignerSettings. An Application can put them in its own layout: <Workspace> <DesignerPalette slot="left" /> <DesignerCanvas slot="main" Width="desktop" [rulers]="true" /> <DesignerInspector slot="right" /> </Workspace> The Designer Service is what they share; the code of the Application reads the result from it: var designer = this.$Service('Designer'); designer.Load(function (error) { if (error) return; console.log(designer.Template()); }); See the reference of each of them in the Library section.

Title: Editors and IDEs
Text: Elemenx has extensions for VS Code, the IDEs of JetBrains (WebStorm, IntelliJ IDEA, PhpStorm...) and Visual Studio 2022, and a language server for the other editors. They know the Components, props, events, directives and Services of your project and of ElemenxUI. Installing | Editor | Where | | --- | --- | | VS Code, VSCodium, Cursor, Windsurf | the Marketplace of the editor (VS Code Marketplace or Open VSX): Elemenx | | WebStorm, IntelliJ IDEA, PhpStorm... | Settings → Plugins → Marketplace: Elemenx; it installs LSP4IJ, which it needs | | Visual Studio 2022 (17.10 or later) | Extensions → Manage Extensions: Elemenx | | Neovim, Zed, Sublime Text, Helix... | the language server of the repository: node editors/server/elemenx-language-server.js --stdio | Every release of Elemenx attaches the files of the extensions to its GitHub release as well (elemenx-vscode.vsix, elemenx-intellij.zip, elemenx-visualstudio.vsix), for an installation from disk. The extensions have the version of Elemenx. The plugin of JetBrains, the extension of Visual Studio and the language server need Node.js; ELEMENXNODE names a Node other than the one of PATH. What they do - Completion: Components and their props, bindings ([Variant]), events ((click)) and the options of a prop (Variant="ghost"); directives (if, for, tip...); the fields and functions of the Component in the expressions of its template; Services in $Service('...'); references in $Ref('...') and $Refs('...'). - Hover: the documentation of a Component, a prop, a directive, a Service, a field or a reference. - Go to definition (Ctrl+click): a Component, a Service, a field or a function of the template, a directive (the core ones too), a prop (its key in the definition), an event (the $Emit that sends it), a reference (#Name and $Ref('Name') lead to each other), $T (its definition in elemenx.js) and the key of $T('ui.call.leave') (its phrase in the nearest locales/.json, English first; its hover shows the phrase in each language). - Diagnostics: an unknown Component or directive, a prop or an event a Component does not have, a $Ref with no element of that name in the template. - Colors: Components, bindings, events, directives, references and {{ }} take colors of their own, and their expressions are colored as JavaScript.
