A project that has only the built files (dist/elemenx.all.min.js) still gets all of it: the extensions carry the sources of their version of Elemenx and ElemenxUI. The template and its Component The template of a Component is its $TemplateURL, the .html of its name beside it (Board.html next to Board.js), or a <template id="x"> of a page for a definition with $TemplateID: 'x'. A name in $Template ('#x') is marked as an error. The expressions of the template see what Elemenx gives them: the fields and functions of the Component, the variables of the loops around them, $T and $index. In WebStorm and IntelliJ IDEA the expressions are JavaScript of the IDE, with the types of the fields taken from their values: Title: '' is a string, Rows: [{ID: 1}] an array of {ID: number}, so Rows[0]. completes ID, and the item of for="row of Rows" has the type of the items. A JSDoc above a key gives it a type where the value tells too little: Elemenx.Component('Team', { / @type {{Name: string, Online: boolean}[]} / People: [], / @type {?{ID: number, Label: string}} / Selected: null }); Other editors The language server speaks LSP over stdio. In Neovim, for example: vim.lsp.start({ name = 'elemenx', cmd = {'node', '/path/to/elemenx/editors/server/elemenx-language-server.js', '--stdio'}, rootdir = vim.fs.root(0, {'package.json', 'elemenx.config.js'}) }) --meta <file> gives it the meta.json of another Library.

Title: The big picture
Text: This section explains how Elemenx works inside: what happens between a <script> tag and a page that answers clicks. You do not need it to build applications; it helps when something surprises you, when you want to know what a feature costs, or when you simply like to know. Each page is short and starts from a picture. One file, many parts Elemenx is one JavaScript file, elemenx.js, with no dependencies, written in ES5 so it runs anywhere a browser runs. Inside, it is a set of parts that each do one thing and talk to each other through one private object: - Your Application is what you write: components (a template, a style, some state and methods), services (shared logic), routes and guards. - The core turns that into a living page: it starts Applications, compiles templates, keeps the state reactive, renders components, and moves between pages. - The services of the framework give the core and your code the rest of the browser in one shape: the network, storages, events between parts of the page, messages between tabs and workers, languages. - The browser does the real work: the DOM, fetch, localStorage, history. Elemenx adds no layer between your page and the DOM: what you see in the developer tools is what Elemenx made, element for element. - Libraries (ElemenxUI, or your own) are components, services and directives an Application uses, loaded as if they were its own. The ideas behind it HTML is the template language. A template is HTML with a few marks: {{ }} for text, [x] for a value, (x) for an event, x for a directive. A designer can read it; a browser parses it. State is plain objects. A component's state is its fields; assigning one updates the page. There is no setState, no store to subscribe to, no immutable copies. Fine-grained updates. Each {{ }} and each [x] of a template is tied to the exact data it reads. When that data changes, that one text node or attribute is updated, and nothing else is computed or compared. There is no virtual DOM. Callbacks and events, never Promises in the API. Anything that takes time (a request, a guard, a loader) calls you back or emits an event. It works the same in every browser and is easy to cancel and to follow. Development without a build. In development the browser loads your files as they are, following index.js lists. A build is an optimization for production, not a requirement to run. The pages of this section - From a script to the first screen: how an Application starts. - From a template to the page: how a template becomes DOM. - How state updates the page: the reactive system. - The life of a component: creation, props, events, content, sleep and destruction. - Services, events and messages: what components share, and how parts of an application talk. - How a navigation happens: the router, step by step. - Network and storage: resources, protocols, ownership. - What a build does: from a project to dist/.

Title: From a script to the first screen
Text: A page loads elemenx.js, then the app.js of your project, and a moment later shows a working application. Here is what happens in that moment, step by step. 1. The framework loads elemenx.js runs once and defines Elemenx: the functions you call (Elemenx.Application, Elemenx.Component, Elemenx.Service...) and, hidden behind them, its parts. Nothing is drawn yet. If the page already has a copy of the same version, the second one stops at once; another version starts beside it, and the console says so. 2. An Application is declared Elemenx.Application('Shop', { $Component: 'Layout', $Root: 'Shop', $Mount: 'body', $Use: ['ElemenxUI'], $Locales: {URL: 'locales/{language}.json', Languages: ['en', 'ru']}, $Router: {Routes: [...]} }); Elemenx.Application only records the definition and waits for the page to be ready. An Application is the owner of everything that follows: its services are its own, its router belongs to it, and two Applications on one page do not see each other's state. 3. Libraries and the language The Application names its libraries ($Use): their files will be found and their stylesheets attached. Then it picks a language (the one chosen before, the one of the system, or the lang of the page) and loads its dictionaries, its own and those of its libraries. The first screen waits for them, so it shows phrases, never keys. 4. The graph: a bundle, or the files The Application now needs the definitions of its components, services and directives. There are two ways to get them, and Elemenx tries them in this order: - A bundle. A build put every definition in app.js inside Elemenx.Bundle({...}). They are registered without a single request. - Discovery. In development there is no bundle. $Root: 'Shop' names a folder; its index.js lists files and folders (['services', 'Layout/Layout.js']), each folder has its own index.js, and Discovery reads them all to make a map: which name is in which file. The files themselves are not loaded yet. 5. Directives and services before the root A template can only be compiled when its directives are known, and a component may ask for a service in its first line. So the directives and services of the Application and its libraries are loaded (from the bundle, or by a <script> each) before the root component is made. Services are only loaded here, not created: a service is created the first time someone asks for it. 6. The root component The component named by $Component is built: its template compiled, its state made reactive, its $OnCreate run (see From a template to the page). Its template names other components (<Header>, <ProductList>); each is built the same way, down the tree. In development, a component whose file is not loaded yet gets a placeholder; Discovery loads the file, and the component takes its place as soon as it is there. 7. Mounted The root goes into the element of $Mount (or into a shadow root of it, with $Shadow). Every component that is now in the page runs $OnReady; the Application runs its own $OnReady. The splash of the page, if there is one, fades out. 8. The router starts Last, the router reads the URL, finds its route, runs its guards and renders its page into the outlet (see How a navigation happens). From now on the application lives: events change state, state changes the page. When something fails A step that fails (a file that does not load, a component that throws in its $OnCreate) stops that Application, not the page: it shows its $Error (a template you give), calls $OnError, and writes the reason in the console. Another Application of the same page goes on.

Title: From a template to the page
Text:
A template is text. A page is a tree of live elements that change when the data changes. This page follows a template from one to the other. 1. Text becomes a tree

{{Title}}

{{Items.length}} items

The browser's own HTML parser reads the template into a tree of nodes, as it reads any page. Elemenx only prepares the text first: it keeps the case of component names (CartLine, which HTML would lower), closes self-closing component tags, and protects expressions that contain characters HTML would take for markup. Each instance of a component gets its own copy of the tree. 2. The walk Elemenx then walks the copy, every node and every attribute, and sorts what it finds: | In the template | Becomes | | --- | --- | | {{Title}} in a text | a text binding on that text node | | [value], [class.empty], [style.width], [attribute.aria-label] | an element binding: a property, a class, a style or an attribute | | [(value)] | a binding and a listener: a field that follows the input and the other way round | | (click)="Clear" | a listener | | #Name | a ref: this.$Ref('Name') finds the element | | if, for, lazy and your structural directives | a host: the element becomes a template the directive builds and takes away | | tooltip and other behavioral directives | a directive with its hooks | | | a component: an instance of its own, its props given | 3. Expressions become functions {{Items.length}} and !Items.length are JavaScript expressions. Each one is compiled once into a function, and that function is kept by its text: a thousand rows with {{item.Title}} share one function. The function reads names from the state of the component first, then from its methods and the helpers of the framework ($T, $Params). A page whose security policy forbids eval (a browser extension, a strict site) cannot compile at run time: a build with --precompile writes these functions into the code, and the template compiler takes them from there. 4. Bindings become effects Each binding becomes an effect: a small function that evaluates its expression and writes the result into its one node. The effect runs once at the start, and from then on whenever the data it read changes (see How state updates the page). That is the whole update system: no render function for the component, no tree to compare. When Items.length changes, the text node of the count and the class of the paragraph are rewritten; the heading, the button and the lines are not touched. 5. Listeners find their method when the event comes (click)="Clear" adds a listener to the button. It looks up Clear when the click happens, not when the template is compiled, so a method set later (in $OnCreate, say) is found too. On a component tag, (remove) listens to what the child emits (this.$Emit('remove', data)); on an element, to a DOM event, including custom ones a directive dispatches. 6. Structural directives own their element if, for and lazy take their element out of the tree and leave a marker (an empty comment) in its place. The element becomes a template of its own: the directive builds a copy at the marker when it should exist (if true, each item of for) and destroys it when it should not, with the components and effects inside. for with key keeps the copy of each item by its key, so when the list changes, the existing rows move instead of being rebuilt. 7. Components become instances is replaced by an instance of CartLine: its own template, state and effects. [item] becomes a prop: an effect of the parent writes the value into the child, and the child hears $OnProps when it changes. class and style on the tag go on the root element of the child. What is written between the tags of a component is its content: it is compiled in the scope of the parent, and the child places it where its template has a (see The life of a component). What it costs Compiling is done once per instance, and the work is proportional to the size of the template. Updates are proportional to what changed, not to the size of the page. That is why a large page with a few changing numbers stays fast, and why a list of ten thousand rows is slow whatever the framework: ten thousand rows are ten thousand elements, and VirtualList draws only those in view.

Title: How state updates the page
Text: You write this.Total = 42, and the number on the page changes. No call to render, no subscription. This page shows how. The state is behind a proxy When a component is made, its state (the fields of its definition, copied for this instance) is wrapped in a JavaScript Proxy. A proxy looks and behaves like the object, but it sees every read and every write. Objects and lists inside the state are wrapped too, the first time they are reached, at any depth. Only plain objects ({}) and arrays are wrapped. A Date, a Map, an element of the page, an instance of a class are kept as they are: Elemenx does not know what their methods change. To update what shows them, assign a new one (this.Since = new Date()). Reading is tracked An effect is a function Elemenx runs and watches: every binding of a template is one (see From a template to the page). While an effect runs, the proxy notes each field it reads in a table: for this object and this key, these effects depend on it. {{Total}} reads Total, so the effect of that text node is noted under Total. The notes are made fresh at each run: an effect that read Discount only when Member was true depends on Discount only while it is. So an effect never runs for data it no longer reads. Writing triggers When code writes this.Total = 42, the proxy looks up Total in the table and runs its effects again, at once, before the assignment returns. Each writes its one node. Writing the same value again does nothing. Adding a key, deleting one, or changing the length of a list triggers the effects that iterate over it (a for, Object.keys). The update is synchronous: the line after the assignment already sees the new DOM. There is no queue to wait for and no nextTick. Several changes, one update Five assignments run the effects that depend on them five times. When a response of the server sets several fields, batch them: this.$Batch(function (state) { state.Loading = false; state.Items = response.Items; state.Total = response.Total; }); Inside $Batch the effects are collected instead of run; at the end each one runs once. this.$Update({...}) does the same for a set of fields. A method of a list (push, splice, sort) is already one change, however many items it moves. What reacts, and what does not - Fields of a component, and anything plain inside them: yes. - Services are plain JavaScript objects, not reactive: a component copies what it shows from a service when the service tells it (OnChange), as the tutorials do. This keeps the cost of reactivity where the page is, not in every object of the application. - Hooks ($OnCreate, $OnReady, $OnDestroy...) run untracked: what they read does not make them run again. - Helpers called from a template ({{Visible(Items, Filter)}}) are part of the effect that calls them: they run again when what they read changes. A helper must only compute; one that writes a field the template reads makes the effect run again forever. Why no virtual DOM A virtual DOM builds a description of the whole component at each change and compares it with the last one to find what to update. Fine-grained effects know what to update without comparing: the table of dependencies already says which nodes read the data that changed. The cost is a little memory for the table, paid once per binding; the gain is that an update costs what changed, not what is on the page.

Title: The life of a component
Text:
A component is a definition (a template, a style, fields and methods) and, once used, any number of instances of it. This page follows one instance from its birth to its end, and shows how it talks to the components around it. A definition, many instances Elemenx.Component('CartLine', { $TemplateURL: 'CartLine.html', $StyleURL: 'CartLine.css', Item: null, Quantity: 1, Tags: [], Remove: function () { this.$Emit('remove', {ID: this.Item.ID}); } }); Elemenx.Component records the definition; nothing is built yet. A definition with $TemplateURL or $StyleURL loads those files the first time an instance is needed; its style is added to the page once, whatever the number of instances. Birth When a template meets , an instance is made: 1. State. The fields of the definition are copied: plain objects and lists deeply, so two instances never share Tags: []. The props given by the tag ([item]="item") are set over them. The state is made reactive. 2. Template. The template is compiled for this instance: its bindings, listeners, directives and child components (see From a template to the page). 3. $OnCreate. Your code runs: the state and the template are there, the element is not in the page yet. This is the place to set fields, to ask services, to subscribe. 4. In the page. The element goes into its place. $OnReady runs: now the element has a size, the focus can go to it, a library that needs a real element can start. Props down, events up A parent gives data to a child through props, and the child tells the parent what happened through events. Neither reaches into the other. - [items]="List" is an effect of the parent: when List changes, the new value is written into the child's Items, and the child's $OnProps hears it. The child should not change its props itself: the next update of the parent would overwrite them. - this.$Emit('select', data) in the child calls the method of the parent named in (select)="Picked", with data. - this.$Parent() and this.$Ref('Name') exist for the rare case a component must call another directly. Content and slots What is written between the tags of a component is its content:

{{Product.Name}}

{{Product.Description}}

 The content belongs to the parent: its expressions read the parent's state, its listeners call the parent's methods. The child decides where it goes: takes the elements with slot="header", the rest. When a slot is inside an if of the child that turns false, the content placed there is destroyed with it and built again when it turns true; with keep it sleeps instead and comes back as it was. class and style written on the tag of a component go on the root element of its instance, beside its own classes, so works as it reads. Living While it lives, the component's effects keep its element up to date, its listeners call its methods, and its props follow its parent. A component whose definition is still loading (in development, or with a remote template) shows a placeholder, its pending template if it has one, and takes its place when it is ready; a failure shows its error template. Sleep and wake When an if turns false, or the router leaves a page, the instance is normally destroyed. With Elemenx.Cache keeping instances (or keep, or $KeepAlive), it sleeps instead: its element leaves the page but stays whole in memory, with its state and its scroll. $OnSleep runs: stop timers and streams there. When it is needed again it wakes in its place, $OnWake runs, and nothing is rebuilt. An instance asleep too long, or beyond the number the cache keeps, is destroyed. Death $OnDestroy runs, and then Elemenx releases everything the instance had: the effects of its bindings, the listeners it added through its template, its directives (each runs its own $OnDestroy), the network resources, events and messages it opened through $Network, $Events and $Messaging, and its child components, deepest first. What you added yourself (a listener on window, a timer, an observer) is yours to remove in $OnDestroy.

Title: Services, events and messages
Text: Components show things. What they share (a session, a cart, a client of an API) lives in services, and what they tell each other without knowing each other goes through events and messages. This page shows who owns what, and which way a message goes. A service: one object for the Application Elemenx.Service('Cart', { $OnCreate: function () { this.Items = []; }, Add: function (product) { this.Items.push(product); } }); this.$Service('Cart') in any component, service, guard or directive of the Application returns the same object. It is made the first time someone asks for it (its $OnCreate runs then), and lives as long as its Application; its $OnDestroy runs when the Application goes. Two Applications of one page have two carts: a service belongs to its Application, never to the page. A service is a plain object, not reactive (see How state updates the page). A component that shows its data copies what it shows into its own fields when the service tells it: the service keeps listeners (OnChange), the component adds one in $OnCreate and removes it in $OnDestroy. This keeps a service usable anywhere, in a test without a page included, and keeps the cost of updates in the components that show something. Guards are functions the router calls before a navigation, with the same this.$Service (see How a navigation happens). Events: inside the page When two parts of a page should not know each other (a header that shows a count, a page that changes it), one says that something happened on a channel, and whoever listens hears it: this.$Events().Emit('cart:changed', {Count: 3}); this.$Events().On('cart:changed', function (event) { self.Count = event.Data.Count; }); Delivery is synchronous, in the same page, with the object itself. A socket made by this.$Events() belongs to its component or service and is closed with it, so a destroyed component never hears an event again. Prefer a service when there is state to keep (the count itself), and an event when there is only news to tell (a toast to show, a sound to play). Messages: between tabs, frames and workers Elemenx.Messaging carries messages on channels between every place Elemenx runs: the other tabs of the site, the frames and windows a page opens, its web workers and its service worker. A socket does not need to know where the others are: the runtimes find each other (through BroadcastChannel and postMessage) and pass the messages along. this.$Messaging().Send('cart:changed', {Count: 3}); A message is copied, as everything that crosses a boundary of the browser: send data, not objects with methods. A tab that signs out can tell the others; a worker that finished a long computation tells the page. Who owns what | Made by | Belongs to | Ends | | --- | --- | --- | | this.$Service('Cart') | the Application | with the Application | | this.$Events(), this.$Messaging(), this.$Network()... in a component | the component | when the component is destroyed | | the same in a service | the service | with the service, so with its Application | | Elemenx.Events() in plain code | nobody | when you call Destroy() | Ownership is what keeps a long-lived application from leaking: what a component opened is closed when it goes, without code of yours.

Title: How a navigation happens
Text: A click on a link to /orders/42, and a moment later the page of the order shows, the URL has changed, and Back returns. Between the two, the router takes seven steps, and any of them may stop or redirect the way. 1. It starts A navigation starts in one of three ways: a click on an <a href> of the same site (the router catches it, unless it opens a new tab or a download), a call in code (this.$Router().Go('/orders/42'), or Replace), or Back and Forward of the browser. All three take the same path below. A new navigation that starts while one is on its way makes the older one count for nothing (NavigationCancel). 2. Match The router reads the path against its routes, from the outer to the inner: /orders/:id matches and gives $Params.id = '42'; the query (?tab=items) and the hash go to $Query and $Hash. Nested routes give a chain: the layout of /orders, then the page of the order inside its outlet. No route matches: the NotFound component of the router, or the browser follows the link itself. 3. Leave The page that shows now may refuse to go: its $OnRouteLeave(context) answers like a guard. A form with unsaved changes asks "Leave without saving?" and answers false to stay. Routes the old and the new path share (a common layout) are not left at all. 4. Guards Each guard of the new route is asked in turn (Guard: 'SignedIn', or a list): | A guard returns | The router | | --- | --- | | true | goes on to the next guard | | false | stops; the page stays, GuardFailed shows if the route has one | | a path ('/login?return=/orders/42') | starts a navigation there instead | | this.$Wait(function (done) {...}) | waits for done(answer), showing the Waiting component meanwhile | | this.$Fail(reason, data) | stops, with a reason for GuardFailed | Guards answer with a value or a callback, never a Promise. A guard keeps a page from showing; the data behind it are protected by the server. 5. Load The components of the route must be defined. From a bundle they are there; in development, the router asks Discovery for their files and waits (see From a script to the first screen). A file that does not load ends the navigation with NavigationError, and the URL goes back to where it was. 6. Commit Now the router changes the page: the URL becomes the new one (NavigationCommit), the component of each level renders into its outlet (outlet="Content" in the layout above it) with its $Params, $Query and $Hash, and the old one is destroyed, or sleeps when Elemenx.Cache keeps pages. A page asleep under the same route and parameters wakes instead of being built. The same route with other parameters keeps its component and only changes its values: a template that reads $Params.id follows by itself. 7. History and title The browser history gets an entry (Go) or has its entry replaced (Replace). A component with $Title names the tab. When the components of the route and those inside them that loaded later are all rendered, NavigationEnd comes: the moment to move the focus, to send an analytics event, to scroll. Where the route lives | Mode | The URL | For | | --- | --- | --- | | history | /orders/42 | a site served over http; the server answers every path with index.html | | hash | /#/orders/42 | a host that cannot rewrite paths | | memory | does not change | a file, a browser extension, a desktop window; the default where there is no http | The steps are the same in every mode; only the place of the route differs.

Title: Network and storage
Text: A browser has many ways to talk to a server (a request, a stream, server-sent events, a socket, a peer connection) and many places to keep data (local and session storage, cookies, IndexedDB), each with an API of its own. Elemenx gives each group one shape, and ties what a component opens to the component. One shape for every connection Every resource of Elemenx.Network (XHR, Stream, LongPolling, SSE, WebSocket, WebRTC, Transfer) has the same life: 1. Make it, with its settings: this.$Network().WebSocket({URL: 'wss://...', Protocol: 'Chat'}). Nothing goes on the wire yet. 2. Listen to what it will report: On('Transport.Open'), On('Transport.Error'), On('Protocol.Message'). Every event is {Namespace, Type, Data, Target}. 3. Start it: Execute() for a request, Connect() for the rest. 4. Stop it: Abort(), Close(), or let its owner go. Because they all report the same way, code that shows progress, retries, or logs works for any of them, and switching from long polling to server-sent events changes one line. None of them returns a Promise: a request can be aborted at any moment, and an event that comes after the component is gone is never delivered. Transport and Protocol Two families of events come from a resource: - Transport. is what happens on the wire: BeforeRequest, Open, Data, Success, Error, Close, Drain. Its data is raw: a text, bytes, a status. - Protocol. is what the messages mean. A Protocol (Elemenx.Network.Protocol('Chat', {Encode, Decode})) stands between the wire and your code: it turns each message that comes into {Type, Data}, emitted as Protocol.<Type>, and each message you send into what the wire takes. Your code listens to Protocol.Message or Protocol.Typing and never parses text. Backpressure A socket or a data channel can be given data faster than the network takes it. Instead of filling the memory, Send returns false once the buffer passes its high mark; a Drain event says when it is low enough to go on. A large file goes through a Transfer: cut into chunks, each sent when there is room, with its progress as events and a TransferReceiver that puts it back together. Owned and closed this.$Network() in a component makes resources that belong to it. When the component is destroyed (its page left, its if false), every resource it made is closed: the socket disconnects, the request aborts, the stream stops, and their late events go nowhere. A service's resources live as long as its Application. That is why a page of a router can open a stream without code to close it. Storage: one shape, and always there this.$Storage gives the storages of the browser one interface: | Storage | Kept | For | | --- | --- | --- | | Local | until cleared | settings, drafts, a cart | | Session | while the tab lives | the state of a flow | | Cookie | as you set it, sent to the server | what the server must read | | IndexedDB | until cleared, large | records, files, offline data | Local.Namespace('cart') keeps the keys of one part of an Application apart from the others; values are JSON in and out. Where the page may not use the storages of the browser (a sandboxed frame, a blocked site, a test without a DOM), Local, Session and Cookie keep their values in memory for the page instead of throwing: the application works, and forgets at reload. IndexedDB keeps the same model as the network: an operation is made, listened to and executed (Store('Notes').Put(...).On('Success', ...).Execute()), and a transaction writes several records or none (see Working offline).

Title: What a build does
Text: In development the browser loads your files one by one, as they are. That is quick to start and easy to debug, and slow for a visitor: dozens of requests, and every component of every library listed. elemenx build makes the same application small and fast, without changing how it works. 1. It reads the graph The builder starts where the browser would: index.html and app.js. It reads the Application ($Component, $Root, $Use, $Router), then follows the graph as the page would run it: - Tags lead to components. The template of the root names <Header> and <ProductList>; their templates name others; and so on. Routes name the components of the pages. - Names lead to services, guards and directives. $Service('Cart'), Guards: ['SignedIn'], tooltip in a template: each is a definition to keep, and its own code names more. - Uses lead to the parts of the framework. $Router keeps the Router; $Network the Network; $Messaging the Messaging; and so on. A name built at run time ($Service(name)) cannot be followed: name it in quotes somewhere, or build with --full. 2. It trims and packs What the graph did not reach is left out: the components of a library the Application never shows, the services it never asks for, the parts of the framework it never calls (the Router, the Network, the workers...), the packs of a library it does not use (emoji, cities, icon sets), and the phrases of the dictionaries no code names. The build prints what it left out. What stays is packed: - templates ($TemplateURL) and styles ($StyleURL) are put inside their definitions, so no file is requested for them; - the code, the templates and the styles are minified; - $Meta is dropped, unless the Application reads it (Elemenx.Meta, the Designer); - with --precompile (always for extensions and native programs), the expressions of the templates are written as functions, for pages that forbid eval. - a site and a widget are split by their routes: what one route alone needs goes into a part of its own (dist/parts/), fetched when the route is first shown (--no-split keeps one bundle). 3. It writes dist/ dist/ holds index.html, elemenx.js (only its parts the Application uses), app.js (every definition inside Elemenx.Bundle({...}), followed by your app.js), the files of the libraries the Application needs, and the public files of the project. Other builds take the same graph to other places: one HTML file (--single), an isolated widget (--widget), a browser extension (--extension), native programs (--native). 4. In the page: bundle first, Discovery second When the built page runs, every definition is already in Elemenx.Bundle: when a component is needed, it is taken from there, without a request. Discovery (the loading of files by index.js) is still there as a fallback: an Application whose bundle lacks a component, in a page that has its sources, still finds it. That is what makes a build an optimization, not a different program: the same code runs in development and in production, and a build that left out too much fails loudly in development of the build (elemenx serve), where you test it before it goes. What it does not do The builder does not rename your files with hashes, does not split the bundle into chunks, and does not transpile: the code is ES5, so it runs as it is. Cache the files with revalidation (see Putting it online).

Title: A landing page
Text:
A one-page site for a product: a hero, its features, its prices and a form to sign up. It has no router and no server: elemenx build --single makes it one HTML file for any static hosting. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Landing. What you learn: an Application and its Components, lists with for, the components of ElemenxUI (Button, PlanPicker, Form, Field, ThemeSwitch, ToastHost), a Service from code (Toast), and a build for production. 1. The project npx elemenx generate application Landing It makes app.js, index.html, elemenx.config.js, package.json and the folder of the sources, Landing/. The Application uses ElemenxUI and mounts its root Component, App, into the body: Elemenx.Application('Landing', { $Title: 'Notely', $Component: 'App', $Root: 'Landing', $Mount: 'body', $Use: ['ElemenxUI'] }); npm run dev starts it at http://localhost:4301 and reloads it as the files change. 2. The page App is the frame: a header that stays on top, the sections, a footer, and a ToastHost where the toasts of the Toast Service show.
Notely
Features Pricing Sign up
© 2026 Notely · Made with Elemenx
A handler gets the event and the element: Go scrolls to the section the link names. Elemenx.Component('App', { $TemplateURL: 'App.html', $StyleURL: 'App.css', Go: function (event, node) { var target = document.getElementById(node.getAttribute('data-target')); event.preventDefault(); if (target) target.scrollIntoView({behavior: 'smooth'}); } }); Each Component is a folder with its .js, .html and .css, listed in Landing/index.js; npx elemenx generate component Hero makes one. 3. The hero Its fields are its state: {{Title}} shows one, and a change of it changes the page. Its buttons call its methods; one of them asks the Toast Service for a toast. Elemenx.Component('Hero', { $TemplateURL: 'Hero.html', $StyleURL: 'Hero.css', Title: 'Notes that think with you', Text: 'Notely links your notes, finds what you forgot and works without the network.', Start: function () { document.getElementById('signup').scrollIntoView({behavior: 'smooth'}); }, Tour: function () { this.$Service('Toast').Show({Title: 'A tour is on its way', Message: 'Sign up and we send you the video.', Variant: 'info'}); } });
New · version 2

{{Title}}

{{Text}}

Suprematism draws a picture of its seed in the colors of the theme: a placeholder until the product has its own. 4. The features A list in the state, a card for each item with for; key keeps each card when the list changes.

Everything a note needs

{{item.Title}}

{{item.Text}}

[name]="item.Icon" binds a prop to an expression; Size="28" is a literal. 5. The prices PlanPicker draws the plans, switches the monthly and the yearly prices, and tells the plan chosen:

Simple prices

The Component keeps what was chosen: the picker shows what it is given, and its events ask for a change. Chosen: function (detail) { this.Plan = detail.ID; this.$Service('Toast').Show({Message: 'A good choice: the ' + detail.ID + ' plan.', Variant: 'success'}); }, Switched: function (detail) { this.Period = detail.Period; } 6. The form Form checks its Fields: Required, Email and the others are the rules of a field, their errors show once a field is left or the form is sent, and submit comes only when everything is valid, with the values by their Name.

Title: A blog
Text:
A blog of posts written in Markdown: the list of the posts, the posts of a tag, a post, and comments under it. The posts are files, so any static hosting serves the blog. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Blog. What you learn: the router (routes, parameters, links, a page not found), a Service that loads data, the Markdown component, the storage of the browser, and the title of the tab. 1. The routes npx elemenx generate application Blog The Application declares its router: a path of each route and its component. :tag and :id are parameters; a path no route has shows NotFound. Elemenx.Application('Blog', { $Title: 'Field notes', $Component: 'Layout', $Root: 'Blog', $Mount: 'body', $Use: ['ElemenxUI'], $Router: { NotFound: 'NotFound', Routes: [ {Path: '/', Component: 'PostList'}, {Path: '/tag/:tag', Component: 'PostList'}, {Path: '/post/:id', Component: 'PostPage'} ] } }); The root Component is the frame of every page; outlet="Content" is where the router puts the page of the route:
Field notes A blog of small experiments
The links are plain : the router takes a click on a link of the page, and the Back and Forward of the browser. 2. The data The posts are files of data/, copied into the build as they are: the list in data/posts.json, each post in data/posts/.md. [ {"ID": "grid-in-five-lines", "Title": "A grid in five lines of CSS", "Date": "2026-10-20", "Tags": ["css"], "ReadTime": 3, "Excerpt": "auto-fit and minmax do what a framework of grids did."} ] A Service loads them: one instance for the whole Application, so what it loaded once is there for every page. Its methods take a callback (error, result). Elemenx.Service('Posts', { $OnCreate: function () { this.Loaded = null; this.Texts = {}; }, / A file of data/ as a text. / Load: function (url, callback) { var request = this.$Network().XHR({URL: url, ResponseType: 'text'}); request.On('Transport.Success', function (event) { if (event.Data.Status === 200) callback(null, event.Data.Response); else callback(new Error('Not found: ' + url)); }); request.On('Transport.Error', function () { callback(new Error('The network failed: ' + url)); }); request.Execute(); }, List: function (callback) { var self = this; if (this.Loaded) { callback(null, this.Loaded); return; } this.Load('/data/posts.json', function (error, text) { if (error) { callback(error); return; } self.Loaded = JSON.parse(text); callback(null, self.Loaded); }); } }); Text(id, callback) loads a post the same way (see the project). 3. The list PostList is the component of two routes: / and /tag/:tag. The router gives it the parameters of its route as $Params, which its template reads; the function Shown takes them as an argument, so the list follows the route when the tag changes. Elemenx.Component('PostList', { $TemplateURL: 'PostList.html', $Title: 'Field notes', Posts: [], Loading: true, Failed: '', $OnCreate: function () { var self = this; this.Shown = function (posts, params) { return posts.filter(function (post) { return !params.tag || post.Tags.indexOf(params.tag) !== -1; }); }; this.$Service('Posts').List(function (error, posts) { self.Loading = false; self.Failed = error ? error.message : ''; self.Posts = posts || []; }); } });

{{$Params.tag ? '#' + $Params.tag : 'All posts'}}

{{Failed}}
A function a template calls is a method, or a helper set in $OnCreate (this.Shown = function ...) as here; the handlers of the events are found the same two ways. 4. A post The router keeps PostPage from one post to another (a link from a post to the next one): the component loads the post of the route when it is ready, and again when a navigation ends on another post. Elemenx.Component('PostPage', { $TemplateURL: 'PostPage.html', ID: '', Text: '', Failed: '', $OnReady: function () { var self = this; this.Open(); this.$Router().On('NavigationEnd', function () { if (self.$Params.id !== self.ID) self.Open(); }); }, Open: function () { var self = this; var id = this.$Params.id; this.ID = id; this.Text = ''; this.Failed = ''; this.$Service('Posts').Text(id, function (error, text) { if (id !== self.ID) return; if (error) { self.Failed = 'This post does not exist.'; return; } self.Text = text; self.$Title((/^# (.+)$/m.exec(text) || ['', id])[1] + ' · Field notes'); }); } });
← All posts
{{Failed}}
Markdown shows the text as HTML with its tables and its highlighted code, and runs nothing of it: a post cannot put a script into the page. $Title names the tab of the browser. 5. Comments The comments live in the storage of the browser, under a namespace of their own (a real blog sends them to its server): $OnCreate: function () { var store = this.$Storage.Local.Namespace('blog-comments'); this.Store = function () { return store; }; this.Items = store.Get(this.Post) || []; }, Add: function () { var text = this.Draft.trim(); if (!text) return; this.Items = this.Items.concat([{ID: Date.now(), Author: 'You', Text: text, Time: new Date().toISOString()}]); this.Draft = ''; this.Store().Set(this.Post, this.Items); } A new list replaces the old one (concat), so the template sees the change. The storage stays out of the state: Store() gives it to the methods, and Add, the handler of the button, is a method of the definition. 6. Build npm run build dist/ holds the pages, the framework and the posts. The router uses the paths of the URL (/post/grid-in-five-lines): the server answers every path with index.html, as elemenx serve does. On a hosting that cannot, the hash mode of the router keeps the route after # (see Router). Next - An admin panel: guards, tables and forms. - Languages: a blog in several languages.

Title: An admin panel
Text: The admin panel of a shop: a page to sign in, a dashboard of figures and a chart, and a table of users to sort, filter, page, edit and remove. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Admin. What you learn: a guard that sends a guest to the page to sign in and back, Services that hold the session and the data, a frame that follows the session, Table, Chart, Drawer, the dialogs and toasts of code, and a form that edits a record. 1. Routes behind a guard Elemenx.Application('Admin', { $Title: 'Shop admin', $Component: 'Shell', $Root: 'Admin', $Mount: 'body', $Use: ['ElemenxUI'], $Router: { Routes: [ {Path: '/login', Component: 'LoginPage'}, {Path: '/', Component: 'DashboardPage', Guard: 'SignedIn'}, {Path: '/users', Component: 'UsersPage', Guard: 'SignedIn'} ] } }); The guard lets a signed-in user in; anyone else goes to /login, with the page they asked for in the query: Elemenx.Guard('SignedIn', function () { if (this.$Service('Session').SignedIn()) return true; return '/login?return=' + encodeURIComponent(this.$To.Path); }); A path returned by a guard is a redirect. A guard can also refuse with this.$Fail(...) and show a component of its own, or wait for a server with this.$Wait(...) (see Guards). 2. The session A Service is one for the Application: every page asks the same Session. It keeps the user in the session storage of the tab and tells its listeners when it changes. Elemenx.Service('Session', { $OnCreate: function () { this.Store = this.$Storage.Session.Namespace('admin'); this.Listeners = []; }, User: function () { return this.Store.Get('user') || null; }, SignedIn: function () { return !!this.User(); }, SignIn: function (email, password, callback) { var self = this; / The server of a real panel checks them; here any password of 8 characters will do. / window.setTimeout(function () { if (String(password).length < 8) { callback(new Error('The email or the password is wrong.')); return; } self.Store.Set('user', {Email: email, Name: email.split('@')[0]}); self.Changed(); callback(null, self.User()); }, 300); } }); SignOut, OnChange, OffChange and Changed complete it (see the project). The Api Service holds the data the same way, and answers after a pause as a server would: a real panel makes its methods ask the server with this.$Network().XHR(...), and nothing else changes. 3. Sign in

Title: A shop
Text:
A small shop: a catalogue by category, the page of a product, a cart that every page shares and keeps after a reload, and a checkout with the fields of a payment card. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Shop. What you learn: state shared by the pages through a Service, a component for each item of a list, a badge on a button, a drawer, a guard that redirects, and the fields of phones and cards. 1. The routes Elemenx.Application('Shop', { $Title: 'Old Town Goods', $Component: 'Layout', $Root: 'Shop', $Mount: 'body', $Use: ['ElemenxUI'], $Router: { Routes: [ {Path: '/', Component: 'CatalogPage'}, {Path: '/product/:id', Component: 'ProductPage'}, {Path: '/checkout', Component: 'CheckoutPage', Guard: 'CartNotEmpty'} ] } }); The checkout wants something in the cart; an empty cart goes back to the catalogue: Elemenx.Guard('CartNotEmpty', function () { return this.$Service('Cart').Count() > 0 ? true : '/'; }); 2. The cart: one for every page A Service lives as long as the Application, one instance for all of it: the button in the header, the cards of the catalogue and the checkout all ask the same Cart. It keeps its lines in the storage of the browser, so they live on after a reload, and tells its listeners each change. Elemenx.Service('Cart', { $OnCreate: function () { this.Store = this.$Storage.Local.Namespace('shop'); this.Lines = this.Store.Get('cart') || []; this.Listeners = []; }, Add: function (product, color) { var line = this.Find(product.ID, color); if (line) line.Count++; else this.Lines.push({ID: product.ID, Title: product.Title, Price: product.Price, Color: color || '', Count: 1}); this.Changed(); }, Changed: function () { var self = this; this.Store.Set('cart', this.Lines); this.Listeners.slice().forEach(function (callback) { callback(self); }); } }); Remove, Find, Count, Total, Clear, OnChange and OffChange complete it (see the project). Catalog, the other Service, holds the products; a real shop loads them from its server. 3. The header and the cart drawer Layout reads the cart into its state and reads it again at each change; the button shows the count as a badge. $OnCreate: function () { var self = this; var cart = this.$Service('Cart'); this.Read = function () { self.Lines = cart.Lines.slice(); self.Count = cart.Count(); self.Total = cart.Total(); }; this.Money = function (value) { return '€' + Number(value).toFixed(2); }; this.Read(); cart.OnChange(this.Read); }, $OnDestroy: function () { this.$Service('Cart').OffChange(this.Read); }
Total {{Money(Total)}}
Lines is a copy (slice()): a new list each time, so the template sees the change. The handler of a native button gets the event and the element: Remove reads the line from its data- attributes. 4. A component for each product The handler of an event of a Component gets what the event carries (here {Color, Size} of the card), not the card. So each product gets a small Component of its own, which knows its product: Elemenx.Component('ProductTile', { $TemplateURL: 'ProductTile.html', Product: null, $OnCreate: function () { var catalog = this.$Service('Catalog'); this.Colors = function (product) { return catalog.Colors(product); }; }, Added: function (detail) { this.$Service('Cart').Add(this.Product, detail.Color || this.Product.Colors[0]); this.$Service('Toast').Show({Message: this.Product.Title + ' is in the cart.', Variant: 'success', Duration: 2500}); } }); The catalogue is then a list of them, filtered by the tab of a category:
5. The checkout The fields of a card are made for it: CardNumberInput finds the brand and checks the number by Luhn, and hides its middle once it is typed; CardExpiryInput refuses a date that is past; PhoneInput writes the number in the mask of its country.

Title: A media collection
Text:
A home collection of films, music and games: a home page with a featured title and shelves, a page for each kind with filters, and a page for each title with its tracks or its cast. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Collection. What you learn: the media components of ElemenxUI (MediaHero, MediaShelf, MediaCard, FacetFilter, TrackList, CastList), the parameters of a route, filters that count what they would leave, and favorites shared by the pages. 1. The routes Elemenx.Application('Collection', { $Title: 'Elemenx Collection', $Component: 'Layout', $Root: 'Collection', $Mount: 'body', $Use: ['ElemenxUI'], $Router: { Routes: [ {Path: '/', Component: 'HomePage'}, {Path: '/browse/:kind', Component: 'BrowsePage'}, {Path: '/title/:id', Component: 'TitlePage'} ] } }); 2. The titles: one Service Library holds the titles, each {ID, Kind, Title, Year, Genres, Score, Poster, Progress} and, by its kind, the Tracks of an album, the Cast of a film or a game, the Platforms of a game. It turns a title into an item of a shelf, and keeps the favorites in the storage of the browser: Item: function (title) { return {ID: title.ID, Title: title.Title, Subtitle: title.Year + ' · ' + title.Length, Image: title.Poster, Rating: title.Score, Progress: title.Progress, Tags: title.Genres, Href: '/title/' + title.ID}; }, Favorite: function (id, on) { this.Favorites = this.Favorites.filter(function (each) { return each !== id; }).concat(on ? [id] : []); this.Store.Set('favorites', this.Favorites); } A real collection loads its titles from a server; the posters of the project are drawn as SVG, so it fetches no picture. 3. The home page: a hero and shelves MediaHero is the head of the page: the backdrop, the poster, the facts, the score, the genres and the story, with the buttons to play and to keep. A title begun (Progress between 0 and 1) shows how much of it was seen, and its button says Resume. Each MediaShelf draws its items as cards in a row that scrolls across; open gives back the item pressed, more the link to all of them: Ratio gives each kind the shape of its picture: a poster, a cover, a frame of a game. 4. Browsing with facets FacetFilter takes the facets and the items. A facet without options takes them from the field of the items (an array of genres counts each genre), and each option tells how many items it would leave with the other facets as they are. filter gives the items left: Facets: function (kind) { var facets = [ {ID: 'genre', Label: 'Genre', Field: 'Genres'}, {ID: 'year', Label: 'Year', Field: 'Year', Type: 'range', Min: 2000, Max: 2025}, {ID: 'score', Label: 'Score', Field: 'Score', Type: 'rating', Max: 10} ]; if (this.Kind(kind).Kind === 'game') facets.splice(1, 0, {ID: 'platform', Label: 'Platform', Field: 'Platforms'}); return facets; }
The template gives its methods $Params.kind, the part of the path the route names: the same page shows films, music and games. 5. The page of a title An album lists its tracks: a press plays one, a press on the one playing pauses it. A film or a game lists its people, and every title ends with more of the same genre: The tracks here only change a state; the Audio Service of ElemenxUI, or a MediaPlayer, plays them for real. 6. Try it node elemenx-cli.js dev examples/Tutorials/Collection Open Music, check Jazz, open an album and press its first track; keep a title with the heart and reload the page: it is still kept.

Title: Widgets on another site
Text:
The shop of another site, which is not an Elemenx application, gets three widgets: the cart in its header, a button to buy under each product, and the reviews of a product. They are one Application, so they share one cart. The finished project is examples/Widgets. What you learn: a build of widgets, the places a page marks for them, the props they take from it, the events the page hears, and the isolation that keeps the styles of the page and of the widgets apart. 1. The project module.exports = { Application: 'Shop', Entry: 'app.js', Index: 'index.html', Output: 'dist', / One widget.js for the page of another site: the framework, ElemenxUI and the Application, isolated. / Widget: true }; npm run build makes dist/widget.js: the framework, ElemenxUI and the Application in one script, which gives the window no Elemenx of its own. 2. The Application and its widgets The Application has no root Component and no mount: the page decides where the widgets go. Elemenx.Widgets names them. Elemenx.Application('Shop', { $Root: 'Shop', $Use: ['ElemenxUI'] }); Elemenx.Widgets .Define('Cart', {Component: 'CartButton', Application: 'Shop', Events: ['checkout']}) .Define('AddToCart', {Component: 'AddToCart', Application: 'Shop', Events: ['added']}) .Define('Reviews', {Component: 'Reviews', Application: 'Shop'}); / Every place of the page, now and later. / Elemenx.Widgets.Watch(); / The code of the page reaches them too: ShopWidgets.Mount(element, 'Reviews', {Product: 'Lamp'}). / window.ShopWidgets = Elemenx.Widgets; 3. One cart for every widget The widgets are one Application: the Cart Service is one for all of them. The button of a product puts the product into it; the cart in the header listens to it. Elemenx.Component('AddToCart', { $TemplateURL: 'AddToCart.html', $StyleURL: 'AddToCart.css', Product: '', Price: 0, Currency: 'EUR', Taken: 0, $OnCreate: function () { var self = this; var cart = this.$Service('Cart'); this.Read = function () { self.Taken = cart.Items.filter(function (item) { return item.Product === self.Product; }).length; }; this.Read(); cart.OnChange(this.Read); }, $OnDestroy: function () { this.$Service('Cart').OffChange(this.Read); }, Added: function () { this.$Service('Cart').Add(this.Product, this.Price); this.$Emit('added', {Product: this.Product}); } }); $OnDestroy lets the listener go: a place removed from the page takes its widget away, and the cart must not call a widget that is gone. 4. The page The page of the other site loads widget.js once, in its head, and marks the places; data-props gives each widget its props as JSON:

Old Town Goods

Brass lamp

A place added later (a product loaded by the page) gets its widget at once; a place removed loses it. The events named in Events bubble from the place as DOM events: document.addEventListener('added', function (event) { console.log('added', event.detail.Product); }); 5. Isolation Each widget renders in a shadow root of its place. The page of the example has rules that would break any button (button { text-transform: uppercase; border-radius: 0 }): the buttons of the widgets keep their look, and the styles of the widgets do not reach the page. A page with an Elemenx of its own, of any version, keeps it: the widget runs its own copy. 6. Try it npm run dev The development page of the project is the shop with the widgets in their places; npm run build and npm run serve serve dist/, the page and widget.js as another site would load it. Next - Widgets on other sites: every option of Elemenx.Widgets. - A shop: the same cart in an Application of its own.

Title: A chat
Text:
A chat of rooms: a name to write under, the rooms in a sidebar, the messages, a composer with emoji, and a bot in one of the rooms. The messages reach the other tabs of the browser at once, without a server. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Chat. What you learn: the Chat layout and its parts, Elemenx.Messaging between tabs, a Service that tells its listeners, and how the same code talks to a server through a WebSocket. 1. The layout Chat is the frame: a sidebar, a header, the messages and the composer in its slots. The list of messages follows the new ones while the reader is at its end, and stays in place while the reader scrolls back.
Rooms
#{{Room}}
Position tells a message where it stands in a run of one author (first, middle, last, single): the name shows on the first message of a run and the avatar on the last, as in a messenger. $index is the place of the item in its for. 2. The rooms and their messages A Service holds them: it keeps them in the storage of the browser, sends each new one to the other tabs, and tells its listeners. Elemenx.Service('Rooms', { $OnCreate: function () { var self = this; this.Store = this.$Storage.Local.Namespace('talk'); this.Listeners = []; this.Seen = {}; this.Socket = this.$Messaging(); / A message of another tab: kept by that tab already, told to the listeners of this one. / this.Socket.On('talk:message', function (message) { self.Told(message.Data); }); }, Messages: function (room) { return this.Store.Get(room) || []; }, Send: function (room, author, text) { var message = {ID: Date.now() + '-' + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 6), Room: room, Author: author, Text: text, Time: new Date().toISOString()}; this.Store.Set(room, this.Messages(room).concat([message]).slice(-50)); this.Socket.Send('talk:message', message); this.Told(message); if (room === 'help') this.Bot(text); }, / Each message once: the socket of this tab may hear its own messages too. / Told: function (message) { if (this.Seen[message.ID]) return; this.Seen[message.ID] = true; this.Listeners.slice().forEach(function (callback) { callback(message); }); } }); this.$Messaging() is a socket of the Service: Send reaches every socket that listens to the channel, in this tab and in the others (a BroadcastChannel joins the tabs of a site), in its frames and in its workers. OnMessage, OffMessage and the bot complete it (see the project). 3. The component listens $OnCreate: function () { var self = this; var rooms = this.$Service('Rooms'); this.Rooms = rooms.List; this.Messages = rooms.Messages(this.Room); this.Heard = function (message) { if (message.Room === self.Room) self.Messages = self.Messages.concat([message]); }; rooms.OnMessage(this.Heard); }, $OnDestroy: function () { this.$Service('Rooms').OffMessage(this.Heard); }, Sent: function (text) { this.$Service('Rooms').Send(this.Room, this.Name, text); } The composer sends with Enter (Shift+Enter is a new line), grows with its text, and offers emoji for the word at the caret. 4. A server Between tabs is a demo; between people the messages go through a server. The Service changes, and nothing else: a WebSocket in place of the socket of Messaging. $OnCreate: function () { var self = this; this.Listeners = []; this.Seen = {}; this.Socket = this.$Network().WebSocket({URL: 'wss://chat.example.com/'}); this.Socket.On('Transport.Data', function (event) { self.Told(JSON.parse(event.Data.Data)); }); / A WebSocket does not reconnect by itself: again, a moment after it closed. / this.Socket.On('Transport.Close', function () { window.setTimeout(function () { self.Socket.Connect(); }, 2000); }); this.Socket.Connect(); } Send then writes this.Socket.Send(JSON.stringify(message)), which returns false while the socket is closed or full (see WebSocket; a Protocol can encode and decode the messages for you). Next - A call with video: CallStage, CallTile and CallControls of ElemenxUI, and WebRTC. - Messaging: frames, windows and workers.

Title: An application that works offline
Text:
Notes that the user installs from the browser as an application of the system, that run without the network, and that update when the user says so (a PWA). The finished project is examples/PWA. What you learn: the PWA of elemenx.config.js, the service worker a build makes, Elemenx.Install (the prompt to install, the state, the updates), and data kept on the device. 1. The build makes the PWA module.exports = { Application: 'PWA', Entry: 'app.js', Index: 'index.html', Output: 'dist', / The icon of the Application: the page, and the icons of the installed application (192 and 512 pixels). / Icon: '/icons/app.png', PWA: { Name: 'Elemenx notes', ShortName: 'Notes', Description: 'Notes that work without the network: an installable Elemenx application.', Theme: '#2f4fd8', Background: '#f4f5f7', Update: 'prompt' } }; npm run build writes the manifest, the icons of every size from Icon, and a service worker that keeps the files of the build: once the page has loaded, it runs without the network. Nothing of it is written by hand. Update decides what a new build does: auto takes it for the next start, prompt waits until the Application applies it (checked at the start and every hour), manual waits and checks only when asked. 2. The state of the installation Elemenx.Install.State() is {Available, Installed, Manual, Waiting, Version}; OnChange tells each change. The component keeps it in its state, so the template follows: $OnCreate: function () { var self = this; this.Store = this.$Storage.Local.Namespace('ElemenxNotes'); this.Notes = this.Store.Get('Notes') || []; this.Online = navigator.onLine !== false; this.Install = Elemenx.Install.State(); this.Heard = function (state) { self.Install = state; }; this.Network = function () { self.Online = navigator.onLine !== false; }; Elemenx.Install.OnChange(this.Heard); window.addEventListener('online', this.Network); window.addEventListener('offline', this.Network); }, $OnDestroy: function () { Elemenx.Install.OffChange(this.Heard); window.removeEventListener('online', this.Network); window.removeEventListener('offline', this.Network); }
Network{{Online ? 'online' : 'offline'}}
Build{{Install.Version || 'not kept yet'}}
Application{{Install.Installed ? 'installed' : Install.Available ? 'can be installed' : Install.Manual ? 'Share, Add to Home Screen' : 'in the browser'}}
3. The button that installs The browser offers to install the page by itself; Elemenx.Install keeps that prompt so the Application shows it when it wants, from its own button: Installed: function () { var self = this; Elemenx.Install.Prompt(function (error, result) { self.Said = error ? error.message : result.Outcome === 'accepted' ? 'Installed.' : 'Not now.'; }); } On a system that installs only by its own menu (Safari on iOS: Share, Add to Home Screen), Manual is true: the page tells the user how. 4. Updates when the user says Checked: function () { var self = this; this.Busy = true; this.Said = 'Checking...'; Elemenx.Install.Update(function (error, result) { self.Busy = false; if (error) self.Said = error.message; else self.Said = result.Available ? 'A new build is ready: ' + result.Version + '.' : 'This is the newest build.'; }); }, Updated: function () { var self = this; this.Said = 'Updating...'; Elemenx.Install.Apply(function (error) { self.Said = error.message; }); } Apply takes the new build at once: every page of the application reloads with it. Its callback is called only when it cannot. 5. Data on the device The notes are in the storage of the browser (this.$Storage.Local), on the device: they are there without the network. A larger application keeps them in IndexedDB (see IndexedDB) and sends them to its server when the network comes back. 6. Try it npm run build npm run serve Open the page, then turn the network off in the developer tools of the browser and reload: the notes are still there. Build again with a change and press Check for updates. Next - Builds: every option of PWA. - A desktop program: the same Application as a program of Windows, macOS and Linux.

Title: A desktop program
Text: The same Application as a program of Windows, macOS and Linux, with Electron: its own title bar and menu, the tray, notifications, the dialogs to open and save files, and an installer. The finished project is examples/Native. What you learn: Native.Desktop of elemenx.config.js, the Platform Service of ElemenxUI (the system from the page), TitleBar and NativeMenu, and the builds of a program. 1. Electron in the project npx elemenx native add desktop It installs Electron and its packager into the project, once (Elemenx carries neither: Electron is about 100 MB, and the project picks its version). elemenx dev still runs the Application in a browser, where the Platform Service does what the web can. 2. The program module.exports = { Application: 'Native', Entry: 'app.js', Index: 'index.html', Output: 'dist', / The icon of the Application everywhere: the page, the program, its installer, the phones. / Icon: '/icons/app.png', / The splash of its page: shown until the Application is ready, in the window and on the phone too. / Splash: {Image: '/icons/tray.png', Text: 'Elemenx native', Background: '#1e1f22', Color: '#dfe1e5', MinTime: 600}, Native: { Desktop: { Name: 'Elemenx native', Width: 960, Height: 640, Frame: 'hidden', CloseToTray: true, Tasks: [ {ID: 'compose', Label: 'New note', Description: 'Write a new note'}, {ID: 'inbox', Label: 'Inbox'} ], Targets: ['zip', 'installer', 'portable'] } } }; Frame: 'hidden' keeps the buttons of the system over a title bar the Application draws; CloseToTray hides the window in the tray when it closes; Tasks are the items of its jump list; Targets the files a build makes. 3. The title bar and the menu TitleBar is the bar the user moves the window by; NativeMenu declares the menu of the program as a menu of the page. A MenuItem with a Role does what the system does (undo, copy, quit...); a Shortcut is a hotkey of the program. <TitleBar Title="Elemenx native" Image="/icons/app.png"> <NativeMenu (select)="MenuChosen" (apply)="MenuApplied"> <MenuItem [label]="$T('native.menu.file')"> <MenuItem ID="note" [label]="$T('native.menu.newNote')" Shortcut="Mod+N" /> <MenuItem ID="open" [label]="$T('native.menu.open')" Shortcut="Mod+O" /> <MenuItem ID="save" [label]="$T('native.menu.save')" Shortcut="Mod+S" /> <MenuItem Separator="true" /> <MenuItem [label]="$T('native.menu.quit')" Role="quit" /> </MenuItem> <MenuItem [label]="$T('native.menu.edit')"> <MenuItem [label]="$T('native.menu.undo')" Role="undo" /> <MenuItem [label]="$T('native.menu.copy')" Role="copy" /> <MenuItem [label]="$T('native.menu.paste')" Role="paste" /> </MenuItem> </NativeMenu> </TitleBar> <NativeMenu Target="tray" (select)="MenuChosen"> <MenuItem ID="show" [label]="$T('native.menu.show')" /> <MenuItem [label]="$T('native.menu.quit')" Role="quit" /> </NativeMenu> On the web the menu is a MenuBar of the page without the items of the system, and the menu of the tray shows nothing. 4. The system from the page The window runs no Node: the page asks the system through the Platform Service, as a callback (error, result): Opened: function () { var self = this; this.$Service('Platform').Open({Accept: ['.txt', '.md', '.json'], Read: 'text'}, function (error, files) { if (error) { self.Said('Open: error, ' + error.message); return; } self.Said('Open: ' + files.map(function (file) { return file.Name + ' (' + file.Size + ' bytes)'; }).join(', ') || 'nothing'); }); }, Saved: function () { this.$Service('Platform').Save({Name: 'elemenx.txt', Text: 'Saved by Elemenx at ' + new Date().toISOString() + '\n'}, this.Answer('Save')); } Said and Answer are helpers of the example that show the result. Platform() tells where the Application runs (electron, capacitor or web), and Has(feature) whether the system can do a thing (tray, notifications, taskbar, hotkeys...): a button of a feature the system lacks can hide. In a browser the same calls do what the web can: a file input, a download, a notification of the browser. 5. Build npx elemenx build --native desktop dist/native/desktop-bin is the program for this system, and dist/native/desktop-dist its zip, its installer and its portable program. Native.Desktop.Platform and Arch build for another system. Next - A mobile application: the same project on Android and iOS. - Builds: every option of Native.Desktop.

Title: A mobile application
Text: The same project as the programs of Android and iOS, with Capacitor: the Application in a native window of the phone, its icon and splash screen, and the features of the phone through the same Platform Service. The finished project is examples/Native. What you learn: Native.Mobile of elemenx.config.js, the Capacitor project the build makes, and how one Application reads the phone, the desktop and the web. 1. Capacitor in the project npx elemenx native add mobile It installs Capacitor and its platforms into the project, once. To build the programs you need Android Studio (Android) and Xcode on a Mac (iOS). 2. The program of the phone Native: { Mobile: { AppID: 'dev.elemenx.nativeexample', Name: 'Elemenx native' } } AppID is the identity of the program in the stores; Icon and Splash of elemenx.config.js become its icon and its splash screen, of every size the platforms want. 3. One Application, three places The Platform Service tells where it runs, and what the system can do: $OnCreate: function () { var native = this.$Service('Platform'); this.Platform = native.Platform(); this.Features = ['dialogs', 'notifications', 'external', 'tray', 'taskbar'].filter(function (feature) { return native.Has(feature); }); } A layout made of ElemenxUI follows the screen already: on a narrow screen a Menu or a ContextMenu with Sheet="auto" opens as a sheet from the bottom, a Workspace puts its panels over the main area, and Swipe (swipe) takes the gestures of a finger. 4. Build and run npx elemenx build --native mobile The build writes the Application into dist/native/mobile, adds the platforms installed, and copies the Application into them. Then: npx cap open android Android Studio opens the project, and runs it on a phone or an emulator; npx cap open ios opens Xcode. npm run android of the example builds and runs it on Android in one step. A program of Android of your own An existing program in Java or Kotlin can show an Elemenx Application without Capacitor: elemenx build --native android-library makes a module of Gradle with ElemenxView (see Builds). Next - A desktop program. - An application that works offline: installed from the browser, no store.

Title: A browser game
Text:
A small game: a hero on a map looks for five gems, round the water and the rocks; the HUD counts them, a menu starts and pauses the game, and an achievement comes with the last gem. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Game. What you learn: GameWorld and the things declared in it, its events and its methods, a HUD over it, GameMenu, the Achievements Service, and the keys and the gamepad. 1. The world GameWorld draws a map of cells on a canvas and walks its units round what blocks them. Its map is declared inside it: a GameLayer of rows of text (a character a kind of ground: . grass, ~ water, = a ford, ^ hills, T a forest, # rock), the units, the buildings and the things.
Gems
{{Target ? 'Going to ' + Target : 'Press a cell: the hero goes there'}} · Escape pauses
Rows: [ '..........~~........', '..TT......~~....^^..', '..TT......=~........', '..........~~...##...', '....##....~~...##...', '....##..............', '..........~~....TT..', '..........~~....TT..' ] The gems are a list of the state: a gem taken out of the list leaves the map. The hud slot is drawn over the world. Projection="orthogonal" shows the map from above; isometric at an angle, as many strategy games do (without it, the projection of the map). 2. Orders and arrivals The world tells a press on a cell (cell, {X, Y, Button, Object}) and a unit at the end of its way (arrive, {ID, X, Y}). ready gives the world itself, whose methods give orders: Order(ids, target) sends units, Change(id, changes) moves one at once. $OnCreate: function () { / The world, once it is ready: its methods (Order, Change, CenterOn...). It stays out of the state. / var world = null; this.World = function (instance) { if (instance) world = instance; return world; }; }, Ready: function (world) { this.World(world); }, / A cell pressed: the hero goes there, round what blocks the way. / Pressed: function (detail) { if (this.Menu || !this.World()) return; this.Target = detail.X + ', ' + detail.Y; this.World().Order(['hero'], {X: detail.X, Y: detail.Y}); } The world is kept in a variable of $OnCreate, not in a field: the state holds data, and a field holding a component would be watched for nothing. World() gives it to the methods. The handlers of the events (Ready, Pressed) are methods of the definition: the template binds them as it renders, before $OnCreate could add any. Arrived: function (detail) { var found = this.Gems.filter(function (gem) { return gem.X === detail.X && gem.Y === detail.Y; })[0]; if (!found) return; this.Gems = this.Gems.filter(function (gem) { return gem !== found; }); this.Found++; if (!this.Gems.length) { this.$Service('Achievements').Show({Title: 'Gem hunter', Text: 'All five gems found.', Rarity: 'epic', Points: 50, Icon: 'trophy'}); this.Started = false; this.Menu = true; } } 3. The menu and the pause
Paused of the world stops its units while the menu is open; Escape opens it, a listener of the document that $OnDestroy takes away. AchievementHost shows the achievements of the Service, one at a time, as a console does. 4. A gamepad Nothing to add: the Gamepad Service makes a pad work the page as the keyboard does. The d-pad moves the focus between the items of the menu, A presses, B is Escape. GameMenu takes the arrows; a game of its own hears the buttons with this.$Service('Gamepad').On('button', ...). 5. More - A larger world: buildings, teams, the fog of war (Fog), a minimap (Minimap), a map of Tiled (Map="maps/level.tmj", see the GameMaps Service). - The loop of a game of your own, at a fixed step whatever the screen: the GameLoop Service. - The inventory, the quests, the dialogues: GameInventory, GameQuests, GameDialogue. Next - GameWorld in the reference of the Library. - An application that works offline: a game installed, playable without the network.

Title: An editor in the manner of an IDE
Text: An editor of code: the files of a project in a tree, each open file in a tab over a code editor, a terminal under them, a palette of commands, and panels that resize and remember their size. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Editor. What you learn: the frame of Workspace and its tool windows, Tree, Tabs, CodeEditor, Terminal, CommandPalette and a hotkey, and drafts kept apart from the saved files. 1. The frame Workspace places what its slots hold: a toolbar on top, tool windows on the left, the right and the bottom, the main area, and a status bar. The edge of a panel resizes it; Persist remembers the sizes in the browser. Studio

Title: Elemenx on the pages of a server
Text: A site of PHP, Django, Rails or any other server renders its pages itself. Elemenx can take one part of such a page and make it interactive, with no build and no change to the rest: here a table of orders that filters and sorts, and a form that posts to the server. The finished page is examples/Tutorials/Backend/index.html. What you learn: Elemenx from one script, a Component defined in the page with a template of the page, data the server writes into the page, an Application mounted into one element, and a request to the server. 1. One script elemenx.all.min.js is the framework and ElemenxUI: their components, styles and icons come with it. (The example takes /elemenx.js from the server of the project, which serves the sources of the repository.) 2. The data of the page The server knows the data when it renders the page: it writes them into the page as JSON, and the Application reads them without a request. A template of the server writes it the way it writes any text, escaped for the page (jsonencode in PHP, jsonscript in Django). 3. The template in the page The Component takes its template from a A script of type text/html is neither run nor shown: Elemenx renders its template where the Application mounts. The servers of Elemenx write a

Title: Forms and validation
Text: A form to sign up, as a real service has it: the rules of each field, a rule of the whole form, a name the server checks while it is typed, a list that grows, and the errors only the server knows. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Signup. What you learn: a model of a form made in code with the Forms Service, validators of a field, of a group and async ones, the errors of a field and when they show, a list of fields, and the answer of a server shown on the field it is about. 1. Two ways, one model A short form needs no code: a Form makes its model of its Fields (Required, Email, MinLength, Match...), as in the guide on forms. Once a form has rules of its own, a server to ask or a list of fields, make the model in code and hand it to the Form: the template stays the same, the logic moves to the component. 2. The model $OnCreate: function () { var forms = this.$Service('Forms'); var rules = forms.Validators; this.Account = forms.Group({ Name: forms.Control('', {Validators: [rules.Required, rules.MinLength(3), rules.Pattern('[A-Za-z0-9]+')], Async: [free]}), Email: forms.Control('', [rules.Required, rules.Email]), Password: forms.Control('', [rules.Required, rules.MinLength(8), digit]), Repeat: forms.Control('', [rules.Required]), Phones: forms.Array([forms.Control('', [rules.Pattern('\\+?[0-9 ]{6,}')])]), Terms: forms.Control(false, [rules.RequiredTrue]) }, [rules.Equal('Password', 'Repeat')]); } - A Control is one value and its validators. - A Group is a set of named nodes; its own validators see all of them: Equal('Password', 'Repeat') is a rule of two fields, so it belongs to the group. - An Array is a list of nodes: the phones. The model is a plain object in the state of the component: its Value, Valid, Status (valid, invalid, pending) and the Errors of each node render as they change. 3. Validators of your own A validator is a function: the control in, null or the errors out. An error may carry its own text: function digit (control) { return !control.Value || /[0-9]/.test(control.Value) ? null : {digit: 'Add a digit'}; } Leave the empty value to Required: a rule that also fails on an empty field shows two errors for one cause. 4. Asking the server An async validator takes a callback. While it runs, the control is pending (the form waits for it on submit), and only the answer for the present value counts, so an old answer that comes late changes nothing: function free (control, callback) { var name = control.Value; window.setTimeout(function () { if (control.Value !== name) { callback(null); return; } accounts.IsFree(name, function (error, isFree) { if (error) callback({network: 'The name could not be checked'}); else callback(isFree ? null : {taken: 'This name is taken'}); }); }, 250); } The pause asks the server once the name stays the same for a moment, not at each key. Async validators run only once the others pass: a name of two letters is not sent. The server of the project is a few lines of elemenx.config.js, Server.Request: elemenx dev and elemenx serve answer /api/... with it. A real project asks its own server; the Accounts Service is the only place that knows the URLs. 5. The template

Title: A live dashboard
Text:
The numbers of a shop as they happen: the visitors on the site, the orders and the revenue, a chart of the last minute and the newest orders, streamed by the server. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Dashboard. What you learn: server-sent events with Network.SSE, a Protocol that turns the text of the stream into typed messages, a Service that owns the connection, reconnection and resuming without losing or repeating a message, and pausing a stream nobody looks at. 1. Why SSE The numbers go one way, from the server. Server-sent events are made for that: an ordinary HTTP response the server keeps open and writes into, which the browser reconnects by itself when it breaks. A WebSocket is for messages both ways (a chat, a game); asking every few seconds wastes requests and still comes late. 2.
