The server A stream is a response of type text/event-stream with messages separated by a blank line. Each one has an id: when the connection breaks, the browser sends the last one back (Last-Event-ID), and the server goes on from there. The project streams from Server.Request of its elemenx.config.js, which elemenx dev and elemenx serve call for every request: Request: function (request, response, pathname) { var id; var timer; if (pathname !== '/api/stream') return false; id = Number(request.headers['last-event-id'] || new URL(request.url, 'http://localhost').searchParams.get('after')) || 0; response.writeHead(200, {'Content-Type': 'text/event-stream', 'Cache-Control': 'no-cache', Connection: 'keep-alive'}); response.write('retry: 1000 '); function send () { id += 1; response.write('id: ' + id + ' data: ' + JSON.stringify(tick(id)) + ' '); } send(); timer = setInterval(send, 1000); request.on('close', function () { clearInterval(timer); }); return true; } retry tells the browser how long to wait before it reconnects. Stop the timer when the request closes: a stream left writing into a closed socket is a leak of the server. Any server does the same: Express, PHP, Go, a proxy in front of them that must not buffer the response. 3. A Protocol The data of a message is text. A Protocol decodes it once, so the rest of the code hears typed messages instead of parsing text everywhere: Elemenx.Network.Protocol('Shop', { Decode: function (text) { try { return {Type: 'Tick', Data: JSON.parse(text)}; } catch (error) { return {Type: 'Invalid', Data: text}; } } }); A resource with Protocol: 'Shop' emits Protocol.Tick with the object, and Protocol.Invalid for a message it cannot read. A server that sends several kinds names them in the JSON ({"Type": "Order", ...}), and the Protocol returns that Type: Protocol.Order, Protocol.Price. 4. A Service owns the connection The connection belongs to a Service, not to a component: one stream for the whole application, whatever shows its numbers, and its state in one place. Open: function () { var self = this; if (this.Stream) return; this.Stream = this.$Network().SSE({URL: '/api/stream' + (this.Last ? '?after=' + this.Last : ''), Protocol: 'Shop'}); this.Stream.On('Transport.Open', function () { self.Tell('live'); }); this.Stream.On('Transport.Error', function (event) { self.Tell(event.Data.ReadyState === 0 ? 'reconnecting' : 'paused'); }); this.Stream.On('Protocol.Tick', function (event) { self.Take(event.Data); }); this.State = 'connecting'; this.Stream.Connect(); this.Tell(this.State); } - Transport.Error with ReadyState 0 means the browser is reconnecting by itself: show it, do nothing else. 2 means it gave up. - Take(tick) keeps the last minute of points (slice(-60), so the memory does not grow for hours), the five newest orders, and their count and sum. - Tell(state) calls the listeners of the Service (OnChange), as in the other tutorials. 5. Resuming without gaps The browser sends Last-Event-ID only when it reconnects the same EventSource. A new one, after a pause, starts from nothing, so the server would send the first ticks again: the same order twice in the list. The Service remembers the last ID it took and names it in the URL of a new stream (?after=); the server reads both. The end-to-end test of the project pauses and resumes the stream, and checks that no order comes twice: it failed before this line was written. 6. Nobody looks, nothing streams A tab in the background needs no numbers. The Service closes the stream when the page is hidden and opens it again, from the last tick, when it shows: document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', function () { if (!self.Wanted) return; if (document.hidden) self.Close('paused'); else self.Open(); }); Wanted keeps a stream the person paused paused when the tab comes back. The server keeps fewer connections open, and a phone saves its battery. 7. The component The component copies what it shows at each change of the Service: Show: function (live) { var last = live.Points[live.Points.length - 1]; this.State = live.State; this.Visitors = last ? last.Visitors : 0; this.Orders = live.Orders; this.Revenue = live.Revenue; this.Recent = live.Recent; this.Labels = live.Points.map(function (point) { return new Date(point.Time).toLocaleTimeString(); }); this.Values = live.Points.map(function (point) { return point.Visitors; }); } {{States[State]}}
  • #{{order.ID}} · {{order.Customer}}{{Money(order.Amount)}}
- role="status" reads a change of the state to a screen reader; aria-live="polite" the new orders, without interrupting. - key="order.ID" keeps the rows of the orders already there: a new one is added on top, the rest are not built again. - Min="0" holds the bottom of the chart, so the area does not jump as the numbers move. - The $OnDestroy of the component takes its listener away and pauses the stream. 8. Try it cd examples/Tutorials/Dashboard npm install npm run dev Stop the server for a few seconds and start it again: the badge says Reconnecting, then Live, and the numbers go on from where they stopped.

Title: A board of live telemetry
Text: A board of live telemetry: a race car, a server cluster or a spaceship, each a scene of 36 to 60 channels, their values coming over a WebSocket from 1 to 120 times a second. The board draws them on dials, bars, numbers, sparklines, signals and lamps, keeps a log of the alarms, and tells its own frames, packets and updates a second. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Telemetry. What you learn: a WebSocket of the server of the CLI, a Protocol of JSON, and the rules of a board that keeps up with a fast feed: the packets stay out of the state, the state changes once a frame, the buffers have a fixed length. 1. The feed of the server Server.WebSocket of elemenx.config.js is the feed, for elemenx dev and elemenx serve. A connection gets the channels of its scene, then their values at its rate. The packets go by the clock, not by the interval of the timer: a timer of the system may tick every 15 milliseconds or so, and 20 packets a second would be 16. function start (connection) { var began = Date.now(); var sent = 0; clearInterval(connection.Timer); connection.Timer = setInterval(function () { var due = Math.floor((Date.now() - began) connection.Hz / 1000); while (sent < due) { packet(connection); sent++; } }, 5); } The browser asks for another scene ({Type: 'scene', Scene}) and another rate ({Type: 'rate', Hz}). 2. The packets stay out of the state The Feed Service receives the packets. A Service is not reactive state: a packet lands in a plain field and costs an assignment, not a render, however many come. this.Socket.On('Protocol.data', function (event) { self.Latest = event.Data; self.Seq = event.Data.Seq; self.Received++; }); 3. The state changes once a frame The board reads the latest packet in a requestAnimationFrame loop. Many packets between two frames cost one render, and every binding of the board reads the same Values: function frame (now) { own.Frames++; if (!self.Paused && feed.Latest && feed.Seq !== own.Seq) self.Draw(feed.Latest); own.Frame = window.requestAnimationFrame(frame); } Draw builds the new values first, outside of the state, then gives them to it in one assignment each. The histories of the sparklines are buffers of 90 values, and the log keeps its last 30 lines: history.push(value); if (history.length > 90) history.shift(); series[item.ID] = history.slice(); this.Values = packet.Values; this.Series = series; this.Lit = lit; One more rule keeps a busy computer in step: a frame with an update lasts its script and the layout and the painting that follow, and what it took past a frame the next update waits. The board takes half of the time of the page at most; on a slow processor it skips frames and stays close to the feed, instead of filling every frame and letting the packets queue behind it. A frame of more than a second is the page held up, not the board: the update after it waits a second at most. 4. A widget for each kind The template draws each channel by its kind: <Meter if="item.Kind === 'dial'" Shape="dial" Needle="true" [value]="Math.round(Values[item.ID] || item.Min)" [min]="item.Min" [max]="item.Max" [high]="item.Alarm" [label]="item.Label" [unit]="item.Unit" ShowValue="true" Size="small" /> <Meter if="item.Kind === 'bar'" [value]="Values[item.ID] || item.Min" [min]="item.Min" [max]="item.Max" [high]="item.Alarm" [label]="item.Label" [unit]="item.Unit" ShowValue="true" Size="small" /> <Sparkline if="item.Kind === 'spark'" [values]="Series[item.ID] || []" Type="area" Width="160" Height="36" [min]="item.Min" [max]="item.Max" Dot="true" /> <Signal if="item.Kind === 'signal'" [value]="Values[item.ID] || 0" Bars="4" /> A scene gives the board a theme of its own, whatever the page shows: this.$Service('Theme').Scope(this.$Element(), 'scifi'). 5. What it costs The header tells the frames the page draws a second (FPS), the packets it receives and the updates it shows. At 20 packets a second every packet is shown and the page keeps its frames; at 120 the updates follow the frames (about 60), the packets between them merged. The dials, bars and lines of a scene take a few milliseconds to update on a desktop computer: the budget of a frame is 16. 6. Try it node elemenx-cli.js dev examples/Tutorials/Telemetry Move the rate to 120, switch to the cluster (60 channels) and watch the FPS; pause the board and the packets go on, counted.

Title: Working offline: sync
Text: Notes that work the same with a network and without: written to the browser first, sent to the server when it can be reached, taken from the server on another device. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Notes. What you learn: local-first data with IndexedDB, an outbox of changes written in the same transaction as the data, a sync that sends and then takes, deletions as marks, the newest change winning a conflict, and a state a person can trust. The PWA tutorial makes the page itself open without a network; this one keeps the data working. A real offline application needs both. 1. The idea: the browser first An application that asks the server for every change stops when the train enters a tunnel. Turn it around: every change is written to the database of the browser at once, and the page shows what is there. The server is a copy that catches up when it can. change ──► IndexedDB: Notes + Outbox (one transaction) ──► the page shows it │ online? ──► POST the outbox ──► remove what was sent ──► GET what changed since the last version 2. The database this.Database = Elemenx.Storage.IndexedDB('Notes', { Version: 1, Stores: { Notes: {KeyPath: 'ID'}, Outbox: {KeyPath: 'Seq', AutoIncrement: true}, State: {} } }); - Notes: the notes, by an ID the browser makes, so a note made offline has its key before the server knows it. - Outbox: the changes not yet sent, numbered in their order. - State: the version of the server at the last sync. 3. A change: both or neither Save: function (note) { var self = this; var change = {ID: note.ID || Date.now().toString(36) + Math.random().toString(36).substring(2, 8), Text: note.Text || '', Updated: Date.now(), Deleted: !!note.Deleted}; this.Database.Transaction(['Notes', 'Outbox'], 'readwrite', function (transaction) { transaction.Store('Notes').Put(undefined, change); transaction.Store('Outbox').Put(undefined, change); }).On('Success', function () { self.Load(function () { self.Sync(); }); }).Execute(); return change.ID; } The transaction writes the note and its place in the outbox together: a tab closed in the middle cannot leave a note that will never be sent. A deletion is a change too (Deleted: true): a note simply removed here would never be removed on the server or on the other devices. 4. The sync Sync: function () { if (this.Busy) { this.Again = true; return; } if (!navigator.onLine) { this.Tell(); return; } this.Busy = true; / Send the outbox, remove from it what was sent, then Pull() what changed on the server. / } - One sync at a time: a change made while one runs asks for another (Again) instead of starting a second. - Only what was sent leaves the outbox, by its Seq: a change made during the request waits for the next sync instead of being lost. - Pull() asks for the notes changed after the version of the last sync (?since=), writes them and the new version in one transaction, and keeps a note changed here since: its newer text is in the outbox and goes up next. The sync starts when the Service starts, after each change, when the browser comes back online (the online event), and every ten seconds while changes wait (a server that failed is asked again). 5. Conflicts Two devices change the same note offline; whose text stays? The project keeps the newest one: each change has its Updated time, and the server refuses an older change than the one it has. It is the simplest rule and fits notes; a shared document needs more (merging the texts, or keeping both and asking). Choose the rule for your data, write it on the server, and test it. 6. A state to trust The person must know whether the notes are safe. The Service gives one state: if (!navigator.onLine) this.Status = 'offline'; else if (this.Busy) this.Status = 'syncing'; else if (this.Failed) this.Status = 'error'; else if (this.Pending) this.Status = 'pending'; else this.Status = 'synced'; and the page says it in words, with the count of the changes waiting: Offline · 2 waiting, then Synced. role="status" reads it to a screen reader as it changes. 7. The test The end-to-end test of the project goes offline with context.setOffline(true), adds a note and edits another, checks Offline · 2 waiting, goes back online and waits for Synced, asks the server what it has, deletes a note, and opens the page in a new browser with an empty database, where the notes come from the server. 8. Try it cd examples/Tutorials/Notes npm install npm run dev In the developer tools, Network, choose Offline: write, edit and delete notes, then go back online and watch them go up.

Title: Signing in
Text: Signing in as a real application does it: a password checked by the server, a short access token kept in memory, a refresh token in a cookie the page cannot read, a session that survives a reload, a token renewed by itself when it expires, and pages closed to guests. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Auth; the user is ada@example.com with the password correct horse 7. What you learn: access and refresh tokens and where each one lives, a JWT signed and checked on the server, rotation of the refresh token, a guard that waits for the session, a request that renews its token, a safe return after signing in, and what OAuth adds. 1. Two tokens sign in ──► server: password ok ──► access token (JSON, 5 minutes) ──► memory of the page └─► refresh token (30 days) ──► cookie: HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Path=/api/auth a request ──► Authorization: Bearer <access token> 401 ──► POST /api/auth/refresh (the cookie goes by itself) ──► a new access token and a new refresh token - The access token goes with every request. It is short-lived: a stolen one is worth minutes. It lives in a variable of the Session Service, not in localStorage, where any script injected into the page (a bad dependency, an XSS) would read it. - The refresh token only buys new access tokens. It lives in a cookie with HttpOnly (no script reads it), SameSite=Strict (no other site sends it) and Path=/api/auth (it goes to the endpoints of the session only). In production add Secure: HTTPS only. 2. The server The project signs its tokens itself, with HMAC-SHA256: a JWT is three parts in base64url, a header, the claims (sub, the user; exp, the expiry) and the signature of both. function sign (payload) { var head = base64url(JSON.stringify({alg: 'HS256', typ: 'JWT'})) + '.' + base64url(JSON.stringify(payload)); return head + '.' + base64url(crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(head).digest()); } verify(token) computes the signature again, compares it with crypto.timingSafeEqual (a plain comparison tells an attacker by its time how many characters are right), and refuses an expired token. A real server takes a library for JWT and keeps the secret out of the code. Three more rules of the server, each one line in the project: - A password is kept as a slow hash with a salt (crypto.scryptSync), never as it is. - A wrong email and a wrong password get the same answer: nobody learns which emails have accounts. - Rotation: each refresh replaces the refresh token, and the old one stops working. A stolen refresh token works once at most, and the next use of the real one shows the theft. With no session, /api/auth/refresh answers 204: a guest is not an error. 3. The Session Service $OnCreate: function () { var token = ''; this.User = null; this.Token = function (value) { if (value !== undefined) token = value; return token; }; } The token is a variable of a closure, not a field of the state: it never renders, never reaches the developer tools of the state, and goes with the tab. Restore(callback) trades the cookie for an access token after a reload. A guard and the header both want the user at the start: the first call asks the server, the others wait for its answer, and later calls know the answer already. Request(method, url, data, callback) adds Authorization: Bearer; a 401 means the access token expired, so it restores once (force) and asks again: this.Call(method, url, data, function (error, status, value) { if (!error && status === 401) { self.Restore(function (signedIn) { if (!signedIn) { callback(new Error('Signed out.')); return; } self.Call(method, url, data, function (again, code, result) { callback(again || (code !== 200 ? new Error(result.Error || 'The server answered ' + code) : null), result); }); }, true); return; } callback(error || (status !== 200 ? new Error(value.Error || 'The server answered ' + status) : null), value); }); The pages never see a token: they call Request, and the Session does the rest. 4. The guard waits After a reload the page has no access token yet. The guard of /account waits for Restore instead of sending a signed-in user to the page to sign in: Elemenx.Guard('SignedIn', function () { var session = this.$Service('Session'); var to = this.$To.Path; if (session.SignedIn()) return true; return this.$Wait(function (done) { session.Restore(function (signedIn) { done(signedIn ? true : '/login?return=' + encodeURIComponent(to)); }); }); }); A guard keeps a page from showing; it protects no data. The data are protected by the server, which checks the token of every request. 5. Back where you were, and nowhere else The page to sign in sends the user back to the page that asked (?return=/account). Take only a path of this site: ?return=//evil.example in a link would otherwise make your own page send the user to a copy of it. self.$Router().Replace(/^\/(?!\/)/.test(self.$Query.return || '') ? self.$Query.return : '/account'); The form gives its fields Autocomplete="username" and "current-password": the password manager of the browser fills and keeps them. 6. Signing out SignOut asks the server to forget the refresh token and to clear the cookie, then forgets the access token. Clearing only the page would leave a refresh token that still works. 7. And OAuth? "Sign in with Google" is OAuth 2.0 with OpenID Connect. Its flow for a web application is the authorization code with PKCE: 1. The page makes a random codeverifier, keeps it, and sends the user to the provider with its hash (codechallenge) and a random state. 2. The user signs in there; the provider sends them back with a code and the state. 3. Your server (or the page) trades the code and the codeverifier for the tokens of the provider; the state must be the one sent, or the answer is refused. The safest place for the end of the flow is your server: it takes the tokens of the provider, finds or creates the user, and then gives the browser the same two tokens as in this tutorial. The page stays the same; only SignIn becomes a link to the provider. Use the library of your server for OAuth: the details (state, nonce, the checks of the ID token) are where the mistakes are. 8. Try it cd examples/Tutorials/Auth npm install npm run dev Open /account, sign in, reload: you stay signed in, and the developer tools show no token in the storages and a cookie the page cannot read. The end-to-end test of the project also answers the first /api/me with 401 and checks the page still shows the account.

Title: An application in several languages
Text:
A hotel to book in English, Russian and Arabic: every phrase from a dictionary, the plural forms of each language, dates and prices written in its manner, and a page that mirrors itself for a language written right to left. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Languages. What you learn: dictionaries and $T, plural forms, Intl for dates and money, switching the language and remembering it, right-to-left layout with logical CSS, and keys that keep their meaning in both directions. 1. The dictionaries One JSON file for each language, in locales/. Nested objects make keys with dots (trip.photos.room); {name} is a parameter: { "trip": { "title": "Seaside", "dates": "{from} – {to}", "nights": {"one": "{count} night", "other": "{count} nights"}, "total": "Total: {sum}" } } The Application names them, and the languages it has: Elemenx.Application('Languages', { $Component: 'TripCard', $Use: ['ElemenxUI'], $Locales: {URL: 'locales/{language}.json', Languages: ['en', 'ru', 'ar']} }); It starts in the language chosen before, else in the language of the system if it has it, else in the lang of the page; its root renders once the dictionary is in, so the first screen shows phrases, never keys. elemenx build takes the dictionaries into the build. 2. Phrases in the template

{{$T('trip.title')}}

{{$T('trip.nights', {count: Nights})}}

$T follows the language: when it changes, every phrase of the page changes with it. Write whole phrases with parameters, never pieces glued in code: the order of the words differs between languages (Total: {sum} is المجموع: {sum}, and another language puts the sum first). 3. Plural forms A phrase that is an object of forms is chosen by count, through Intl.PluralRules of the language. English has two forms; Russian three; Arabic six: "nights": {"one": "{count} ночь", "few": "{count} ночи", "many": "{count} ночей", "other": "{count} ночи"} "nights": {"zero": "لا ليالٍ", "one": "ليلة واحدة", "two": "ليلتان", "few": "{count} ليالٍ", "many": "{count} ليلة", "other": "{count} ليلة"} 1 ночь, 3 ночи, 5 ночей, 21 ночь: the rules know them; never write count === 1 ? ... : .... 4. Dates and money Dates, numbers and currencies are not phrases: Intl writes them in the manner of the language. Dates: function (nights, language) { var format = new Intl.DateTimeFormat(language, {day: 'numeric', month: 'long'}); var from = new Date(this.Arrival + 'T12:00:00'); var to = new Date(from.getTime() + nights 86400000); return Elemenx.Locale.Text('trip.dates', {from: format.format(from), to: format.format(to)}); }, Money: function (amount, language) { return new Intl.NumberFormat(language, {style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR'}).format(amount); } July 14, 14 июля, and €252.00, 252,00 €. The template passes Language to these methods (Dates(Nights, Language)): a text written in code is not a $T, so the component keeps the language in its state, set by Elemenx.Locale.OnChange, and the expression follows it. The Format Service of ElemenxUI (Money, Date, Relative) follows the language by itself. 5. Choosing the language Switched: function (value) { Elemenx.Locale.Language(value, function () {}); } Language(code, callback) loads the dictionaries of the language, switches, sets lang and dir of the page, and remembers the choice for the next visit. Name each language in itself (Русский, العربية): a person who does not read English must find their own. 6. Right to left For Arabic, Hebrew, Persian or Urdu the page gets dir="rtl", and the browser lays the text and the flow of the boxes from the right. Help it with logical CSS: inline and block instead of width and height, start and end instead of left and right: .trip { max-inline-size: 520px; margin-block: 40px; margin-inline: auto; padding-inline: 16px; } A rule with margin-left stays on the left in Arabic; margin-inline-start goes to the right by itself. The components of ElemenxUI are written so already. Pictures that mean a direction (an arrow, a "next") are mirrored by a rule; pictures that do not (a clock, a check mark, a logo) are not: [dir='rtl'] .trip-arrow svg { transform: scaleX(-1); } 7. Keys in both directions ArrowRight means "next" in English, and "back" in Arabic, where the reading goes to the left. Elemenx.Locale.Key(event) swaps the two arrows on an element laid out right to left, so the code is written once: Stepped: function (event) { var key = Elemenx.Locale.Key(event); if (key === 'ArrowRight') this.Next(); else if (key === 'ArrowLeft') this.Previous(); } 8. The phrases of ElemenxUI ElemenxUI speaks English and Russian. In another language its components fall back to English until you add its phrases: Elemenx.Locale.Add('ar', {ui: {select: {placeholder: 'اختر'}}}), or a file of your own with the keys of libraries/ElemenxUI/locales/en.json. 9. Try it cd examples/Tutorials/Languages npm install npm run dev Move the slider in each language and watch the forms of the nights; switch to Arabic, use the arrow keys on the photo, and reload: the page remembers the language.

Title: A browser extension
Text: A reading list in the button of the browser: press it on a page, save the page in one click, find it later on every browser you sign in to. The same project builds as a page and as an extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Extension. What you learn: elemenx build --extension and its surfaces, the manifest and the permissions it asks for, the APIs of the extension with a fallback for development, chrome.storage.sync, and what the policy of an extension forbids. 1. One project, two builds npm run dev # the page in a tab, as any project: fast to write and to test npm run extension # elemenx build --extension: dist/extension/chrome, dist/extension/firefox, and a zip of each The settings of the extension are in elemenx.config.js: Extension: { Surface: 'popup', Name: 'Reading list', Description: 'Keeps the pages to read later, on every browser you sign in to.', Manifest: { permissions: ['activeTab', 'storage'] } } - Surface: where the page shows. popup, the window of the button; tab, a tab of its own opened by the button; side, the side panel of Chrome and the sidebar of Firefox. - Manifest: keys added to the Manifest V3 the builder writes. Ask for the least: activeTab gives the page of the tab only when the user presses the button, where tabs and hostpermissions would warn of "reading all your data on all websites" at the install. - The version comes from package.json; Firefox needs an ID to publish. 2. The APIs of the extension, and a stand-in In an extension the page has chrome.storage and chrome.tabs; in elemenx dev it does not. The Service checks once, and stands in with the storage of the page and the page itself, so the whole application runs and is tested as a page: $OnCreate: function () { this.Items = []; this.Extension = typeof chrome !== 'undefined' && !!chrome.storage && !!chrome.storage.sync; this.Local = this.$Storage.Local.Namespace('reading'); }, Current: function (callback) { if (this.Extension && chrome.tabs) { chrome.tabs.query({active: true, currentWindow: true}, function (tabs) { callback(tabs[0] ? {Title: tabs[0].title || tabs[0].url, URL: tabs[0].url} : null); }); return; } callback({Title: document.title, URL: location.href}); } Only the Service knows about chrome: the component calls Save, Remove and Open, and does not change between the two builds. Firefox has the same chrome namespace, so one code runs in both. 3. A storage that follows the user chrome.storage.sync keeps small data (100 KB in all, 8 KB an item) in the account of the browser: the list shows on every computer the user signs in to. chrome.storage.local holds more, on this computer only. Listen to its changes: another window of the extension, or another computer, changes the list while this one is open: chrome.storage.onChanged.addListener(function (changes, area) { if (area === 'sync' && changes.items) self.Take(changes.items.newValue || []); }); 4. A popup is a small page that does not last - It is as wide as its page asks, up to 800 pixels: the page asks for 360 (.reading { width: 360px; }). - It closes when it loses the focus, and everything in it ends: keep nothing in memory you need later, write it to the storage at once. - A link would open in the popup: the Service opens a page in a new tab (chrome.tabs.create). 5. The policy of an extension The page of an extension may not run code made from a text: no inline <script>, no eval, no new Function. The builder precompiles the expressions of the templates into functions (Elemenx.Expressions), so the templates work; and it stops on an inline script of the page, which would not run there. The router of an extension keeps its route in memory: its page is always index.html. 6. Install it, and publish it In Chrome or Edge, open chrome://extensions (edge://extensions), turn on the mode for developers, and load dist/extension/chrome as an unpacked extension; in Firefox, about:debugging, This Firefox, a temporary add-on: dist/extension/firefox/manifest.json. The zips are what the stores take: the Chrome Web Store, Microsoft Edge Add-ons and addons.mozilla.org. 7. The tests The page is tested as any project (tests/examples/tutorials.spec.js saves, reloads and removes a page). A second test builds the extension, loads it into Edge with --load-extension, saves a page and reads chrome.storage.sync: what runs in the store is what was tested.

Title: A video call
Text: A call for a few people: a room joined by its name, everyone's video on a CallStage, the microphone and the camera on its controls. The browsers find each other through a WebSocket of the server, and then send their video directly to each other. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Call. What you learn: the parts of a WebRTC call (signaling, offer and answer, ICE candidates, tracks), Network.WebSocket and Network.WebRTC with one Protocol, a mesh of connections, a data channel beside the media, the camera and the microphone, and the components of a call. 1. How two browsers meet Ada server (/signal) Grace │ join {Room} ───────────────►│ │ │◄─────────── welcome {Peers: []} │ │ │◄──────────────── join {Room} ───────│ │◄─────────── peer {Grace} │ welcome {Peers: [Ada]} ──────────►│ │ │◄──────── signal {To: Ada, Offer} ───│ Grace offers │◄─ signal {From: Grace, Offer}│ │ │── signal {To: Grace, Answer}►│── signal {From: Ada, Answer} ──────►│ │◄════════ candidates both ways, then video, sound and data directly ═══════►│ The server only passes the messages of the signaling: it never sees the video. Each browser describes what it sends (an offer, an answer: codecs, tracks) and the addresses where it may be reached (ICE candidates); then the two talk directly. A STUN server tells a browser its public address; where a firewall closes every direct path, a TURN server relays the media, and a real service needs one. 2. The signaling Server.WebSocket of elemenx.config.js gives elemenx dev and elemenx serve a socket at /signal. It keeps the rooms: a join gets the list of the others (welcome), the others hear of the newcomer (peer), and a signal is passed to the one it names. Its whole code is in the project, forty lines. On the page, one Protocol encodes and decodes the JSON of the socket and of the data channels, so each Type is an event: Elemenx.Network.Protocol('Signal', { Encode: function (value) { return JSON.stringify(value); }, Decode: function (text) { var data; try { data = JSON.parse(text); } catch (error) { return {Type: 'Invalid', Data: text}; } return {Type: data.Type || 'Invalid', Data: data}; } }); this.Socket.On('Protocol.welcome', function (event) { event.Data.Peers.forEach(function (peer) { self.Peer(peer.ID, peer.Name, true); }); }); this.Socket.On('Protocol.peer', function (event) { self.Peer(event.Data.ID, event.Data.Name, false); }); Who offers is decided once: the one who came later offers to everyone there. Both offering at the same time is the classic bug of a first call. 3. One connection for each person var peer = this.$Network().WebRTC({Configuration: {iceServers: [{urls: 'stun:stun.l.google.com:19302'}]}, Protocol: 'Signal'}); peer.On('Transport.ICECandidate', function (event) { if (event.Data.Candidate) self.Send(id, {Candidate: event.Data.Candidate}); }); peer.Connect(offering); peer.Connection().addEventListener('track', function (event) { person.Stream = event.streams[0]; }); this.Local.getTracks().forEach(function (track) { peer.Connection().addTrack(track, self.Local); }); if (offering) { peer.CreateOffer(function (error, offer) { if (!error) self.Send(id, {Offer: offer}); }); } - Connect(offering) makes the RTCPeerConnection (and, for the one who offers, the data channel); Connection() is that native connection, where the tracks are added and heard. - The tracks are added before the offer, so it describes them. - The other side answers with AcceptOffer(offer, callback), the first one takes it with AcceptAnswer(answer, callback). Each person has a connection to each other one: a mesh. It is simple and needs no media server, and it holds about four to six people; beyond that each browser sends its video too many times, and a call goes through a media server (an SFU) that forwards one stream to everyone. 4. Candidates that come early A candidate can arrive before the offer it belongs to has been accepted, and adding it then fails. Keep them until the description is set: else if (data.Candidate) { if (person.Ready) person.Peer.AddICECandidate(data.Candidate); else person.Waiting.push(data.Candidate); } Ready(person), called once AcceptOffer or AcceptAnswer is done, adds those that waited. 5. The camera and the microphone navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({audio: true, video: {width: 640, height: 360}}).then(function (stream) { callback(stream); }, function () { callback(null); }); The browser asks the person first, and only on https:// or localhost. A refusal is not the end: the call goes on without them, to see and hear the others. To mute, turn the track off (track.enabled = false): the connection stays, and turning it on again needs no new negotiation. To leave, track.stop() every track: only then does the light of the camera go off. 6. A data channel beside the media The connection carries a data channel too. The state of the microphone and the camera goes there, from browser to browser, without the server: peer.On('Protocol.state', function (event) { person.Muted = !!event.Data.Muted; person.Camera = !!event.Data.Camera; }); The same channel can carry a chat, reactions or a raised hand. 7. The stage <CallStage if="State === 'joined'" Layout="grid"> <CallTile slot="participants" for="person of People" key="person.ID" [name]="person.Name" [stream]="person.Stream" [muted]="person.Muted" [camera]="person.Camera" /> <CallTile slot="self" [name]="Self.Name" [stream]="Self.Stream" [muted]="Self.Muted" [camera]="Self.Camera" Self="true" /> <CallControls slot="controls" [muted]="Self.Muted" [camera]="Self.Camera" [hide]="['share', 'hand', 'react', 'chat', 'people', 'layout']" (mute)="Muted" (camera)="Filmed" (leave)="Left" /> </CallStage> CallTile plays a MediaStream ([stream]), shows an avatar while the camera is off, and mirrors the own video as a mirror would. CallStage places the tiles in a grid and the own video in a corner; CallControls emits mute, camera and leave, and the component calls the Room Service. 8. Try it cd examples/Tutorials/Call npm install npm run dev Open the page in two windows, join the same room with two names: each window shows the other. On two computers of a network, open the address of the computer that serves it, over HTTPS: the camera is refused on a plain http:// address other than localhost. The tests of the project join two pages to a room and check that each one sees the other and hears its microphone go off; another one starts Chrome with its fake camera and checks that the video of each plays in the tile of the other.

Title: A library of your own
Text: Acme, a small library of components a company shares between its applications: a card for a number that matters, a price, a text to copy. With its own service, its phrases in two languages, its design tokens built on those of ElemenxUI, and a showcase that writes its reference from what the components declare. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Kit. What you learn: the layout of a library, declaring it and using it, components that use a service of their library, phrases and tokens of a library, $Meta and Elemenx.Meta, and what a build takes of a library. 1. The layout Kit/ ├── app.js Elemenx.Library('Acme', ...) and the Application ├── index.html ├── Kit/ the Application: its showcase └── libraries/Acme/ ├── index.js ['index.css', 'services', 'components'] ├── index.css the tokens of Acme ├── locales/en.json, ru.json ├── services/ index.js, Prices.js └── components/ index.js, StatCard/, PriceTag/, CopyField/ A library is laid out as an Application: index.js files list what is there, in order; a folder named in a list has an index.js of its own. Each component is a folder with its .js, .html and .css. 2. Declaring it Elemenx.Library('Acme', { $Root: 'libraries/Acme', $Locales: {URL: 'locales/{language}.json', Languages: ['en', 'ru']} }); Elemenx.Application('Kit', { $Component: 'Showcase', $Root: 'Kit', $Use: ['ElemenxUI', 'Acme'] }); $Use names the libraries of the Application. A tag it does not know (<StatCard>) is looked for in them; their services load before the root starts, and the CSS their index.js lists is attached once. To share it between projects, publish the folder as a package and give $Root its path. 3. Components that use their library PriceTag writes its prices through Prices, a service of the same library: Price: function (amount, currency) { return this.$Service('Prices').Format(amount, currency); } A component of a library is written as any other. Give its classes the name of the library (acme-price, acme-stat): the styles of a library meet those of every application that uses it, and a short name like .price would collide. 4. Phrases The texts of the components are keys of the library, never words in the templates: <button type="button" class="acme-copy-button" (click)="Copy">{{Copied ? $T('acme.copy.done') : $T('acme.copy.action')}}</button> locales/en.json and ru.json hold them under the name of the library (acme.copy.action), so they never meet the keys of an application. An application may change a phrase or add a language: Elemenx.Locale.Add('de', {acme: {copy: {action: 'Kopieren'}}}). 5. Tokens :root { --acme-brand: var(--elemenx-accent); --acme-surface: var(--elemenx-surface); --acme-line: var(--elemenx-border); --acme-good: var(--elemenx-success); --acme-bad: var(--elemenx-danger); --acme-radius: var(--elemenx-radius); } The components use only --acme-. Built on the tokens of ElemenxUI, they follow its light and dark schemes and its themes for nothing; a product changes its brand in one line (:root { --acme-brand: #7c3aed; }), and no color is written twice. 6. What a component declares $Meta: { Group: 'data', Icon: 'tag', Description: 'A price, with the old one struck through and the discount.', Props: { Amount: {Type: 'number', Description: 'The price.'}, Currency: {Options: ['EUR', 'USD', 'GBP', 'RUB'], Description: 'Its currency.'}, Old: {Type: 'number', Description: 'The price before, struck through.'}, Size: {Options: ['small', 'medium', 'large'], Description: 'Its size.'} }, Sample: {Amount: 79, Old: 99, Currency: 'EUR'} } $Meta tells tools what a component is: its group and icon in a palette, its public props (a type, or the options of a list), its events, a sample to show. It is never state. Elemenx.Meta(name) returns it normalized, with the default value of each prop read from the definition: this.Metas = this.Names.map(function (name) { return Elemenx.Meta(name); }); The showcase of the project makes its reference of it: a table of the props of each component, its events, written once, beside the code that they describe. The UI Builder of Elemenx reads the same $Meta to put the components of a library in its palette and its inspector. 7. The build A build takes of a library only the components the Application renders, by their tags in its templates and then in theirs; the rest is left out. The $Meta is left out too, unless the Application reads it (Elemenx.Meta in its code, or the Designer), as the showcase does: then it stays. 8. Try it cd examples/Tutorials/Kit npm install npm run dev Add a prop to StatCard and to its $Meta: the reference of the showcase shows it at the next reload.

Title: A directive of your own
Text:
Two directives a real application needs: inview, which tells when an element comes into the screen (to animate it, to count a view, to load more), and media, which builds an element only while a media query holds. The first adds behavior to an element; the second decides whether the element exists. What you learn: when a directive is the right tool, the hooks of a behavioral directive and its Data, cleaning up, sleeping and waking, a structural directive with Mount and Unmount, and testing a directive. 1. A directive, a component or a service? - A component has its own markup: a card, a picker. - A service has state and logic and no element: a session, a cart. - A directive adds behavior to an element that someone else wrote: any element, any component's root, without wrapping it. copy, hotkey, draggable of ElemenxUI are directives. If you would otherwise add the same addEventListener in $OnReady of ten components, it is a directive. 2. inview: the hooks / inview tells when its element comes into the screen: it gets the class in-view and emits inview with {Visible}. The value is {Threshold (0 to 1, the share that must show), Once (stop after the first time)}, or nothing. / Elemenx.Directive('inview', { $Meta: { Description: 'inview tells when its element comes into the screen: the class in-view and the event inview with {Visible}.' }, $OnCreate: function (context) { context.Data.Seen = function (entries) { var visible = entries[entries.length - 1].isIntersecting; var options = context.Value || {}; context.Element.classList.toggle('in-view', visible); context.Element.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('inview', {detail: {Visible: visible}})); if (visible && options.Once) context.Data.Observer.disconnect(); }; }, $OnUpdate: function (context) { var threshold = Number((context.Value || {}).Threshold) || 0; / A new value of the expression with the same threshold: nothing to do. / if (context.Data.Observer && context.Data.Threshold === threshold) return; if (context.Data.Observer) context.Data.Observer.disconnect(); context.Data.Threshold = threshold; context.Data.Observer = new IntersectionObserver(context.Data.Seen, {threshold: threshold}); context.Data.Observer.observe(context.Element); }, $OnSleep: function (context) { context.Data.Observer.disconnect(); }, $OnWake: function (context) { context.Data.Observer.observe(context.Element); }, $OnDestroy: function (context) { if (context.Data.Observer) context.Data.Observer.disconnect(); } }); - $OnCreate runs once, when the element is in the template, before its value; $OnUpdate runs with the first value and again each time what the expression reads changes; $OnDestroy when the element goes. - context.Data is the directive's own object for this element: two elements with inview never share an observer. - Clean up everything you started in $OnDestroy: an observer, a listener on window, a timer. A directive that forgets it leaks on every page of the router. - A component kept by the cache sleeps instead of going: $OnSleep and $OnWake stop and resume what costs while nobody sees it. - The event is a DOM event of the element, so the template listens to it as to a click:
...
.feature { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(16px); transition: opacity 0.4s, transform 0.4s; } .feature.in-view { opacity: 1; transform: none; } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .feature { opacity: 1; transform: none; transition: none; } } Respect prefers-reduced-motion: an animation that moves the page makes some people sick. 3. media: a structural directive / media="'(min-width: 800px)'" builds its element while the media query holds, and takes it away when it does not. / Elemenx.Directive('media', { Structural: true, $OnUpdate: function (context) { if (context.Data.Query) context.Data.Query.removeEventListener('change', context.Data.Changed); context.Data.Query = window.matchMedia(context.Value); context.Data.Changed = function () { if (context.Data.Query.matches) context.Mount(); else context.Unmount(); }; context.Data.Query.addEventListener('change', context.Data.Changed); context.Data.Changed(); }, $OnDestroy: function (context) { if (context.Data.Query) context.Data.Query.removeEventListener('change', context.Data.Changed); } });
...
A structural directive owns its element: Mount() builds it (once), Unmount() takes it away, with the components inside. CSS could only hide the sidebar; media does not build it at all on a phone, so its components, their requests and their timers never start there. An element has one structural directive at most (if, for, lazy, media); for two, nest two elements. 4. Where to declare them Register a directive before the templates that use it are compiled: list its file in the index.js of the Application or of its library, before the components. A name is written in lower case (inview, long-press); registered twice, it throws. In a library, add $Meta with its Description: the tools and the reference show it. 5. Testing A directive is tested in a browser, on an element of a small component: it('inview marks its element and tells it', async function () { var seen = []; var host = Elemenx.Component('Host', { $Template: '
', Seen: function (event) { seen.push(event.detail.Visible); } })(); document.body.appendChild(host.$Element()); await waitFor(function () { return seen.length; }); expect(host.$Element().querySelector('div').classList.contains('in-view')).toBe(true); expect(seen).toEqual([true]); host.$Destroy(); }); Test the cleaning too: after $Destroy, the observer or the listener must be gone (a spy on disconnect or removeEventListener). Example The two directives, registered here before the component of the example is made. Scroll so the box leaves the screen and comes back; make the window narrower than 800 pixels:
Shown {{Times}} times · {{State}}
Scroll down ↓
I am in view

This line exists only on a window at least 800 pixels wide.

Title: An accessible application
Text:
One person in five lives with a disability; everyone has a broken arm, a bright sun on a phone or a slow network some day. An accessible application works with a keyboard alone, with a screen reader, at a large zoom, in high contrast and without animation. Most of it is free if it is built in from the start, and costly to add later. What you learn: what ElemenxUI does for you, and what is still yours: the order of headings and landmarks, names of controls, the focus, messages that are read aloud, color and motion, and how to test it all. 1. What the components give The components of ElemenxUI are built for it, and the tests of the project check it: - A Field names its control by its Label (aria-labelledby) and marks it required (aria-required); its error is a role="alert" read when it shows. - Dialog and Drawer are elements: the focus goes in, stays in, and comes back to the button that opened them; Escape closes them. - Select, Menu, Tabs, RadioGroup, Tree and the others follow the patterns of the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: their roles, their states (aria-expanded, aria-selected), and their keys (arrows, Home, End, typing a letter). - ToastHost is a live region: a toast is read without taking the focus. - The focus is always visible (:focus-visible), the animations stop under prefers-reduced-motion, and the contrast theme raises every contrast (this.$Service('Theme').Use('contrast')). - In a right-to-left language the components mirror themselves, and their arrow keys keep their meaning (Elemenx.Locale.Key). None of it helps if the page around them is a pile of divs. 2. The page: landmarks and headings
