A screen reader lists the landmarks (header, nav, main, footer) and the headings, and jumps between them: that is how a page is read without seeing it. One h1 for each page, levels without gaps. The router changes the page without loading it: give each route a $Title (it becomes the title of the tab, which is read), and move the focus to the h1 of the new page, so the reader starts there and not at the link that was pressed: $OnReady: function () { var heading = this.$Element().querySelector('h1'); heading.setAttribute('tabindex', '-1'); heading.focus(); } 3. Every control has a name A button with only an icon says nothing to a screen reader:

Title: Testing an application
Text: A list of tasks, and its tests: the logic alone in unit tests, the whole application in a browser. The finished project is examples/Tutorials/Todo. What you learn: where the logic of an application goes so a test can reach it, unit tests with Vitest in a real browser, end-to-end tests with Playwright against the build, and what each kind is for. 1. The logic in a Service A component shows; a Service decides. Everything a test should check without a page (adding a task, refusing an empty one, the count of the tasks left) lives in the Todos Service: Elemenx.Service('Todos', { StorageKey: 'tasks', $OnCreate: function () { this.Store = this.$Storage.Local.Namespace('todo'); this.Items = this.Store.Get(this.StorageKey) || []; this.Listeners = []; }, Add: function (text) { var title = String(text || '').trim(); if (!title) throw new Error('A task needs a title'); this.Save(this.Items.concat([{ID: Date.now() + '-' + this.Items.length, Title: title, Done: false}])); }, Left: function () { return this.List('active').length; } }); The component TodoApp only reads the Service and calls it from its events (see the project). This split is the whole trick: the Service is tested in a few milliseconds, the component through the page. 2. The tools npm install --save-dev vitest @vitest/browser-playwright @playwright/test npx playwright install chromium Elemenx needs a DOM, its storage and its events, so the unit tests run in a real browser too, not in a fake DOM. vitest.config.mjs: import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config'; import { playwright } from '@vitest/browser-playwright'; export default defineConfig({ test: { include: ['tests//.test.js'], browser: { enabled: true, provider: playwright(), instances: [{browser: 'chromium'}], headless: true } } }); 3. A unit test The test loads elemenx.js and the file of the Service, and asks an Application for the Service: every test gets a fresh one, from an empty storage. import { beforeEach, describe, expect, it } from 'vitest'; import '@qybercom/elemenx/elemenx.js'; import '../Todo/services/Todos.js'; describe('Todos', function () { var todos; beforeEach(function () { localStorage.clear(); todos = Elemenx.Application('Tests' + Math.random(), {}).$Service('Todos'); }); it('refuses a task without a title', function () { expect(function () { todos.Add(' '); }).toThrow('A task needs a title'); }); it('ticks, filters and clears the tasks done', function () { todos.Add('One'); todos.Add('Two'); todos.Toggle(todos.List()[0].ID); todos.ClearDone(); expect(todos.List().map(function (item) { return item.Title; })).toEqual(['Two']); }); }); npx vitest run runs them. A Service of an Application is made once for it: a new Application name gives a new instance, so the tests do not share state. A component may be tested the same way: define it with an inline $Template, make it (Elemenx.Component('Name')(props)), put its element in the page and check its DOM. Its methods are on the instance (instance.Add()), its events reach a listener given as (event) of a host component. 4. An end-to-end test The real thing: the build, served as in production, used by a browser as a person would. playwright.config.mjs builds and serves the project before the tests: import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test'; export default defineConfig({ testDir: 'tests', testMatch: '/.spec.js', use: { baseURL: 'http://127.0.0.1:4318' }, webServer: { command: 'npx elemenx build && npx elemenx serve', url: 'http://127.0.0.1:4318', reuseExistingServer: true } }); import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test'; test('adds a task, ticks it, filters and clears it', async function ({ page }) { await page.goto('/'); await page.getByLabel('New task').fill('Buy milk'); await page.getByLabel('New task').press('Enter'); await expect(page.locator('.todo-left')).toHaveText('1 left'); await page.getByText('Buy milk').click(); await page.getByRole('button', {name: 'Clear done'}).click(); await expect(page.locator('.todo-empty')).toBeVisible(); }); Look for elements as a person does: by their label (getByLabel), their role and name (getByRole('button', {name: 'Add'})), their text. The components of ElemenxUI give their fields labels and their buttons names, so these work without test IDs. 5. What to test where - Unit tests for the rules: validation, computations, the state a Service keeps. They are fast and many. - End-to-end tests for the paths a person takes: sign in, buy, write. A few, but on the real build, as it ships. - A bug gets a test that fails before the fix, at the cheapest level that shows it. npm test in the project runs both (vitest run && playwright test).

Title: A fast application
Text:
Most slow pages are slow for a few reasons: too much code to load, too much built at once, work done again for nothing, and a list of ten thousand rows in the DOM. Each has a tool in Elemenx. Measure first: speed you have not measured is a guess. What you learn: measuring, a smaller build, building less and later (lazy, if, structural directives), lists with key and VirtualList, fewer updates ($Batch, computed values), keeping what costs (Elemenx.Cache, $OnSleep), and work off the main thread. 1. Measure - Lighthouse in the developer tools of Chrome, on the build (elemenx serve), in the mode of a phone: the first paint, the largest paint, the total blocking time, and the shifts of the layout. - Performance, the panel: record a slow action, then look at the long tasks (over 50 milliseconds) and at what ran in them. Elemenx names its work in the stacks (render, $OnUpdate, the name of your method). - In the field: PerformanceObserver for largest-contentful-paint and event reports what real people get, on their machines. Measure on a slow machine: the panel of Performance slows the processor four or six times. A page fast on a developer's laptop is not fast on the phone of a customer. 2. Load less elemenx build already takes only what the Application uses: the components it renders, the services it names, the parts of the framework it calls, the packs of its libraries. It says what it left out. Keep it able to see: - Name services and components in quotes ($Service('Toast')): a name built at run time ($Service(name)) cannot show its use, and the build must keep more. - Large data (a list of cities, a catalog) goes in a file loaded when it is needed, not in the code. - Images: the right size for the screen (srcset), a modern format (AVIF, WebP), loading="lazy" below the first screen, and a width and height so the layout does not jump when they come. - Compression and caching on the server: see Putting it online. 3. Build less, and later The first screen should build the first screen, not the whole page.
lazy builds its element when it comes within a screen of the view, or when the browser is idle, one at a time in the order of the page; a placeholder of the height given keeps its place, so nothing jumps. What is inside does not exist before: its components, their requests and their timers start then. What a person may never open (a tab, a dialog, the settings) is built by if when it opens, not hidden by CSS from the start. A structural directive of your own can decide too: media of A directive of your own builds a sidebar only on a wide screen. 4. Lists
  • ...
    • key names each item: when the list changes, an item keeps its element and its components and moves with them, and only the new ones are built. Without it, removing the first item rebuilds the others in their new places. Use a real ID, never $index. A list of thousands is a different problem: thousands of elements are slow to build, to lay out and to keep, whatever the framework. VirtualList draws only the rows in view: A hundred thousand rows cost as much as forty. Table pages its rows (PageSize) for the same reason. 5. Update less A change of state updates what reads it, at once. A few rules keep that cheap: - Several changes, one update: this.$Batch(function (state) {...}) or this.$Update({Loading: false, Items: items}) after an answer of the server, instead of five assignments that update the template five times. - Compute once: a helper called in a template (Visible(Items, Filter)) runs at every update of what it reads. If it is costly (sorting thousands, formatting dates), compute the result when its inputs change and keep it in a field. - Copy from services what you show, not more: a component that holds the whole catalog updates for every change of it. - Do not replace what did not change: assigning the same value does nothing, but a new list with the same items rebuilds a for without key. 6. Keep what costs A page left and opened again is built again, its data loaded again. Elemenx.Cache keeps it asleep instead: Elemenx.Cache({Instances: {Scope: 'router', MaxAge: 300000, Max: 10}}); The pages of the router sleep for five minutes, ten at most, and wake as they were: their DOM, their state, their scroll. A component that sleeps hears $OnSleep: stop its timers and its streams there, and take them up in $OnWake. A tab hidden in the background deserves the same (document.hidden, as the stream of A live dashboard does). 7. Off the main thread A computation of a second freezes the page for a second: the clicks wait, the animations stop. Move it to a worker (Elemenx.WebWorker): parsing a large file, searching thousands of records, compressing, image processing. Split what must stay on the page into pieces between frames (requestAnimationFrame, requestIdleCallback). 8. A list to keep - Measured on a slow phone, on the build, before and after. - The build left out what it could; data and images load when needed. - The first screen builds the first screen; the rest is lazy or if. - key on every for; VirtualList or pages for long lists. - $Batch for several changes; costly values computed once. - Pages that come back are cached; timers stop while asleep or hidden. - No long task over 50 milliseconds on an interaction.

Title: Putting it online
Text: The way from npm run dev to an address on the internet: the build, what any static host needs to know about it, the settings of nginx, of the common hosts and of a container, caching, HTTPS and the headers of security, and a check before every release. What you learn: what dist/ holds, the fallback of routes, caching files whose names do not change, compression, a Content Security Policy for Elemenx, and a deployment that runs on its own. 1. The build npm run build # elemenx build: dist/ npm run serve # elemenx serve: dist/ as production would serve it, at http://127.0.0.1:<ProductionPort> dist/ is a static site: index.html, elemenx.js, app.js (the Application, its templates and styles, and the parts of its libraries it uses), the files of the libraries it needs, and the public files of the project. No server code runs it: any host of static files will do. Always try the build with elemenx serve before it goes: a component found in development but not in the build (a name built at run time) shows there, not in elemenx dev. The Server.Request and Server.WebSocket of elemenx.config.js, which the tutorials use as their API, belong to the development server: in production that API is your own server. 2. Three rules for any host 1. Every path of the router serves index.html. With $Router: {Mode: 'history'}, a reload of /orders/42 asks the server for that path; the server must answer with index.html, and the router shows the page. A file that exists (/app.js, /images/logo.png) is served as it is. elemenx serve does it; a host must be told. 2. The files are revalidated, not cached blindly. The names of the files of a build do not change from one build to the next (app.js stays app.js), so a browser that keeps app.js for a year never sees the new version. Send Cache-Control: no-cache (or max-age=0, must-revalidate, as elemenx serve does) with an ETag: the browser asks each time, and the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body while nothing changed. That costs one short request per file; with HTTP/2 they go together. Images and fonts whose content never changes under the same name may be cached longer. 3. Compress the text. elemenx.js, app.js, the HTML, the CSS and the JSON shrink four or five times with gzip or Brotli. elemenx serve follows all three (Compression, CacheControl in Server of elemenx.config.js): read its headers in the developer tools, and make the host send the same. 3. nginx server { listen 443 ssl http2; servername app.example.com; root /var/www/app/dist; gzip on; gziptypes text/css application/javascript application/json image/svg+xml; location / { tryfiles $uri $uri/ /index.html; addheader Cache-Control "no-cache"; } location /images/ { addheader Cache-Control "public, max-age=604800"; } location /api/ { proxypass http://127.0.0.1:3000; } } tryfiles ... /index.html is rule 1; nginx sends ETag and answers 304 by itself. A proxy in front of a stream (server-sent events) must not buffer it: proxybuffering off; in its location. 4. The common hosts | Host | The fallback of routes | | --- | --- | | Netlify | a file redirects in dist/: / /index.html 200 | | Vercel | vercel.json: {"rewrites": [{"source": "/(.)", "destination": "/index.html"}]} | | Cloudflare Pages | none to write: a site without a 404.html serves index.html for unknown paths | | GitHub Pages | no rewrites: use $Router: {Mode: 'hash'} (/#/orders/42), or copy index.html to 404.html | | S3 + CloudFront | the error page for 403 and 404 is /index.html with the code 200 | Files that must be in dist/ (redirects, robots.txt, CNAME) go in the project as public files: the build copies them. 5. A container FROM node:22-alpine AS build WORKDIR /app COPY package.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . RUN npx elemenx build FROM nginx:1.27-alpine COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf The first stage builds, the second serves only dist/ with nginx: the image holds no Node and no sources. 6. HTTPS and the headers of security HTTPS is not optional: the camera, the microphone, the clipboard, service workers, push notifications and installation as an application work only on https:// (and on localhost). Let's Encrypt gives certificates for free; most hosts do it for you. The headers every page should get: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; connect-src 'self' wss://app.example.com; frame-ancestors 'none' A Content Security Policy is the strongest defense against an injected script. Elemenx compiles the expressions of its templates with new Function: a policy without 'unsafe-eval' needs a build with --precompile, which writes them as code. Components put styles on their elements, hence style-src 'unsafe-inline'. connect-src names your API and your sockets. 7. A deployment that runs on its own name: deploy on: push: branches: [main] jobs: deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: 22 - run: npm ci - run: npm test - run: npx elemenx build - run: npx wrangler pages deploy dist --project-name app env: CLOUDFLAREAPITOKEN: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLAREAPITOKEN }} The tests run first; a red test stops the deployment. The last step is the command of your host (netlify deploy --prod --dir dist, vercel deploy --prod, an rsync to your server); its key lives in the secrets of the repository, never in the code. 8. Before every release - npm test is green, and the end-to-end tests ran against the build (elemenx build && elemenx serve). - A reload on a deep route works on the host, not only on /. - The developer tools show 304 for unchanged files on a second visit, and gzip or br on the scripts. - A new release reaches a browser that had the previous one (a PWA: see its update). - The console of the page is empty.

Title: For those who know Vue, React or Angular
Text:
The ideas are the same: components with state, templates that follow it, services, a router. This page puts the words of Elemenx next to the ones you know, then shows one component written four ways. The same component A counter with a step, its total shown, a reset that the parent hears. Elemenx.Component('Counter', { $Template: '
{{Count}}
', Step: 1, Count: 0, Add: function () { this.Count += Number(this.Step); }, Reset: function () { this.Count = 0; this.$Emit('reset', null); } }); The fields of the definition are its state and its props at once: a parent sets them by attributes (Step="5") or bindings ([step]="Size"), and a change of a field renders what reads it. There is no setState, no ref(), no signal to call: this.Count += 1 is the change. Words | Vue | React | Angular | Elemenx | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | data(), props | useState, props | fields, @Input() | the fields of the definition | | {{ value }} | {value} | {{ value }} | {{Value}} | | :title="x" | title={x} | [title]="x" | [title]="X" | | @click="go" | onClick={go} | (click)="go()" | (click)="Go" | | v-model="name" | value and onChange | [(ngModel)]="name" | [(value)]="Name" on a native field; [value] and (change) on a component | | v-if / v-for | && / .map() | ngIf / ngFor | if / for (with key) | | ref="box" | useRef | #box, @ViewChild | #Box and this.$Ref('Box') | | $emit('reset') | a callback prop | @Output() | this.$Emit('reset', data) | | computed | useMemo | a getter, computed() | a function the template calls with what it reads: {{Total(Items)}} | | mounted | useEffect(..., []) | ngOnInit, ngAfterViewInit | $OnCreate (before the first rendering), $OnReady (rendered) | | unmounted | the cleanup of useEffect | ngOnDestroy | $OnDestroy | | provide / inject, Pinia | context, a store | services, DI | Elemenx.Service and this.$Service('Name'): one per Application | | Vue Router | React Router | the Router | $Router of the Application, outlet, guards | | | children | | and slot="name" | |

Title: Overview
Text:
Elemenx.Network gives one model to every way a page talks to a server or to another page: a request, a stream of a response, a long poll, server-sent events, a WebSocket, a WebRTC data channel, a large transfer split into chunks, and the measurement of the traffic of any of them. Each one is a resource with the same shape: it is configured, it is started, it reports what happens as events, and it is closed or destroyed. None of them returns a Promise. | Resource | What it is | Start | Stop | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | XHR | one request and its response | Execute() | Abort() | | Stream | a response read chunk by chunk while it comes (fetch) | Connect() | Close() | | LongPolling | a request held by the server until it has news, made again and again | Connect() | Close() | | SSE | server-sent events (EventSource) | Connect() | Close() | | WebSocket | a two-way socket, with backpressure | Connect() | Close() | | WebRTC | a peer-to-peer data channel, with backpressure | Connect(), CreateOffer() | Close() | | Transfer | a large value (files, an object with files) sent or received in chunks with progress | Send(), Execute() | Abort() | | TransferReceiver | the receiving side of a chunked Transfer | (listens) | Destroy() | | Metrics | bytes and speeds of a resource | Start(), Begin() | End(), Stop() | Two more parts shape them: a Protocol turns what a resource sends and receives into typed messages, and a Context gives several resources the same protocol, listeners and settings. Creating a resource A resource is made by a factory of Elemenx.Network, with its settings in an object, or by its setters one after another: var request = Elemenx.Network.XHR({Method: 'GET', URL: '/api/hello', ResponseType: 'json'}); var same = Elemenx.Network.XHR() .Method('GET') .URL('/api/hello') .Header('Accept', 'application/json'); Setters return the resource, so they chain; a setter called while the resource runs (an executing request, an open socket) is ignored. Owned resources Inside a component, a service or an Application, use this.$Network() instead of Elemenx.Network. The resources it makes belong to their owner: when the component is destroyed, its requests are aborted, its sockets are closed and its transfers are destroyed, so nothing keeps running for a page that is gone. A resource made after its owner was destroyed throws Elemenx Network owner is destroyed. Elemenx.Component('Weather', { $Template: '

{{Text}}

', Text: 'Loading...', $OnReady: function () { var self = this; this.$Network().XHR({URL: '/api/weather', ResponseType: 'json'}) .On('Transport.Success', function (event) { self.Text = event.Data.Response.Summary; }) .Execute(); } }); this.$Network('Name') gives a facade whose every resource takes the context Name (see Contexts). An Application declares a context with this.$Network('Name', definition). Events Every resource reports through On(name, callback) and Off(name, callback) (Off(name) removes all the listeners of that name). An event has a namespace and a type, and a listener chooses how much it hears: - On('Transport', callback): every event of the transport (BeforeRequest, Open, Data, Close...); - On('Transport.Success', callback): one type of them; - On('Protocol.JSON', callback): a message decoded by the Protocol of the resource; - On('Transfer.Progress', callback) and On('Metrics.Update', callback): the events of a Transfer and of Metrics. The callback gets (event, context). The event is {Namespace, Type, Data, Target}: Data holds what the event is about (the response, the received data, the close code...), Target the resource. A Protocol event also gets as its context the transport event that carried it. An exception thrown by a listener is reported as an uncaught error, as the DOM does for its listeners; the other listeners still run. Times Every resource keeps the times of its life: $StartedAt() (when it was made), $ConnectedAt() (when it opened, or the request started) and $ClosedAt() (when it closed or finished); a time that has not come is null. Which one to use - One request with an answer: XHR. Its upload and download progress are events. - A long response to show while it comes (a log, lines of JSON, a generated text): Stream. - News from the server, one way: SSE where the server can keep a response open, LongPolling where it cannot (an old proxy, a serverless function). - Messages both ways: WebSocket. - Between two browsers, without the server in the middle: WebRTC. - Files and large values, with progress, pause and retries: Transfer over any of them. The examples of this section run against the server of this reference: /api/hello, /api/echo, /api/events, /api/poll, /api/stream and the socket /api/socket.

Title: XHR
Text:
Network.XHR is one HTTP request and its response, on XMLHttpRequest: the upload and the download report their progress, and the steps of the request are events. A request may be executed again once it has finished. var request = this.$Network().XHR({ Method: 'POST', URL: '/api/orders', Headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'}, Data: JSON.stringify({Product: 7, Count: 2}), ResponseType: 'json', Timeout: 10000 }); request.On('Transport.Success', function (event) { console.log(event.Data.Status, event.Data.Response); }); request.On('Transport.Error', function (event) { console.log('The request failed', event.Data.Event); }); request.Execute(); Settings | Setting | Setter | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | Method | Method(value) | GET by default | | URL | URL(value) | the address | | Data | Data(value) | the body: a text, a FormData, a Blob, an ArrayBuffer... (sent as it is, or encoded by the Protocol) | | Headers | Header(name, value) | request headers; a value may be a list, and Header adds to what is there | | Protocol | Protocol(value) | a Protocol (its name or its definition) that encodes Data and decodes the response | | Timeout | | milliseconds before the request gives up (Timeout event) | | ResponseType | | '', 'text', 'json', 'blob', 'arraybuffer', 'document', as XMLHttpRequest has them | Data goes as it is: an object needs JSON.stringify (or a Protocol whose Encode does it), and a FormData sets its own content type. Methods - Execute() sends the request; while it runs, a second Execute() does nothing. - Abort() stops it (Abort event). - XHR() returns the native XMLHttpRequest of the current request. - On(name, callback), Off(name, callback), $StartedAt(), $ConnectedAt(), $ClosedAt(). Events In the order they come: | Event | Data | | --- | --- | | Transport.BeforeRequest | {Method, URL, Data, XHR}: the request is about to be sent (a context adds headers here) | | Transport.RequestProgress | the ProgressEvent of the upload | | Transport.AfterRequest | the upload is complete | | Transport.BeforeResponse | {Status, StatusText, Headers, URL, XHR}: the headers of the response are in | | Transport.ResponseProgress | the ProgressEvent of the download | | Transport.AfterResponse | {Status, StatusText, Headers, Response, ResponseText, URL, XHR} | | Protocol. | the response decoded by the Protocol | | Transport.Success | the same as AfterResponse: the request is over | | Transport.Error, Transport.Abort, Transport.Timeout | {Event, XHR}: it failed, was aborted, or took too long | Success means an answer came, whatever its status: a 404 is a success of the transport, so look at Status. Example

{{Steps}}

{{Result}}
Progress of an upload var upload = this.$Network().XHR({Method: 'POST', URL: '/api/upload', Data: file}); upload.On('Transport.RequestProgress', function (event) { if (event.Data.lengthComputable) self.Percent = Math.round(event.Data.loaded 100 / event.Data.total); }); upload.Execute(); For a file that must survive a broken connection, or for several files inside one object, use a Transfer over the request: it reports one progress, and over a socket it resends what was lost.

Title: Stream
Text:
Network.Stream reads a response while it comes, chunk by chunk, through fetch and a ReadableStream: a log that grows, lines of JSON that a server writes one after another, a text a model generates. The reading can be paused and resumed (the browser stops taking bytes from the network meanwhile), and closed at any moment. var stream = this.$Network().Stream({URL: '/api/logs?follow=1'}); var decoder = new TextDecoder(); stream.On('Transport.Data', function (event) { self.Log += decoder.decode(event.Data.Data, {stream: true}); }); stream.On('Transport.End', function () { self.Done = true; }); stream.Connect(); Settings Method, URL, Data (the body of a request that is not GET or HEAD), Headers and Protocol, as for XHR, with the same setters. Methods - Connect() starts the request and reads the response. - Pause() stops reading (Pause event); Resume() reads on (Resume event). - Close() cancels the reading and the request (BeforeClose, then Close). Events | Event | Data | | --- | --- | | Transport.BeforeConnect | {Method, URL, Data} | | Transport.Open | {Status, StatusText, Headers, URL, Response}: the headers are in | | Transport.Data | {Data, Bytes, Response}: a chunk, a Uint8Array | | Protocol. | the messages the Protocol found in the chunks | | Transport.End | the response is complete | | Transport.Pause, Transport.Resume | {URL} | | Transport.BeforeClose, Transport.Close | {URL} | | Transport.Error | {Error}, or {Reason: 'ReadableStreamUnavailable'} where the browser cannot read a body as a stream | Messages across chunks A chunk ends anywhere: in the middle of a line, of a character of UTF-8. A Protocol with Push(chunk) keeps what is left over between chunks and returns the messages that are complete (see Protocols). Here the server writes a line of JSON every 400 milliseconds, ten of them:

{{Status}} · {{Bytes}} bytes

  • #{{line.Index}}: {{line.Text}}
A Transfer without data over a Stream receives a large response with its progress (Loaded, Total, Speed) and lets the user pause the download.

Title: LongPolling
Text:
Network.LongPolling asks the server for news with a request the server holds until it has some; as soon as the answer comes, the next request goes. It brings messages from the server where a response cannot stay open (an old proxy, a serverless function, a host that cuts long responses). After an error or a timeout the next request waits Retry milliseconds. var feed = this.$Network().LongPolling({URL: '/api/notifications', Retry: 2000, Timeout: 30000}); feed.On('Transport.Data', function (event) { self.Notifications.push(JSON.parse(event.Data.Data)); }); feed.Connect(); Settings | Setting | Setter | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | Method, URL, Data, Headers, Protocol | as for XHR | every request of the poll sends them | | Retry | Retry(milliseconds) | the pause after an error or a timeout, 1000 by default | | Timeout | | milliseconds a request may wait (Timeout event, then a retry) | Methods - Connect() starts polling (BeforeConnect, Open, then the requests). - Close() stops it and aborts the request that waits (BeforeClose, Close). - XHR() is the request that waits now. Events | Event | Data | | --- | --- | | Transport.BeforeConnect, Transport.Open | {URL} | | Transport.BeforeRequest | {Method, URL, Data, XHR}: before every request | | Transport.BeforeResponse | {Status, StatusText, XHR} | | Transport.Data | {Data, Status, StatusText, XHR}: Data is the text of the answer | | Protocol. | the answer decoded by the Protocol | | Transport.AfterResponse | {Status, StatusText, Response, XHR} | | Transport.Error, Transport.Timeout | {Event, XHR}: the next request waits Retry | | Transport.BeforeClose, Transport.Close | {URL} | Example The server of this reference holds /api/poll for 600 milliseconds and answers with a number that grows. The Protocol decodes the JSON of every answer:

{{Polling ? 'Polling' : 'Stopped'}} · {{Answers.length}} answers

  • #{{answer.Sequence}} at {{answer.Time}}
The server answers every request: with news, or with nothing after a while (a 204, an empty list), so that proxies do not cut a request that waits too long.

Title: SSE
Text:
Network.SSE receives server-sent events through EventSource: a response the server keeps open and writes messages into, data: ... followed by a blank line. The browser reconnects by itself when the connection breaks, and sends the id of the last message it received (Last-Event-ID), so the server can go on from there. var events = this.$Network().SSE({URL: '/api/prices', Protocol: 'JSON'}); events.On('Protocol.JSON', function (event) { self.Price = event.Data.Price; }); events.Connect(); Settings | Setting | Setter | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | URL | URL(value) | the address of the stream | | WithCredentials | WithCredentials(value) | true sends the cookies of another origin (CORS) | | Protocol | Protocol(value) | decodes the data of every message | Methods - Connect() opens the EventSource. - Close() closes it: the browser stops reconnecting. - Source() is the native EventSource, or null while closed. Events | Event | Data | | --- | --- | | Transport.BeforeConnect | {URL, WithCredentials} | | Transport.Open | {Event, Source}: also after every reconnection | | Transport.Data | {Data, LastEventID, Origin, Event, Source}: one message | | Protocol. | the message decoded by the Protocol | | Transport.Error | {ReadyState, Event, Source}: ReadyState 0 means the browser reconnects, 2 that it gave up | | Transport.BeforeClose, Transport.Close | {Source} | The server ends its response, and the browser opens it again after retry milliseconds: an Error event with ReadyState 0, then Open. To stop for good, call Close(). Example The server of this reference sends five events, one every 400 milliseconds, then ends the response. The example closes the stream after the fifth one, so the browser does not ask again:

{{Steps}}

  • id {{message.ID}}: event {{message.Index}} at {{message.Time}}
SSE goes one way, from the server. For messages both ways use a WebSocket; where a response cannot stay open, LongPolling.

Title: WebSocket
Text:
Network.WebSocket is a socket that carries messages both ways while it is open. It adds to the browser's WebSocket a Protocol (messages encoded and decoded as typed events) and backpressure: when more is queued than the network takes, Send refuses instead of filling the memory, and a Drain event says when it may go on. var socket = this.$Network().WebSocket({URL: 'wss://example.com/chat', Protocol: 'ChatJSON'}); socket.On('Transport.Open', function () { socket.Send({Type: 'Join', Room: 'general'}); }); socket.On('Protocol.Message', function (event) { self.Messages.push(event.Data); }); socket.Connect(); Settings | Setting | Setter | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | URL | URL(value) | ws:// or wss:// | | Protocols | Protocols(value) | the subprotocols of the WebSocket handshake (a name or a list) | | BinaryType | BinaryType(value) | 'blob' (the default) or 'arraybuffer': how binary messages arrive | | Protocol | Protocol(value) | the Protocol of the messages | | BufferHighWaterMark | BufferHighWaterMark(bytes) | 4 MiB: above this many bytes waiting in the socket, Send refuses | | BufferLowWaterMark | BufferLowWaterMark(bytes) | 1 MiB: below this, after a refusal, Drain comes | | DrainInterval | DrainInterval(milliseconds) | 10: how often the socket checks whether it drained | The water marks and the interval may change while the socket is open; without an argument their setters return the value. Methods - Connect() opens the socket. - Send(message) encodes the message with the Protocol and sends it. It returns true, or false when the socket is not open or under pressure (nothing was sent: try again on Drain). - Writable() is true when the socket is open and not under pressure. - Close(code, reason) closes it. - Socket() is the native WebSocket, or null while closed. Events | Event | Data | | --- | --- | | Transport.BeforeConnect | {URL, Protocols, Socket} | | Transport.Open | {Event, Protocol, Extensions, Socket} | | Transport.BeforeSend, Transport.AfterSend | {Data, BufferedAmount, Socket}: around every message | | Transport.Data | {Data, Origin, Event, Socket}: a message as it came | | Protocol. | the message decoded by the Protocol | | Transport.Backpressure | {BufferedAmount, Bytes, HighWaterMark, Socket}: the socket is full | | Transport.Drain | {BufferedAmount, Socket}: it may take messages again | | Transport.Error | {Event, Socket} | | Transport.BeforeClose | {Code, Reason, Socket} | | Transport.Close | {Code, Reason, Clean, Event, Socket} | A WebSocket does not reconnect by itself: listen to Close and call Connect() again when the Application wants it to. Example The server of this reference answers every message with {Echo, Time}. The Protocol sends objects as JSON and decodes the answers:

{{Status}}

  • {{echo.Echo}} {{echo.Time}}
Sending a lot A loop that sends many messages stops when Send returns false and goes on with the next one on Drain: function pump () { while (index < chunks.length) { if (!socket.Send(chunks[index])) return; index++; } } socket.On('Transport.Drain', pump); pump(); A Transfer does this for you, with acknowledgments and retries, and reports one progress.

Title: WebRTC
Text:
Network.WebRTC is a data channel between two browsers: an RTCPeerConnection with one RTCDataChannel, with a Protocol and backpressure as a WebSocket has them. The negotiation (the offer, the answer, the ICE candidates) goes through methods with callbacks, never through Promises; how the two peers exchange them (a WebSocket, a server, a QR code) is up to the Application. The negotiation var caller = this.$Network().WebRTC({Configuration: {iceServers: [{urls: 'stun:stun.l.google.com:19302'}]}}); caller.On('Transport.ICECandidate', function (event) { signaling.Send({Type: 'Candidate', Candidate: event.Data.Candidate}); }); caller.CreateOffer(function (error, offer) { if (error) return; signaling.Send({Type: 'Offer', Offer: offer}); }); / The other browser: / callee.AcceptOffer(offer, function (error, answer) { signaling.Send({Type: 'Answer', Answer: answer}); }); / Back in the first one: / caller.AcceptAnswer(answer, function (error) { / The channel opens: Transport.Open. / }); / Both, for every candidate the other one found: / peer.AddICECandidate(candidate); Every negotiation method takes an optional callback (error, result) as its last argument, always called after the method returned: CreateOffer and AcceptOffer give the local description, AcceptAnswer the accepted remote one, AddICECandidate nothing. Without a callback, a failed step is a Transport.Error event whose data holds Error, Operation (the method) and Connection. Settings | Setting | Setter | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | Configuration | Configuration(value) | the RTCConfiguration: iceServers... | | ChannelName | ChannelName(value) | the label of the data channel, 'elemenx' | | Channel | Channel(value) | the RTCDataChannelInit: {ordered, maxRetransmits, protocol} | | Protocol | Protocol(value) | the Protocol of the messages | | BufferHighWaterMark, BufferLowWaterMark | setters | 1 MiB and 256 KiB: the bytes waiting in the channel | | QueueHighWaterMark, QueueLowWaterMark | setters | 4 MiB and 1 MiB: the bytes waiting in the queue of Elemenx before the channel | Methods - CreateOffer(callback), AcceptOffer(offer, callback), AcceptAnswer(answer, callback), AddICECandidate(candidate, callback): the negotiation. - Connect(initiator) makes the peer connection without negotiating (initiator false: do not create the channel, wait for the one of the other side). - Send(message) queues a message for the channel and returns true, or false when the channel is not open or the queue is full (Backpressure; go on at Drain). - Writable(), Close(). - Connection() is the RTCPeerConnection, DataChannel() the RTCDataChannel. Events | Event | Data | | --- | --- | | Transport.BeforeConnect | the peer connection is made | | Transport.LocalDescription, Transport.RemoteDescription | the descriptions set | | Transport.ICECandidate | {Candidate, Connection}: send it to the other peer | | Transport.ConnectionState, Transport.ICEConnectionState, Transport.SignalingState | the states of the connection as they change | | Transport.Channel | the data channel is there (set its binaryType here) | | Transport.Open | the channel is open | | Transport.Queued, Transport.BeforeSend, Transport.AfterSend | a message queued, and sent into the channel | | Transport.Data | {Data, ...}: a message received | | Protocol. | the message decoded | | Transport.Backpressure, Transport.BufferedAmountLow, Transport.Drain | the queue is full, the channel took its buffer, the queue may take messages again | | Transport.ChannelClose, Transport.BeforeClose, Transport.Close | | | Transport.Error | {Error, Operation, Connection} | Example Two peers in this page talk to each other: the offer and the answer go from one to the other in code, as a signaling server would carry them.

{{State}}

  • {{line}}
For files and large values over the channel use a Transfer: it splits them into chunks the channel takes, waits for the acknowledgments of the other side and resends what was lost.

Title: Transfer
Text:
Network.Transfer moves a large value over another resource and reports one progress for it: a file, a Blob, an ArrayBuffer, or any object that holds files, dates and numbers together. It works in three ways, chosen by what it is given: | Mode | When | How | | --- | --- | --- | | Whole | Data, over a resource without Send (an XHR) | the value goes in one request; the progress is the progress of the upload, then of the response | | Chunked | Data, over a resource with Send (a WebSocket, WebRTC) | the value is cut into chunks; a window of them is in flight at once, each one waits for its acknowledgment and is sent again when it does not come | | Inbound | no Data | it receives: the progress of a download over an XHR or a Stream (pause and resume with a Stream), or the chunks a chunked Transfer of the other side sends | var upload = this.$Network().Transfer({ Transport: this.$Network().XHR({Method: 'POST', URL: '/api/upload'}), Data: {Title: 'Holiday', Taken: new Date(), Photos: [fileA, fileB]} }); upload.On('Transfer.Progress', function (event) { self.Percent = Math.round(event.Data.Progress 100); }); upload.On('Transfer.Complete', function (event) { self.Done = true; }); upload.Send(); Values with files A plain object or a list goes as a structured envelope (application/x-elemenx-structured): an 8-byte header, a JSON manifest of the value with a placeholder for each binary part ({$ElemenxBinary: index}) and each date ({$ElemenxDate: iso}), then the bytes of the parts, one after another. The receiving side of Elemenx (TransferReceiver) gives the same object back, with File and Blob objects in their places. A server reads the header (the magic number 0x45585354 and the length of the manifest), the manifest, and the parts by their sizes. A Blob, a File, an ArrayBuffer or a typed array goes as it is. Settings | Setting | Setter | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | Transport | Transport(resource) | the resource it goes over | | Data | Data(value) | what to send; without it the Transfer receives | | ChunkSize | ChunkSize(bytes) | 64 KiB: the size of a chunk | | WindowSize | WindowSize(count) | 8: the chunks in flight at once | | Retry | Retry(milliseconds) | 1500: how long a chunk waits for its acknowledgment before it goes again | | MaxRetries | MaxRetries(count) | 8: how many times a chunk goes again before the Transfer fails | | Encoder | Encoder(function) | encodes each chunk (or the whole value) before it is sent: compression, encryption | An Encoder is function (value, context) returning the encoded value, or function (value, context, done) calling done(error, value) once; a Promise is refused with an error. Methods - Send(value) sends a value (or the Data already set); Execute() starts what was set: sending with Data, receiving without. - Pause(), Resume(), Paused(): a download over a Stream. - Abort() stops it (the other side of a chunked Transfer is told), Destroy() stops it and lets its transport go. - Phase(): Idle, Sending, WaitingComplete, WaitingResponse, Receiving, Complete, Error, Abort; Active(). - Receive(packet) gives it a packet by hand, when the packets do not come through a Protocol. Events | Event | Data | | --- | --- | | Transfer.Start | {ID, Name, Type, Size, Mode, ChunkSize, WindowSize, Transport} | | Transfer.Phase | {ID, Phase, Data, Elapsed} | | Transfer.Chunk | {ID, Index, Offset, Bytes}: a chunk went | | Transfer.Retry | {ID, Index, Retry}: a chunk went again | | Transfer.Progress | {ID, Loaded, Total, Progress, Speed, Elapsed, Mode} (Sent too for chunks): Loaded counts what the other side acknowledged | | Transfer.Data | {ID, Data, Bytes, Loaded, Total}: a part received (inbound) | | Transfer.Pause, Transfer.Resume | {ID, Loaded, Total} | | Transfer.Complete | {ID, Loaded, Total, Elapsed, Mode, Metrics: {SendElapsed, WaitElapsed, ResponseElapsed, TotalElapsed}}, and in the Whole mode Response: the data of the Success of the transport ({Status, Response, ...}) | | Transfer.Error, Transfer.Abort, Transfer.Timeout | {ID, Loaded, Total, Phase, Error} | The chunked protocol A chunked Transfer speaks in packets {Type: 'Transfer', Action, ID, ...}: 1. Start {Name, Mime, Size, ChunkSize, Chunks} opens it; 2. Chunk {Index, Offset, Bytes, Data} carries a part; the receiver answers Ack {Index}; 3. End {Chunks, Size} closes it; the receiver answers Complete; 4. Abort stops it from either side. The Protocol of the transport encodes the packets for the wire (a binary frame, or JSON with the data in base64) and decodes the incoming ones into the type Transfer: {Type: 'Transfer', Data: packet}. A TransferReceiver on the other side listens to Protocol.Transfer of its transport, answers the acknowledgments and emits Transfer.Start, Transfer.Chunk, Transfer.Complete ({ID, Name, Mime, Size, Blob}) and Transfer.Receive (the same, with Data, the object back, for a structured value). Example: a value with a file, over a request The server of this reference answers /api/echo with the size of what it received:

{{Status}}

Example: chunks over a data channel Two WebRTC peers of this page: one sends 2 MB in chunks of 32 KiB, the other receives them with a TransferReceiver and acknowledges each one. The Protocol carries the chunks as JSON with their bytes in base64:

Title: Metrics
Text: Network.Metrics counts the bytes a resource sends (TX) and receives (RX) and their speeds: the current one, and the average, the lowest and the highest of a measurement. It listens to the events of its transport: the upload and download progress of an XHR, the messages of a WebSocket, a WebRTC channel, an SSE or a Stream. var metrics = this.$Network().Metrics({Transport: socket, Interval: 100, Window: 1000}); metrics.On('Metrics.Update', function (event) { self.Upload = Math.round(event.Data.TX.Speed / 1024) + ' KiB/s'; self.Download = Math.round(event.Data.RX.Speed / 1024) + ' KiB/s'; }); Settings | Setting | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Transport | the resource it measures; Transport(resource) changes it while it is stopped, Transport() returns it | | Interval | 50: milliseconds between two Update events and between two samples of the speeds | | Window | 250: the milliseconds of traffic the current speed is computed over | | AutoStart | with a Transport, the metrics start at once unless this is false | Running and measuring Metrics run (Start(), Stop()): while they run they count every byte, and Elapsed is the time since Start. A measurement (Begin(), End()) is a part of that time whose average, lowest and highest speeds are kept: Begin zeroes them, and the time of a direction counts only while bytes go in that direction, so the pause between an upload and its response does not lower the average. End freezes the measurement until the next Begin. Reset() zeroes everything, Active() tells whether a measurement runs, Destroy() stops and lets the transport go. The snapshot Snapshot(), and the data of every event, is: { TX: {Bytes, Speed, SpeedAvg, SpeedMin, SpeedMax, MeasureElapsed, Active}, RX: {Bytes, Speed, SpeedAvg, SpeedMin, SpeedMax, MeasureElapsed, Active}, Total, / TX.Bytes + RX.Bytes / Elapsed, / milliseconds since Start / MeasureElapsed, / milliseconds since Begin / Active, / a measurement runs / Running / the metrics run / } Speeds are bytes per second. Events Metrics.Start, Metrics.Stop, Metrics.Begin, Metrics.End, Metrics.Reset, and Metrics.Update every Interval while they run and on every change of the counters; the data of each one is the snapshot. Example An upload of 16 MB to /api/echo through a Transfer, measured: <Button Label="Upload 16 MB" Variant="primary" [disabled]="Busy" (click)="Upload" /> <Properties Columns="2"> <Property Label="Sent" [value]="Sent" /> <Property Label="Current speed" [value]="Speed" /> <Property Label="Average" [value]="Average" /> <Property Label="Highest" [value]="Highest" /> </Properties> <script> ({ Busy: false, Sent: '0 MB', Speed: '—', Average: '—', Highest: '—', Megabytes: function (bytes) { return (bytes / 1048576).toFixed(1) + ' MB'; }, Upload: function () { var self = this; var request = this.$Network().XHR({Method: 'POST', URL: '/api/echo', ResponseType: 'json'}); var metrics = this.$Network().Metrics({Transport: request, Interval: 100, Window: 500}); var transfer = this.$Network().Transfer({Transport: request, Data: new Blob([new Uint8Array(16 1048576)])}); this.Busy = true; metrics.Begin(); metrics.On('Metrics.Update', function (event) { self.Sent = self.Megabytes(event.Data.TX.Bytes); self.Speed = self.Megabytes(event.Data.TX.Speed) + '/s'; self.Average = self.Megabytes(event.Data.TX.SpeedAvg) + '/s'; self.Highest = self.Megabytes(event.Data.TX.SpeedMax) + '/s'; }); transfer.On('Transfer.Complete', function () { metrics.End(); self.Busy = false; }); transfer.Send(); } }) </script>

Title: Protocols
Text: A Protocol stands between a resource and the wire: it encodes what the Application sends and decodes what comes into typed messages. Without one, a resource sends what it is given and reports only Transport.Data; with one, every message that comes is also a Protocol. event, so a component listens to Protocol.Price or Protocol.ChatMessage instead of parsing text everywhere. Elemenx.Network.Protocol('JSON', { Encode: function (value) { return JSON.stringify(value); }, Decode: function (text) { var data; try { data = JSON.parse(text); } catch (error) { return {Type: 'Invalid', Data: text}; } return {Type: data.Type || 'JSON', Data: data}; } }); var socket = this.$Network().WebSocket({URL: 'wss://example.com/live', Protocol: 'JSON'}); socket.On('Protocol.Quote', function (event) { self.Price = event.Data.Price; }); Elemenx.Network.Protocol(name, definition) registers a Protocol, Elemenx.Network.Protocol(name) returns it (or null). A resource takes a Protocol by its name or as a definition object, in its settings (Protocol: 'JSON') or by its setter (Protocol('JSON')) before it starts. A definition | Member | Called | Returns | | --- | --- | --- | | Encode(value, resource) | for every outgoing value: the Data of a request, a message of Send, a packet of a Transfer | what goes on the wire: a text, a Blob, an ArrayBuffer... | | Decode(input, resource) | for every incoming message: a response, an event of SSE, a message of a socket | {Type, Data}, emitted as Protocol. with Data; null emits nothing | | Push(chunk, resource) | for every chunk of a Stream, instead of Decode | a message {Type, Data}, a list of them, or nothing | this in these functions is the resource, so Push keeps there what is left over between chunks (this.Rest), one buffer for each resource that uses the Protocol. Lines of JSON Elemenx.Network.Protocol('NDJSON', { Push: function (chunk) { var lines; this.Decoder = this.Decoder || new TextDecoder(); lines = ((this.Rest || '') + this.Decoder.decode(chunk, {stream: true})).split('\n'); this.Rest = lines.pop(); return lines.filter(Boolean).map(function (line) { return {Type: 'Line', Data: JSON.parse(line)}; }); } }); Transfers A Transfer in chunks over a socket sends packets {Type: 'Transfer', Action, ID, Index, Data, ...} through Encode, where Data is binary, and waits for Protocol.Transfer events: the Decode of its transport turns the packets that come back (Ack, Complete) into {Type: 'Transfer', Data: packet}, with Data back as an ArrayBuffer. A binary Protocol frames each packet (a header of JSON, then the bytes); a text one puts the bytes in base64. Example A Protocol made for one request: it decodes the response of /api/hello into a type of its own.

Title: Contexts
Text: A context is what several resources share: a Protocol, listeners (headers of authorization, logging, error reports), and any setting a function gives them. It is declared once and named when a resource is made. Elemenx.Network.Context('API', { Protocol: 'JSON', On: { 'Transport.Error': function (event) { console.warn('Network error', event.Target); } }, BeforeRequest: function (event) { event.Data.XHR.setRequestHeader('Authorization', 'Bearer ' + Session.Token()); }, Configure: function (resource, type) { if (type === 'XHR') resource.Header('Accept', 'application/json'); } }); var orders = this.$Network('API').XHR({URL: '/api/orders'}); var live = this.$Network('API').WebSocket({URL: 'wss://example.com/live'}); A definition | Member | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Contexts | a name or a list of the contexts this one builds on: they apply first | | Configure(resource, type) | called with every resource and its type ('XHR', 'WebSocket'...) before anything else; returning false leaves the context out for that resource | | Protocol | the Protocol every resource takes | | On | {eventName: listener}: listeners added to every resource | | BeforeRequest(event) | a listener of Transport.BeforeRequest (requests: headers, signatures) | | BeforeConnect(event) | a listener of Transport.BeforeConnect (connections) | A context that names itself through its Contexts (directly or through others) is applied once: the cycle stops there. Using a context - Elemenx.Network.Context(name, definition) declares it; Elemenx.Network.Context(name) returns it. - An Application declares one for its components: this.$Network('API', definition) in its definition. - this.$Network('API') returns a facade whose every resource takes the context; Elemenx.Network.XHR(settings, 'API') does it for one resource, and resource.Context('API') adds a context to a resource made before. - A context may also be a definition object instead of a name, for a single use. Example A context that counts the requests of the page and adds a header to each one:

Title: Storage
Text: Elemenx.Storage gives the storages of the browser one shape: Local (localStorage: kept until it is cleared), Session (sessionStorage: kept while the tab lives), Cookie (document.cookie: sent to the server with every request) and IndexedDB (a database of objects, see IndexedDB). A namespace keeps the keys of one part of an Application apart from the others, and a context gives several parts the same namespaces and database. var local = Elemenx.Storage.Local; local.Set('settings', {Theme: 'dark', Size: 14}); local.Get('settings'); / {Theme: 'dark', Size: 14} / local.Has('settings'); / true / local.Remove('settings'); Where the page may not use the storages of the browser (a sandboxed frame without allow-same-origin, storage the user blocked, Node), Local, Session and Cookie keep their values in memory, for the page alone: an Application still loads and runs, and what it keeps goes with the page. Local and Session | Method | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Get(name) | the value, or null when there is none (or it is not a value Elemenx wrote) | | Set(name, value) | stores any value JSON can hold: numbers, texts, lists, objects; returns the storage | | Has(name) | whether there is a value | | Remove(name) | removes it | | Clear() | removes every key of the namespace (of the whole storage without one) | | Namespace(name) | the same storage under the prefix name.: Local.Namespace('cart').Set('items', [...]) writes cart.items | A value is stored as {"Value": ...}, so Get gives back the same type it was given: a number stays a number, false stays false. Cookie A cookie holds a text. Set(name, value, options), Remove(name, options) and Clear(options) take the options of a cookie: | Option | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Path | the paths that receive it, '/' for the whole site | | Domain | the domain and its subdomains | | MaxAge | seconds it lives | | Expires | the moment it ends: a Date or a text | | SameSite | 'Strict', 'Lax' or 'None' | | Secure | only over HTTPS | A cookie is removed with the Path and Domain it was set with. Get, Has and Namespace work as for Local. Contexts Elemenx.Storage.Context('Shop', { Namespace: 'shop', IndexedDB: { Name: 'Shop', Version: 2, Stores: {Orders: {KeyPath: 'ID'}, Products: {KeyPath: 'ID', Indexes: {Category: {}}}} } }); Elemenx.Storage.Context('ShopCart', {Contexts: 'Shop', Namespace: 'cart'}); var storage = Elemenx.Storage('ShopCart'); storage.Local.Set('items', [7, 12]); / the key shop.cart.items / storage.IndexedDB().Store('Orders'); / the database Shop / Elemenx.Storage(context) returns {Local, Session, Cookie, IndexedDB} for a context: the namespaces of the context and of the contexts it builds on (Contexts) are joined in order, and their IndexedDB definitions are merged, so IndexedDB() without arguments opens the database they describe (with arguments, IndexedDB(name, definition) opens another one). A context that names itself through its Contexts throws Elemenx circular Storage Context dependency; an unknown one throws Elemenx unknown Storage Context: . In a component or a service this.$Storage('ShopCart') is the same as Elemenx.Storage('ShopCart'). An Application declares a context with this.$Storage(name, definition). Example

Title: IndexedDB
Text:
Elemenx.Storage.IndexedDB(name, definition) is a database of objects in the browser: stores of records by key, indexes to find them by a field, and transactions that change several records at once or not at all. The schema is declared, Elemenx creates it when the database is first opened or its version grows, and every operation reports by events: no Promise, no onsuccess by hand. var db = Elemenx.Storage.IndexedDB('Notes', { Version: 1, Stores: { Notes: {KeyPath: 'ID', AutoIncrement: true, Indexes: {Tag: {KeyPath: 'Tags', MultiEntry: true}}} } }); db.Store('Notes').Put(undefined, {Text: 'Buy milk', Tags: ['home']}) .On('Success', function (event) { console.log('Saved with the key', event.Data); }) .On('Error', function (event) { console.log('Not saved', event.Data); }) .Execute(); The definition | Key | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Version | 1 by default; a higher number upgrades the database: the stores and indexes not there yet are created | | Stores | {Name: {KeyPath, AutoIncrement, Indexes}}: KeyPath is the field of a record that is its key (without it, a key is given with each record), AutoIncrement numbers the records | | Indexes | {Name: {KeyPath, Unique, MultiEntry}}: KeyPath is the field (the name of the index by default), Unique refuses two records with the same value, MultiEntry indexes each item of a list | | Upgrade(context) | called during an upgrade, after the stores are created: {Database, Transaction, OldVersion, NewVersion}, to move or convert the data of an older version | Operations Every operation is an object to listen to and then run: .On('Success', callback), .On('Error', callback), .Execute(). The callback gets {Type, Data}: the result, or the error. Nothing happens before Execute(). | Store | Result | | --- | --- | | Get(key) | the record, or undefined | | GetAll() | every record | | Count() | how many | | Put(key, value) | the key of the record written (give undefined as the key for a store with a KeyPath) | | Remove(key), Clear() | | | Index(name).Get(value), .GetAll(value), .Count(value) | the records of an index; GetAll() without a value gives all of them in the order of the index | The database opens with its first operation and stays open: Close() closes it, Delete() closes and deletes it (an operation too). When another tab upgrades the database, this connection is closed and the next operation opens the new version. Transactions db.Transaction(['Accounts'], 'readwrite', function (transaction) { var accounts = transaction.Store('Accounts'); accounts.Put('alice', {Balance: 90}); accounts.Put('bob', {Balance: 110}); }).On('Success', function () { / Both are written. / }).On('Error', function (event) { / Neither is. / }).Execute(); Transaction(stores, mode, callback) (mode 'readonly' by default, or 'readwrite') calls back with the transaction: Store(name) gives the requests of that store (Get, Put, Remove, Clear, Index(name).Get/GetAll), each with its own On('Success'), and Abort() cancels everything. The operation succeeds when the transaction completes; an error of any request, an exception of the callback or Abort() makes it fail, and nothing of it is kept. Example

Title: Events and pipes
Text: Elemenx.Events is a bus of the page for parts that do not know each other: a component says that something happened on a channel, and every component, service or Application that listens to that channel hears it. The delivery is synchronous, in the same JavaScript runtime, with the object itself (no copy). Across tabs, frames and workers use Messaging. / Anywhere: a socket, and a message on a channel. / var events = Elemenx.Events(); events.On('cart:changed', function (event) { console.log(event.Channel, event.Data, event.Source); }); events.Emit('cart:changed', {Count: 3}); Sockets Elemenx.Events() makes a socket; inside a component, a service or an Application this.$Events() makes one that belongs to it and is destroyed with it. | Method | Meaning | | --- | --- | | On(channel, callback) | listens to a channel; the same callback is added once | | Off(channel, callback) | stops listening; Off(channel) removes every callback of the channel | | Emit(channel, data) | delivers data to every socket that listens to the channel, this one included; returns the socket | | Channels() | the channels this socket listens to | | Destroy() | removes the socket; a destroyed socket throws Elemenx Events Socket is destroyed | | ID | the identifier of the socket | An event is {Channel, Data, Source, Is}: Source is the socket that emitted it. Declared channels A definition may name its channels and get all of them through one method: Elemenx.Component('CartBadge', { $Template: '{{Count}}', $Events: ['cart:changed', 'cart:cleared'], Count: 0, $OnEvent: function (event) { var self = this; event.Is('cart:changed', function (changed) { self.Count = changed.Data.Count; }); event.Is('cart:cleared', function () { self.Count = 0; }); } }); event.Is(channel) returns whether the event is of that channel; event.Is(channel, handler) also calls the handler when it is. Pipes event.Is(channel, pipes, handler) passes the events of a channel through a pipeline before the handler: a list of pipes, each written {Name: setting}. The pipeline lives as long as the socket that owns the listener, so a pipe remembers what it saw between events. Its place is the order of the Is calls of the listener: keep that order the same at every event. | Pipe | Setting | What passes | | --- | --- | --- | | Debouncer | a count | a value once it came that many times in a row, and not again until another value has come as many times (a flicker of a sensor does not pass) | | Filter | a count | after every that many events, the value seen most often among them (a vote against noise) | | Gate | milliseconds | an event with a true value after that long, unless an event with a false value came meanwhile (a hover that stays, a key held) | event.Is('presence:typing', [{Gate: 500}], function () { self.Typing = true; }); event.Is('sensor:door', [{Debouncer: 3}, {Filter: 5}], function (stable) { self.Door = stable.Data; }); Elemenx.Pipe(name, factory) adds a pipe: factory(setting) returns {Use: function (event, pass) {...}, Destroy: function () {...}}; Use calls pass(event) (or pass with another event) for what goes on, and Destroy frees its timers. Elemenx.Pipe(name) returns a factory. A pipe that is not registered throws Elemenx Pipe is not registered: . Elemenx.Pipe('Throttle', function (milliseconds) { var last = 0; return { Use: function (event, pass) { if (Date.now() - last < milliseconds) return; last = Date.now(); pass(event); } }; }); Messaging uses the same pipes: message.Is(channel, pipes, handler). Title: Messaging
Text:
Elemenx.Messaging carries messages on named channels between every place Elemenx runs: the components of a page, its frames and the windows it opens, the other tabs of the site, and its web workers and service workers. A socket does not need to know where its peers are: the runtimes find each other and pass the messages along. For messages that stay in one runtime, Events are simpler and synchronous. var socket = this.$Messaging(); socket.On('chat:message', function (message) { console.log(message.Data.Text, 'from', message.Source); }); socket.Send('chat:message', {Text: 'Hello'}); Sockets Elemenx.Messaging(context) makes a socket; this.$Messaging(context) makes one that belongs to its component, service or Application and is destroyed with it. | Method | Meaning | | --- | --- | | On(channel, callback) | listens to a channel | | On(callback) | listens to the socket's own channel: the answers sent to it | | Off(channel, callback), Off(callback) | stops listening | | Send(channel, data, options) | sends to every socket that listens to the channel, here and in every connected runtime; {Transferable: true} transfers data (an ArrayBuffer, a MessagePort) instead of copying it, when it goes to one runtime | | ID(value) | names the socket's own channel; ID() returns the name | | Channels() | its own channel and the channels it listens to | | Destroy() | removes it | A message is {Channel, Source, Data, Is}. Source is the own channel of the sending socket: socket.Send(message.Source, answer) answers the sender only. message.Is(channel, pipes, handler) works as for Events, with the same pipes. The data of a message is copied by the structured clone of the browser when it leaves the runtime: plain objects, lists, dates, Blob, ArrayBuffer, Map... but no functions and no DOM nodes. Declared channels Elemenx.Component('OrderStatus', { $Template: '

{{Status}}

', $Messaging: ['orders:status', 'orders:cancelled'], Status: '', $OnMessage: function (message) { if (message.Is('orders:status')) this.Status = message.Data.Status; else if (message.Is('orders:cancelled')) this.Status = 'Cancelled'; } }); $Messaging is a text (the ID of the socket: the messages sent to that channel), a list of channels, or {ID, Channels, Context}; $OnMessage(message) receives every message of them. Every socket of a component also listens to two channels of its own: elemenx: (every instance of that component) and elemenx:: (one of them). Contexts Elemenx.Messaging.Context(name, {ID, Channels, Contexts}) names a set of channels and an ID that sockets take: Elemenx.Messaging('Name'), $Messaging: {Context: 'Name'}. An Application declares one with this.$Messaging(name, definition). Where messages go - Frames and windows. A page of Elemenx inside an iframe announces itself to its parent, and a window opened by another one to its opener; the other side answers and the two are connected, with nothing to call. Repeated announcements are counted once. - Other origins. A frame or a window of another origin is refused unless both sides trust each other: Elemenx.Messaging.Origins('https://other.example.com') (a text or a list) on each one. The first announcement carries no data; the messages after it go to the verified origin only. - Other tabs. The tabs of the same origin share a BroadcastChannel: a message reaches the sockets of every one of them. - Workers. A web worker or a service worker made with Elemenx is connected to its page (see Web workers). - By hand. Elemenx.Messaging.Window(target, {Origin, Transferable}) connects a window that is neither a frame nor an opener: target is a selector of an iframe, an iframe or a Window; Origin is the origin it must have (the origin of the page by default; '' for any). It returns {Target(), Origin(), Active(), Destroy()}. this.$Messaging.Window(...) does the same for an owner, a selector being read inside its element. A message reaches every runtime once, however many paths lead there. Example Two sockets of this page; the second one answers on the first one's own channel. Open this page in a second tab and press Ping the tabs: the other tab answers through the BroadcastChannel.

Title: Web workers
Text: Elemenx.WebWorker runs a script in a worker, off the thread of the page, with Elemenx loaded there and Messaging connected: the page and the worker talk on a channel, as any two sockets do. Long computations, parsing of large files and compression stop freezing the page. var worker = this.$WebWorker('Resizer', {Script: '/workers/resizer.js', StartMode: 'lazy', Channel: 'images:resize'}); this.$Messaging().Send('images:resize', {Image: blob, Width: 320}); The script of the worker: / /workers/resizer.js: Elemenx is already loaded; ElemenxWorkerName and ElemenxWorkerChannel are set. / var socket = Elemenx.Messaging(); socket.On(ElemenxWorkerChannel, function (message) { var result = resize(message.Data.Image, message.Data.Width); socket.Send(message.Source, {Image: result}); }); The definition | Key | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Script | the URL of the script (required) | | StartMode | 'auto' (the default: it starts when the handle is made), 'manual' (it starts on Start()), or 'lazy' (it starts when a message is first sent on its channel) | | Channel | the channel of the worker, its name by default (in the worker: ElemenxWorkerChannel) | | Framework | the URL of elemenx.js for the worker; by default the script the page loaded (a framework inline in a single-file build gives the worker a copy of its text) | Elemenx.WebWorker(name, definition) registers a worker and returns a handle; Elemenx.WebWorker(name) makes another handle of a registered one. this.$WebWorker(name, definition) makes a handle that belongs to its component or service and stops with it; an Application's $WebWorker(name, definition) makes one its components share: this.$WebWorker(name) in a component returns the Application's handle when there is one. The handle | Method | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Start() | starts the worker (from a page only) | | Stop() | terminates it; a lazy worker stopped by hand does not start again by itself | | Destroy() | terminates it for good | | State() | 'Stopped', 'Starting', 'Running' or 'Error' | | Name(), Channel(), StartMode(), Native() | the native Worker | | On(event, callback), Off(event, callback) | Starting, Running (the worker loaded its script), Stop, Error; the callback gets {Type, Worker, State, Data} | A message sent before the worker runs waits: the bridge keeps it until the worker is there. A worker cannot start from a page opened as a file, and a widget build starts no worker. Title: Service workers
Text: Elemenx.ServiceWorker registers a service worker with Elemenx loaded in it and connects it to Messaging, and reports the states of its registration as events. A service worker lives beyond the page: it caches files for the page to work offline, receives push messages, answers requests of the pages of its scope. var worker = this.$ServiceWorker('Offline', {Script: '/offline-worker.js', Scope: '/', Channel: 'offline'}); worker.On('Active', function () { this.$Messaging().Send('offline', {Command: 'cache', URLs: ['/', '/app.js']}); }.bind(this)); The browser registers the framework itself (elemenx.js?elemenxserviceworker=1&...) as the worker; it loads the script of the Application and sets ElemenxWorkerName and ElemenxWorkerChannel, as in a web worker: / /offline-worker.js / var socket = Elemenx.Messaging(); socket.On(ElemenxWorkerChannel, function (message) { if (message.Data.Command === 'cache') caches.open('v1').then(function (cache) { return cache.addAll(message.Data.URLs); }); }); self.addEventListener('fetch', function (event) { event.respondWith(caches.match(event.request).then(function (cached) { return cached || fetch(event.request); })); }); The definition | Key | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Script | the script of the worker (required) | | Scope | the pages it controls, './' by default | | Channel | its channel, its name by default | | Framework | the URL of elemenx.js, the script the page loaded by default | Elemenx.ServiceWorker(name, definition) registers it at once and returns a handle; this.$ServiceWorker(name, definition) makes one that belongs to its owner. A service worker needs HTTPS or localhost. The handle | Method | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Register() | registers again after Unregister or an error | | Update() | asks the browser to check the script for a new version | | Unregister() | unregisters it | | State() | 'Unregistered', 'Registering', 'Installing', 'Waiting', 'Active', 'Unregistering' or 'Error' | | Registered(callback) | calls back true or false: whether the browser has a registration for its scope | | Controlled() | whether a service worker controls this page | | Reachable() | whether the active worker is connected to Messaging | | Registration() | the ServiceWorkerRegistration | | Name(), Channel(), Scope(), Destroy() | | | On(state, callback), Off(state, callback) | an event for each state as it comes: Registering, Installing, Waiting, Active, Unregistering, Unregistered, Error; the callback gets {Type, Worker, State, Data} | Example The service worker of this reference answers on its channel. Title: Accordion
Text: Sections that fold, one under the other: the Sections inside it (Collapsible). Exclusive (true by default) keeps one open at a time: opening a section folds the others, each with its own toggle event. Bordered draws them as one block with lines between them. Properties | Property | Default | | --- | --- | | Exclusive | true | | Bordered | true | | Label | '' | Slots default Example <Accordion> <Section Title="Shipping" Collapsible="true">Delivery in 2 to 4 days, free from 50 €.</Section> <Section Title="Returns" Collapsible="true" Collapsed="true">30 days to send it back, in its box.</Section> <Section Title="Warranty" Collapsible="true" Collapsed="true">Two years, on the parts and the work.</Section> </Accordion> Tests - Accordion keeps one section open: opening one folds the others, each with its toggle — tests/regression/library-new.test.js

Title: AchievementHost
Text: Shows the achievements of the Achievements Service, one at a time, over the whole page, as a game console does: a round badge pops up, opens into a band with the title (a light runs over it), and folds back into the badge before it goes. Place one in the layout of the Application. Placement: bottom (the default) or top, at the middle of the viewport. A press on the band dismisses it. Properties | Property | Default | | --- | --- | | Placement | 'bottom' | Example <Button Label="Unlock an achievement" Icon="trophy" Variant="primary" (click)="Unlock" /> <AchievementHost /> <script> ({ Count: 0, Unlock: function () { var rarities = ['common', 'rare', 'epic', 'legendary']; this.Count++; this.$Service('Achievements').Show({ Title: 'Reader ' + this.Count, Text: 'You opened ' + this.Count + ' pages of the reference.', Rarity: rarities[(this.Count - 1) % rarities.length], Points: this.Count 10, Duration: 4000 }); } }) </script>

Title: Avatar
Text:
The picture of a person, a team or a product. Image shows a picture; without one, or when it does not load, the avatar is made of the Name (or of Seed): Generate initials (the first letters of the first two words, or Initials of its own: a logo of letters), pattern (a symmetric figure of five by five cells, as code hosts give their users) or shapes (an abstract composition of circles, squares and triangles) or suprematism (a picture of the Suprematist Service), always the same for the same name, in a color of the name; Color sets the color of its own. Shape circle, rounded or square; Size small, medium, large, xlarge or a number of pixels. Status puts the dot of a Presence (online, away, busy, dnd, offline, connecting) on its corner. Properties | Property | Default | | --- | --- | | Name | '' | | Image | '' | | Initials | '' | | Generate | 'initials' | | Seed | '' | | Color | '' | | Shape | 'circle' | | Size | 'medium' | | Status | '' | Example

The initials take a color of the name; an image that does not load falls back to them.

Tests - puts what one route alone uses into its part, and keeps the first screen, the shared and what the rest uses — tests/regression/split.test.js - draws it in the page as a component, again when its seed changes, and as an avatar — tests/regression/suprematism.test.js

Title: Barcode
Text:
A barcode of a text (the Barcodes Service): Format code128 (the default), ean13, ean8, upca, code39, itf14, datamatrix, pdf417, or one of its own (Barcodes.Register). Module is the width of a module in pixels (2: a code as wide as its modules twice), Height the height of the bars in pixels (80), ShowText writes the human text under them (FontSize in pixels), Dark and Light its colors (Light transparent for none). Its style: Round (0 to 1: the ends of the bars round), Shape of the modules of a matrix (square, dots, rounded or diamond). Check adds the check digit of Code 39, Bearer false leaves out the frame of ITF-14, Columns and Level shape a PDF417. SVG() returns it as the text of an SVG, Png(scale, callback) as a data URL of a PNG (scale times its size: 2), Download(name, format) saves it as name.png or name.svg; ready gives the component itself, to call them. A text the format cannot write shows nothing and emits error (the reason, as its message). Properties | Property | Default | | --- | --- | | Format | 'code128' | | Module | 2 | | Height | 80 | | ShowText | true | | FontSize | 14 | | Dark | '#000000' | | Light | '#ffffff' | | Round | 0 | | Shape | 'square' | | Check | false | | Bearer | true | | Columns | null | | Level | null | | Label | '' | Events - error: The format cannot write the text: the error. - ready: It is made: the component itself, to call Download, Png or SVG. Methods - SVG() - Png(scale, callback) - Download(name, format, callback) Example

{{Problem || 'Every format takes its own text: digits for EAN, UPC and ITF-14, any text for DataMatrix and PDF417.'}}

Title: Block
Text:
A block: content in a frame, with a title on a band set into the top of the frame. Note is a caption after the title, the actions slot holds controls at the end of the band, the default slot the content. Padding: medium, compact or spacious (the paddings of elemenx-block). HeaderShape 'trapezoid' makes the block a folder: the title (and the note) on a tab as wide as their text, its end sloping down to the body, the actions beyond the slope. Its look comes from the --elemenx-block- tokens of the theme. Properties | Property | Default | | --- | --- | | Title | '' | | Note | '' | | Level | 3 | | Padding | 'medium' | | HeaderShape | 'default' | Slots actions, default Example

A frame whose title is a folder tab.
